item.title: San Diego County investigating highly contagious parasite cases linked to Gaylord Pacific Resort pools
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 5.37
CHULA VISTA (KGTV)- San Diego County public health officials are investigating four cases of a highly contagious parasite linked to the swimming pools at the Gaylord Pacific Resort and Convention Center. The San Diego Public Health Department is investigating four cases of cryptosporidiosis — also known as "crypto" — connected to the resort's pools. Officials are alerting anyone who swam there between July 24 and Aug. 15 that they may have been exposed. Health officials say the Cryptosporidium parasite can survive in water even when a pool is properly maintained. The county has not said the pools were improperly maintained. Brynn Taylor, a family medicine physician with Kaiser Permanente, said the parasite's resilience is what makes it particularly difficult to contain in public pools. "Even in a very well-maintained public swimming pool, these organisms are resistant to chlorine, so it doesn't kill them. So that means that that is a potential source of spread," Taylor said. Doctors say cryptosporidiosis is a very common parasitic infection, with about 800,000 cases reported in the U.S. every year. The most common symptom is watery diarrhea, which typically appears within days of exposure. "The typical symptoms are going to be an acute onset of watery diarrhea. That's usually within about 2 to 10 days from the time of exposure," Taylor said. Taylor also warned that people can continue spreading the infection even after their symptoms resolve. "The tricky thing about this is that even if a person no longer has symptoms, they can still be shedding the oocytes of the parasitic infection, and that's where we see the contamination or that's where we see the spread," Taylor said. Most healthy people recover on their own, but the illness can be more serious for people with weakened immune systems. Some people may have no symptoms at all. Taylor said standard disinfectants may not be enough to stop the spread of this particular parasite. "We think about how to reduce our exposure and sometimes we think about things that are on the go like alcohol-based hand sanitizers, but for this parasitic infection, we actually want to think more about washing our hands with good old soap and water, and then instead of disinfecting surfaces with things like bleach, this one, we're a little more successful in eradicating it with a mix of hydrogen peroxide," Taylor said. I reached out to the Gaylord Pacific Resort for comment and have not heard back. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. item.title: Supervisors OK Grant for East SD County Small Businesses
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 5.25
SAN DIEGO (CNS) — Small businesses in east San Diego County will be eligible for loans of up to $50,000 under a new revolving loan program approved by the county Board of Supervisors, it was announced Wednesday. Supervisors voted unanimously Tuesday to approve a proposal by Supervisors Joel Anderson and Monica Montgomery Steppe establishing the "Empower East County Business Revolving Loan Fund." According to a statement from Anderson and Montgomery Steppe, the grant "will help businesses that may have difficulty accessing traditional financing, providing loans for working capital, equipment, inventory, facility improvements, expansion and job creation." The program will serve businesses in the cities of El Cajon, La Mesa, Lemon Grove and Santee and communities in unincorporated East County, "while pairing financing with technical assistance through the Small Business Development Center," according to the supervisors. The program will allow small businesses to access revolving loans ranging from $1,000 to $50,000 for capital, equipment, inventory or other expansion needs, according to a county news release.

item.title: SD County Supervisors Vote 3-2 to Formally OK Cannabis Policy
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 5.09
By: KAREN WEIL, City News Service SAN DIEGO (CNS) - Five years after its introduction, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors voted 3-2 Wednesday to formally approve a "socially equitable" cannabis policy that will allow for expanded commercial operations in unincorporated areas. The vote amends zoning and regulatory ordinances, certifies an environmental impact report and sets license and permit fees. The policy will take effect in 30 days and cover cultivation, distribution, manufacturing, microbusinesses, retail, temporary events and testing. Mirroring the council's Aug. 19 vote to advance the policy, Supervisors Paloma Aguirre, Terra Lawson-Remer and Monica Montgomery Steppe voted yes, while their colleagues Joel Anderson and Jim Desmond were opposed. Previously, only five cannabis businesses were allowed to operate in the unincorporated regions. Supervisors recently opted for staff policy recommendations over those from the Planning Commission, including a ban on outdoor cultivation and 1,000-foot buffer from day care or youth centers, places of worship, public parks and trails and schools, rather than a 600-foot distance.

item.title: Brengle Fire forces over 100 Vista residents to evacuate as flames reach apartment backyards
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.96
VISTA, Calif. (KGTV) -- More than 100 people were forced to evacuate their homes in a Vista neighborhood Sunday morning after trees in Brengle Terrace Park ignited, sending flames feet from apartments on Meadow Lake Drive in Vista. The fire erupted just after 7 a.m. 1200 block of Vale Terrace Drive and led to an evacuation order and warning for two zones. Residents said they had very little time to grab their loved ones and get out. Debbie Davson, who has lived in the neighborhood next to Brengle Terrace Park for 21 years, said she and her husband were first alerted by what they thought was a storm. "We thought that the storm had [come] in, so my husband went outside to go check on it, and that's when he saw the fire and just started yelling, ‘Fire!’ We ran outside to get everybody else out," Davson said. Davson took video from her apartment before evacuating. "We saw everything. It was literally about 10 feet away from our backyard, so we saw it all. It was a huge blaze … and it moved very quickly from about mid apartment over to this way," Davson said. Her neighbor, Summer Skorheim, woke up to someone banging on her door. "I got up and they stopped and I went and opened the back as I usually do the slider glass slider, and it was right behind my apartment and I grabbed my dog and grabbed my purse and my jacket and came out here," Skorheim said. Jeff Lehman, who captured cell phone video of the flames lighting up palm trees and eucalyptus in the park, said he arrived at the park this morning to play pickleball. "I came out this morning to play pickleball as I regularly do, and we were just about to start a game about 7:10 this morning. And one of my friends said there's a fire, and over here in the creek bed there was smoke and fire coming up from the creek bed," Lehman said. Several crews from across the county responded to help battle the Brengle fire, shooting foam and water in all directions to get the fire under control. Oceanside, San Marcos, North County Fire Protection District, and Cal Fire joined Vista Fire Rescue in the fight. All evacuation orders were lifted by 10 a.m. The cause of the fire is under investigation. item.title: Coastal flooding warning issued for San Diego as high tide expected tonight
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.88
San Diego is under a coastal flooding warning, with high swells anticipated Monday night — but whether residents need to worry depends largely on where they live and how their home is built. In the Mission Beach neighborhood, Nantasket Court offers a clear example of how differently flooding can impact properties just steps apart from one another. Properties raised as little as a foot and a half right on the boardwalk don't flood significantly, even when the ocean reaches the base of the house, according to residents who live in them. But just up the street, the situation changes. "The tide has been coming up decently high on the bayside - comes all the way up onto the boardwalk and sometimes even onto the alley," David McCall, a neighbor off Nantasket, said. Underground garages in the area have flooded during past tidal events, and the uneven impact makes the problem difficult to solve. One resident said elevation and planning ahead have made a significant difference. "Well, we're really lucky that we're inland from both the bay and the beach side, so we don't really get impacted by it, and our house is elevated, which is something we planned a long time ago," McCall said. Whether to sandbag is ultimately a decision left to individual residents — and one that may come down to the construction and elevation of their specific property. item.title: Labor Day travel weekend comes amid higher gas prices
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.77
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) – Many people are either calling it a night after arriving or waking up early on Saturday to get to their Labor Day destinations. AAA said people are looking for ways to make travel work despite higher gas prices. “We know just historically what we've seen, even with the travel being more expensive or gas being more expensive, most people still prioritize travel,” Annllyen Venagas, AAA Southern California Here’s where gas prices stand right now in our region. It’s tipping about $5.92 a gallon for regular gas here in San Diego. That’s 16 cents more than a week ago and essentially a month ago. But regular gas was below $5 a gallon this time last year. AAA said you’re still encouraged to hit the road early, before 10 a.m. on Saturday and before noon on Monday, despite this time period not being the busiest of all holiday travel time periods. If you are driving, you’ll clearly be spending more getting to your holiday destination. AAA Southern California said Labor Day travelers can anticipate spending roughly $18 to $24 more to fill up their gas tank compared to last year’s holiday. “They're finding ways to make it work. They're modifying their trips so that they can still prioritize travel but still save money on gas and travel, even though, like you said, gas prices are higher than a year ago,” Venagas said. AAA said that’s still not stopping people from traveling, just maybe shorter distances if they are driving. Still, some are opting to stay home for Labor Day rather than make a trip out of the weekend. “Well, gas is $6 a gallon, which is crazy. Like I can't afford that. I really can’t,” Julia Campbell said. “If this is how much I have to spend on gas, I can't really spend anything else on anything else, you know.” “For me right now, no, because I got like 4 kids, so it's just really expensive right now here in California,” Melissa Diaz said.

item.title: City of Oceanside reviewing options to relieve traffic issue for the Capistrano neighborhood
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.58
OCEANSIDE, Calif. (KGTV) – The City of Oceanside is looking into relieving a traffic headache for a neighborhood that’s right next door to Camp Pendleton, the Capistrano neighborhood. You’ve probably seen it as you’re flying up I-5 heading up to Orange County or Los Angeles. “The Capistrano neighborhood has long been challenged by access issues,” Jonathan Borrego, the City Manager for the City of Oceanside, said. “When it gets congested, it's incredibly hard, difficult. It's only one way out. So, at times, I just might as well just stay home,” Edgar Morales, Resident But those who live here say this place can turn into a traffic nightmare in the mornings because it’s so close to the main gate at Camp Pendleton and there’s one way in and one way out. “It is terrible to get in and out of here because Camp Pendleton is right over here. The traffic in the morning is terrible,” Michael Villeli, Resident "Two ways in, one way out. So, you know, things get backed up at the light, it gets backed up on the freeway right behind me here every morning with base traffic,” Lane Scaria, Resident So the City of Oceanside is looking into ways to get rid of this traffic headache. “They wanted us to look at different solutions to see if there is a feasible option to get some other point of access in and out of that neighborhood,” Borrego said. “So, we've undertaken that study and are presenting those recommendations.” Out of 10 options presented to the Oceanside City Council last Wednesday, three options are getting a closer look, and one is being taken back to the state to see if an interchange off-ramp can be built. “Those essentially involve making a connection out of that neighborhood to Loretta Street, which actually used to be a roadway that once crossed the riverbed, and that was before Highway 76 existed,” Borrego said. “So there is actually a roadway that exists out there, but it involves the construction of a bridge over the river, which of course drives the cost up, but that connection probably makes the most sense for a variety of reasons.” Now, the funding, design and construction still all need to happen, which Oceanside’s city manager said could take up to 10 years. “For the city to be thinking about that, that's a sigh of relief for us,” Morales said. Those who live here welcome the hope of getting another road out of their neighborhood. “It's good to hear that they're trying to take some action, you know, but, you know, for some of us it's a little too late,” Scaria said. “We just hope that something will happen sooner rather than later.”

item.title: Amber Alert issued in multiple Central, Southern California counties for teen believed to have been abducted
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.50
An Amber Alert was issued in multiple Central and Southern California counties Sunday for a girl believed to have been abducted in Monterey County. The California Highway Patrol issued the alert for the following counties after 14-year-old Diana Galvez Ortega was reported missing in Salinas: Monterey, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Ventura, Kern, Los Angeles, San Bernardino, Riverside, San Diego, Orange, and Imperial. CHP officials believe the teen is with 38-year-old Sergio Galvez Perez. The relationship between the teen and man was not immediately known. The CHP said the pair is traveling in a white Nissan Altima without license plates. According to the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office, arrest warrants were issued Aug. 31 for Galvez Perez and a 14-year-old unidentified female in connection with the death of an infant whose body was found on a Monterey County roadway on Aug. 1. Sheriff’s officials stated, “Detectives have determined that Sergio Galvez Perez is currently concealing the 14-year-old juvenile and preventing law enforcement from locating her.” Anyone who sees the teen and/or the adult male is urged to call 911.

item.title: Campland on the Bay sells out for Labor Day weekend as families make the most of the holiday
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.28
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Families packed Campland on the Bay in San Diego's Pacific Beach for Labor Day weekend, with more than 500 campsites and around 3,000 guests filling the waterfront campground to capacity. Kalin McColery has been visiting Campland on the Bay since she was just a few months old. For her family, trips to the Mission Bay campground throughout the year are a tradition — and this Labor Day marked a first. "This is the first time we're here for Labor Day, so it's a little bit different. We're kind of enjoying it, seeing how it goes. Normally we're at home, so this is pretty fun to be able to come back here," McColery said. The family made the trip from Long Beach for golf cart rides, magnet games, and most importantly, family time. Jen Cammack, who lives in Otay Mesa, said the holiday weekend is about keeping it simple. "We're going to go to the pool pretty soon and then we're going to go to the bay, um, but just seriously, just hanging out with our family around the campgrounds and catching up," Cammack said. Staff say the campground is completely sold out for the holiday. Serena Rodriguez, Director of Recreation and Entertainment at Campland on the Bay, said the location draws visitors looking for a full day of outdoor activities. "We're right on Mission Bay, the big water park of San Diego, and it's just everybody to come on by whether they want to enjoy the beach, take some, rent some jet skis out, and just have a great time when they're here," Rodriguez said. Rodriguez said this year the campground has seen an uptick in guests extending their stays. "Right now our weather has cooled down and people are staying that extra night so they can really embrace the Labor Day and having that day off," Rodriguez said. item.title: American Legion Post 255 celebrates Labor Day with fundraiser
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.24
NATIONAL CITY (KGTV) — American Legion Post 255, also known as Larry E. Bennett Post 255 in National City, marked Labor Day with a community gathering featuring a classic little fundraiser. The fundraiser featured traditional Labor Day dishes like chili dogs and nachos, all for just $5, with proceeds going toward repairs to the post's kitchen. The event drew city leaders like Mayor Ron Morrison and Councilmember Marcus Bush, as well as longtime members. Liliana Armenta, the post commander, said the gathering reflects what the post means to its members year-round. "It feels amazing to have our post open to our members. We have a lot of members who are a little bit older and live alone. Their kids or family have moved away, so this is kind of a second home to them," Armenta said. For some members, the holiday also meant a little grooming. The post offers haircuts on the first Monday of every month for an unbeatable deal of $12. Member Louie Tejeda took advantage of the deal — with a slight modification. "I'm going to get a mustache trimmed from Elsa," Tejeda said. "Can't beat five bucks," Tejeda said. While Labor Day falls at the start of September, the month also holds special significance for the American Legion. The U.S. Congress issued the organization's federal charter on September 16, 1919. More than a century later, the Legion continues to serve as a gathering place where veterans can find community. Member Greg Trammell said the holiday brought back fond memories of the city. "I came to celebrate the holiday with the community," Trammell said. "My dad is from National City, so a lot of memories in National City, great things, and our independent community... we're always helping each other out." The post also welcomed one of its newest members, Jen Lawson. Lawson said she recently moved out of homelessness and into veteran housing in National City with the help of the non-profit organization, PATH. "I qualified as a veteran to be in this veterans program, and they got me an apartment at Union Tower," Lawson said. Her new home is just down the street from the post — a coincidence she embraced. "And I thought, well, there you go, it's meant to be," Lawson said. Armenta is extending an open invitation to any active-duty service member, Veteran, or family member of someone who served to join the National City post. Annual memberships for active-duty service members or veterans are $50, and family memberships are $30.

item.title: More birds are getting caught and hooked by fishing lines in La Jolla
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.54
More birds are getting caught and hooked by fishing lines and its happening in La Jolla. “There's been a drastic rise in entanglements in seabird and marine animal over the last three years,” Azi Sharif says. She’s part of Wildlife Jewels, a nonprofit that protects wildlife from human-caused threats. Her team has been tracking what’s happening along the La Jolla coastline and she says the numbers are concerning. “Since beginning of April, our data shows 84 entanglements of birds just here along the La Jolla coastline between Children's Pool and Point La Jolla. They don't make it,” Sharif says. Sharif says the location makes the problem even more difficult. These birds feed, rest and raise their young along this coastline the same area where her team has been documenting fishing activity. “Right at their feeding spot and nesting and resting spot of these birds, there's lots of fishing activity going on which we have been documenting and witnessing as well,” Sharif says. ABC10 News reporter Olivia González-Britt also reached out to local fishing community members. One man, who wanted to remain anonymous, says he started fishing on local boats at 14. He tells me accidental hookings can happen, but experienced fishermen know how to reduce the chances and safely release a bird if it does get caught. He says most fishermen care about the marine ecosystem, adding that birds can even help fishermen find where the fish are. Sharif says she wants to see changes to prevent more birds from getting caught: “We urgently ask for consideration of expanding the MPA, the marine protected area in this area.” She’s also calling for greater monitoring and enforcement, including the possibility of using drones to identify fishing boats inside protected areas. If you see an injured or entangled bird, Sharif says reporting it can help get that animal rescued while also giving her team more data about where and how these incidents are happening.

item.title: Pentagon 'temporarily rescinds' new testosterone guidelines
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 4.46
Pentagon 'temporarily rescinds' new testosterone guidelines A top official said a "draft" document was "inadvertently" posted. New Pentagon guidelines for mandatory testosterone deficiency screening of male service members aged 30 and above were "temporarily rescinded" from a Defense Department website shortly after they were posted earlier this week, according to a U.S. official. The guidelines emerged from an announcement in mid-July from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that testosterone screenings were to become a part of the military’s annual health check-ups for male service members aged 30 years and older serving on active-duty and the reserves. Hegseth said that if clinicians recommended testosterone replacement therapy for a service member, it would be up to that individual to decide if they wanted to purse the treatment. The announcement drew criticism from some medical experts who questioned the need for such testing and treatment. On Wednesday, the Pentagon issued a press release from Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, that “the Director of the Defense Health Agency issued comprehensive clinical guidance to the Military Departments and medical care providers” setting up “uniform screening and treatment pathways” in the military’s medical system for testosterone treatment. The press release included links to three documents posted on the DHA’s website providing specific medical and clinical guidance, but by the next day, the guidelines had been removed from the website. “Clinical Guidance for Health and Human Performance Optimization' published on September 2, 2026, has been temporarily rescinded to allow for updates,” said a U.S. official. “The 'Interim Guidance on Testosterone Deficiency Screenings for Active Duty and Reserve Component Personnel' remains in effect. The final clinical guidance will be issued shortly,” said the official. In addition to providing specifics for male testing, the guidelines also provided guidance that female service members be asked about fatigue and disrupted menstrual cycles that could be associated with hormonal dysregulation No other reason was offered as to why the guidance had been temporarily rescinded, but on Friday, a top adviser to Hegseth described the documents posted on the website as a "draft" document that had been "inadvertently" posted. "What was posted earlier this week was something that was a draft. It was not approved for release," Tim Parlatore, a senior advisor to Hegseth and his former personal attorney, said in an appearance on CNN. "Somebody had put it out there inadvertently. And so, we needed to pull that back because we need a lot more input to make sure that the information on that reflected the current science and medical science and medical guidance, as opposed to certain antiquated protocols," Parlatore said. It's not yet clear when new DHA clinical guidance for the testosterone screenings of male service members will be made available. Low testosterone levels have been a concern in the military, particularly in the special operations community, where high stress, extreme physical labor, paired with not getting enough calories, could negatively impact testosterone levels -- though research is still ongoing. A very small percentage of men have a medical condition called Testosterone Deficiency. However, some doctors say they are concerned that the online popularity of "low-T" as a medical problem creates a false impression that this is a bigger problem than it really is.

item.title: 25 years later, Michael Strahan recalls days after 9/11
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.73
25 years later, Michael Strahan recalls days after 9/11 The special "9/11: United We Stand -- 25 Years Later" airs Tuesday, Sept. 1. Michael Strahan will never forget looking out his window in Montclair, New Jersey, and seeing the first World Trade Center tower in flames on Sept. 11, 2001. Strahan, a former football star turned "Good Morning America" co-anchor, said he never expected he would end up in New York City but fell in love with it after being drafted to the New York Giants, the team he stayed with for 15 seasons of his career. He's among the athletes, musicians and entertainers who reflected on how their industries worked to bring healing after tragedy for the the ABC News special, "9/11: United We Stand -- 25 Years Later." An ABC News special, "9/11: United We Stand -- 25 Years Later," airs Tuesday, Sept. 1, at 9 p.m. ET on ABC and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu. In the wake of the attacks, Strahan was one of the players who pushed for the cancellation of that weekend's football games out of respect for those lost. He also contributed to an NFL-wide effort to provide disaster relief and support to victims and their families. "What were we gonna do? Sit at home? No, we wanted to collectively get together and offer whatever kind of assistance that we could at Ground Zero," Strahan said. "That's the biggest show that we wanted to give them, was a show of respect." The NFL wasn't the only major sports league to use its platform to foster unity and support victims post-9/11. In fall 2001, the Yankees went to the World Series, and though they ultimately lost the series, commentators say the team's participation in the games that came just over a month after the tragedy unified New Yorkers. "It became more than just playing baseball," Derek Jeter, then Yankees shortstop, said. "Our job was to bring joy, especially to New York at that time." Selena Roberts, then sports columnist at the New York Times, noted that the leagues recognized their role in a difficult time. "After Sept. 11, players and coaches absolutely knew that they had a platform and a responsibility to be there for the public, and I think in so many ways, really did help heal people," she said. That fall, a star-studded concert at Madison Square Garden, organized by singer Paul McCartney, brought some of music's biggest names together for a benefit to honor and raise money for 9/11 victims and first responders. Called The Concert for New York City, the benefit featured singers David Bowie, Mick Jagger, Jon Bon Jovi, Billy Joel and McCartney, among others. Bon Jovi reflected on the meaning of his band's song "Livin' on a Prayer" in that moment. "'We got each other and that's a lot.' That's what it is, right?" the singer said. "In that moment in time, when you felt helpless, to have a lyric that is about just simple unity and faith." Late night talk show hosts also did their part to calm the public's nerves. CBS's David Letterman was the first of the late-night hosts to return on air post-9/11. During his first show back after the attack, Letterman said, "There's only one requirement of all of us, and that is to be courageous." Anthony DeCurtis, an author and music critic, said that immediately after 9/11, there was a moment in which people questioned listening to music or going to the theater. That, though, is precisely why we have art, he said. "At moments like that, you know, you want artists who are going to help us understand and come to terms with the things in our lives that are the most frightening things," Curtis said. "This is what we do, and what better time to do it than now?" Strahan said it was an era where people learned to be more compassionate. "I'd never seen the level of unity that we had during that time."

item.title: Meet the chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.58
Meet the New York City chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks Members of "Operation Chefs With Spirit" reflect on the tragedy 25 years later. Chef Don Pintabona spent years cooking up the finest dishes for celebrities, Wall Street brokers and other VIPs at the Tribeca Grill in downtown Manhattan, but nothing could have prepared him and the rest of the city's restaurant community for their biggest job. In the hours after the World Trade Center was attacked and destroyed on Sept. 11, 2001, Pintabona said he and many other chefs, caters, food service workers and others all yearned to help the city in some capacity with their skills, but didn't immediately know how. But through quick thinking, organizing and the generosity of thousands New Yorkers, Pintabona and the other restaurant members put together a massive operation that fed Ground Zero workers around the clock for two months after the attacks. "Everybody kind of just said, 'Okay, let's jump in,'" Pintabona, 66, told ABC News. He and other volunteers of "Operation Chefs with Spirit" said that even though 25 years have passed since the attacks, the memories of those weeks are still fresh, as is the sense of awe at how they put the operation together. Turning the page on a tragedy Pintabona said he had a desire to do something after the attacks to help the city, but it was a little piece of paper that came to him serendipitously that sparked his idea for the operation. On Sept. 11, he said he watched the destruction of the towers from the roof of his home in Brooklyn, which was so close that pieces of paper debris from the towers were floating in the air near him. One of those was a "P" page from a dictionary and when Pintabona picked it up he said he noticed that one side of the page had words with negative connotations, such as pesky, while the other side had words such as persevere, perseverance, persistence. “9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. "I mean, in my mind, this came straight from heaven, that through the perversion, you gotta persist, you gotta persevere," he said. "So those words were banging around my head for the days and weeks and just trying to figure out how can I live up to this." Pintabona said the next day he was able to get to his restaurant, and he started cooking with what he had in his kitchen. He then brought the food to Stuyvesant High School in lower Manhattan, which was one of the staging areas for first responders. "We had just floods of people coming in to attack the food," he said adding that the meals were gone in a matter of hours. Pintabona said he wanted to continue to feed more people but transporting the meals through the streets, which were damaged and restricted to first responders and the National Guard, would be a challenge. He said he had a eureka moment during a cigarette break while watching the Hudson River. "I saw a barge…And I said, 'Holy s---, this is it. We've got to feed everybody by boat,'" he recalled. A crew assembles, quickly gets into action Pintabona told ABC News he found that that other chefs in the city were also interested in feeding the Ground Zero workers and they all put their heads together. He soon started calling up several contacts within the food industry, the city government and the owner of Spirit Cruises, which operated city sightseeing and party cruises lines, and things quickly began to fall in place. Spirit provided three boats, one at Chelsea Piers that would be used to cook and prepare the meals, another to transport the food to Ground Zero, and a third, a triple decker, stationed in Battery Park City near the pit that was used for the workers to eat and rest. The city's top chefs, such as Charlie Palmer, Danny Meyer and Daniel Boulud, and food workers and volunteers would be doled out with tasks with everything from cutting veggies to organizing forks, spoons and plates. Jim Stewart, a longtime food service coordinator who had experience coordinating food operations at the Meadowlands and other big clients, jumped in when Pintabona made the calls for help. Stewart said he too was compelled to do something after the attacks. "I think at that point, having something to do was sort of helpful, and it gave you some sort of purpose in a very difficult situation," Stewart, 66, a Navy veteran, told ABC News. Stewart used his connections to secure food from the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, which was still in fridges following the end of that year's U.S. Open. Stewart and Pintabona estimated that the food from the tennis center could serve 75,000 meals, but that was all eaten within three days. Fortunately, they weren't the only New Yorkers who were willing to share from their fridges. Stewart recalled how a whole slew of Downtown Manhattan restaurant staff, from small Chinatown restaurants to larger, more elite eateries like the ones under B.R. Guest, were calling him up and ready to offer their food. "So they would be bringing down enormous amounts of food packages to go. All the cooks from down there, they brought meals for like 200 people without question for a month," Stewart said. "I would get a call, and they would go, 'At the airport, there's two pallets of beef from Texas.' It was not just New York," Stewart added. Pintabona said that thousands of New Yorkers arrived at Chelsea Piers ready to volunteer, even those who never cooked a meal in their life. Although Pintabona had to turn many would-be volunteers away because of space and logistics issues, he said he worked out to tailor their skills to fit the operation. "When they would come on, I would try to talk to as many as possible. 'Okay, you work at Smith Barney in the accounting department? You know what? We need you to help us inventory the food that comes in off the trucks,'" he recalled. "A lot of people, obviously servers and whatnot, food service people, I would put them front-facing on the buffets, you know what they're used to." Megan Murphy was a full time bartender at Rue 51 in Manhattan on Sept. 11 and she told ABC News she immediately answered Stewart's call. She helped to serve the food and coordinate with other volunteers right at the pit. "It was my call to duty," Murphy, 51, told ABC News while holding back tears. " I had been doing something because I was helpless. I felt helpless and I just wanted to help. I just want to be…I just needed to be there." 'Nourishing more than their stomachs' By Sept. 14, the operation had kicked off and the volunteers were ready to go and the first set of food was delivered to the pit. The boats would sail from Chelsea Piers nearly 2 1/2 miles south to Ground Zero with a team of volunteers and return back for another round and the operation would continue 24/7. Workers still had soot on them and looked liked they hadn't slept in days but they gladly accepted the meals and cherished the time to step away from the terrible scene. Pintabona said massage therapists joined in on the volunteering and provided the crews with free massages to ease their muscles. He said the meals definitely helped the pit workers have the energy to push through with their work, but the chefs and volunteers all felt that their service meant a lot more than a free lunch. "You'd see the looks on the faces of people that came in, if they'd been on the pile for God knows how many hours and starving and then they got to sit in a clean environment and then talk to other first responders," he said. "So that was the most amazing part of the effort," he added, "[It] kind of nourished a lot more than just stomachs." Murphy, who continued to bartend at night during her volunteer time, said that many who came down to help went beyond just serving food and in many cases offered the pit crews a place to unwind and let out their raw emotions. "I would make an effort just to go to everyone and talk to them, and let them talk to me about the experience," she said. "If after lunch they could walk out and I could walk out with them and they were smiling and getting off their shift and made it a better day, that was what I was there to do," Murphy added. The volunteers and chefs said that while they pushed forward with the operation, with some sleeping on the boats, the stress and hard work did compound. Fortunately, the volunteers had each other's backs, according to Pintabona and Stewart. "It got so ridiculous that one day Jimmy was working the phones and, you know I just had this stupid, selfish craving for a Krispy Kreme doughnut," Pintabona recalled. "I said, 'All right, let's call this guy.' We called them, and the next day a whole truck with like 20 rolling racks of Krispy Kreme donuts showed up," Stewart said. "So [Pintabona] looked at me and was like, I should have known better." Looking back 25 years later The operation ended after roughly two months and roughly a million meals after the Red Cross came in and took care of meals for the Ground Zero pit crew. But Pintabona said that the crew didn't grow apart. He organized a Christmas party at Cipriani in Soho for all of the volunteers and their families and many stayed in touch in the last 25 years. Stewart said he was humbled by the outpouring of support from not only New Yorkers, but people throughout the world who heard about the feeding operation and were moved. "I have these pictures that were sent to me from a class where the children, they drew cartoons," he recalled. "They said like, 'Keep going. You're doing great.' You know, 'thank you for your efforts.'" Murphy said that she is still emotional thinking back to the weeks after the attacks, but the memories of selfless New Yorkers always stand out. "New York is strong, New Yorkers are strong," she said. Pintabona agreed and said for him it all came back to that floating dictionary page and that push to persevere. "You have to turn the page and stay on the positive side. So that's kind of what I've learned through this experience," he said.

item.title: American family missing in apparent crash of small plane off Bahamas coast
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.55
4 family members killed in Bahamas small plane crash identified Two grandparents and two grandchildren were aboard the plane, the family said. The bodies of four family members from Miami were recovered Tuesday following a small plane crash near the Bahamas, family members said. A family statement provided to ABC News identified the passengers as Mario Lamar Sr., 80, and Lili Lamar, 79, and their grandchildren Sofi Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22. Mario Lamar was "an experienced pilot with more than 40 years of flying experience," according to the family. "Our relatives ultimately located our loved ones and had to bring them aboard their own vessels," the family said in a statement Tuesday. The cause of the crash is still under investigation, according to the Aircraft Accident Investigation Authority (AAIA) of The Bahamas. The agency said as of Tuesday afternoon it has not found the plane or any wreckage. Around 2 p.m. on Monday, "the Royal Bahamian Defense Force requested Coast Guard assistance following a report of a downed airplane with four people aboard approximately 15 miles off Andros Island, Bahamas," the Coast Guard said. The Bahamas Police Department identified the plane as a PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft. It took off from Great Harbour Cay around 11:12 a.m. Monday and was bound for Miami Executive Airport, officials said. "Air Traffic Control subsequently lost contact with the aircraft approximately 13 miles west of Andros Island," Bahamas Police said, adding that poor weather had postponed the search. The investigation into the crash is ongoing, officials said. The family said it is asking for privacy. "We are deeply grateful to everyone who supported us, searched alongside us, and kept our family in their prayers," they said in a statement.

item.title: Witkoff hails 'meaningful discussions' on Ukraine-Russia war in Zelenskyy meeting
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.24
Witkoff hails 'very meaningful discussions' on Ukraine-Russia war in Sunday meeting with Zelenskyy Witkoff and Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday. LONDON -- President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff hailed what he described as "very meaningful discussions" regarding the Ukraine-Russia war, saying the talks in Kyiv Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy were "substantive [and] important." Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, arrived in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday in a renewed White House push for progress on ending Russia's full-scale invasion of its neighbor, now in its fifth year. "President Trump asked us to convey his personal regards to you and to the people of Ukraine," Kushner told Zelenskyy in comments before reporters, adding that Trump "wanted us to convey that he sees this as a very, very hard and complex problem, but it's a very worthy problem worth solving." He added that Trump was committed not only to ending the conflict, but also to securing a lasting peace that would enable Ukraine "to build itself into the great nation that they [Ukraine] have the fullest potential to achieve." Zelenskyy thanked the United States for its continued support and expressed gratitude to Trump for "allowing the American group to be here in Ukraine today." "After the meetings in the Russian Federation, it was very important for us to have President Trump's chief negotiators in Ukraine today," Zelenskyy said. The U.S. delegation traveled to Ukraine following talks in Moscow on Saturday, during which Witkoff and Kushner sat down with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss what a White House official told ABC News were "substantive plans for next steps" on the path toward a peace deal, despite few signs peace is any closer. The visit to Kyiv by Witkoff and Kushner is their first during the full-scale invasion. The pair have visited Russia several times during the conflict. They arrived from Poland by train before being welcomed by President Zelenskyy outside the historic Saint Sophia Cathedral in the center of the capital. Zelenskyy embraced the two the men before leading them inside the cathedral. Prior to their arrival, Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X that he had met with Ukraine's negotiating team and was expecting a "substantive conversation" with the U.S. envoys. "Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive. We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready," he wrote in a post to X. The national security advisers of France, Germany and the U.K. were among senior European officials who also traveled to Kyiv to take part in Sunday's talks. A source told ABC News the American delegation was serious about the meetings in Moscow and Kyiv, adding that the visits are "not just for show." According to the source, the American side wants to end the war before winter, while Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelenskyy's office, believes this will not be possible and that Russia will only be genuinely ready for negotiations in the spring or summer 2027. The American negotiating pair spent more than three hours with Putin in the Kremlin on Saturday, with U.S. and Russian officials both praising the discussions. But Putin afterward gave no sign of compromise. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told the state-run Tass news agency that Putin told Witkoff and Kushner that it was necessary to eliminate "all root causes of the Ukrainian conflict," a phrase routinely used by officials in Moscow hinting at maximalist Russian demands that Ukraine be forced to accept neutrality, cut down its military and abandon any NATO aspirations. Putin also "noted the successes of Russian forces" in the ongoing war effort "and expressed confidence in achieving its goals," Ushakov said. Most experts believe Putin's position in recent weeks has only hardened, with signs he believes Russia is winning the war and is more determined to use military force to try to force concessions from Kyiv, including by targeting its energy system this winter. In the last two weeks, Russia has significantly intensified its air attacks on Kyiv, using jet-powered drones to relentlessly terrorize the capital. At the start of Saturday's meeting, Witkoff thanked Putin for hosting the American delegation and noted the "incredible" stories and memories that he, Kushner, Ushakov and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill Dmitriev will have when they retire. "Yours will be right at the top of it all," Witkoff said. Witkoff also conveyed Trump's best wishes and thanked Putin on behalf of the Gilman family for helping secure the return of Rob Gilman. Putin said that the credit belonged to Trump. A White House official told ABC News that Kushner and Witkoff were joined by officials from the National Security Council, State Department and Treasury Department during the discussions on "proposals to bring peace to this conflict." Witkoff further thanked Putin for supporting what he described as a temporary "no-shoot" arrangement around Kyiv and Moscow, which allowed the American delegation to travel safely to and from Russia. Putin and Zelenskyy have both publicly said they will not strike each other's capitals during the American delegations visits. While no Russian strikes struck Kyiv overnight Saturday, drones were reported to have targeted the nearby city of Boryspil. Russian strikes continued in the rest of Ukraine. The Kremlin meeting did little to encourage Ukrainians, Oleksandr Merezhko -- a member of the Ukrainian parliament and the chair of the body's foreign affairs committee -- told ABC News on Sunday. "We are expecting Trump's envoy but I don't have any hopes at all," he said from Kyiv. This is something that Trump doesn't understand -- Putin believes that there is no way back for him. He has committed so many crimes that, as he believes, he can save his skin only if Ukraine capitulates." Merezhko said he was among those skeptical of Witkof and Kushner's ability to chart a path to a settlement, describing the pair as "amateurs without necessary knowledge and experience." Both Russia and Ukraine continued long-range overnight strikes. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 108 drones and an unspecified number of cruise missiles into the country overnight into Sunday morning. Air defenses downed 82 drones and six cruise missiles, the air force said, with impacts reported across 11 locations. Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported at least one attack in the Kyiv region, where a Russian strike caused a "large-scale fire" at an infrastructure facility. Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said its forces downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight, with craft reported shot down over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. ABC News' Oleksiy Pshemyskiy contributed to this report.

item.title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.10
The steel 'embodies his soul': 9/11 family takes World Trade Center beam across US Stephen Siller Jr. was just 9 months old when his firefighter dad died on 9/11. On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner. "He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News. "When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan." He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center. Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old. Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired. The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News. 9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful." At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago." To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's. "Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across." The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many." As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11. "And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot." "Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel." Siller Jr. found one of the most memorable stops to be Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he learned of the attacks. "We normally have stairs that go up to the steel truck," Siller Jr. explained, but on this May visit to the school, it was pouring rain. Still, the children "were begging the firemen, 'Hey, can we get up? We just want to touch the steel,'" Siller Jr. said. As the kids were lifted up, they began "praying over this steel," he recalled. "Little kids who understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history ... it once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day," he said. "I was really shocked at how interested they were," he said. To Frank Siller and Siller Jr., educating the next generation was a key goal of the Steel Across America campaign. "These kids were incredible; they were patient ... and they consistently showed up," Siller Jr. said. "No matter where we were in the country, there were families there, which was beautiful -- fathers and mothers wanting to teach their kids." "I was 9 months old on 9/11 -- if you were born after me, and not in New York City, you know, there's a high chance that you have no real understanding of that day," he continued. "It's important that that lesson is taught to these kids -- there's so much to be pulled from the sacrifices made." The Steel Across America campaign is part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, started by Frank Siller in honor of his brother's run from the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the World Trade Center. The foundation supports military members, first responders and their families across the U.S. The foundation is currently providing wounded veterans and first responders with mortgage-free, specially-adapted smart homes. "We didn't let Stephen just perish in that rubble and let that story end there. No, we took his act of courage and sacrifice and said, 'We're going to do good with it,'" Frank Siller said. "Would Stephen make that run again through the tunnel, knowing he was gonna die? I think he knew he was gonna die," Frank Siller said. "At the very least, he knew it was a strong possibility that he might not be coming home. And to think that he did that, knowing how much he loved Sally and his kids, people like that are few and far between. ... And it's got to be recognized and never forgotten."

item.title: 9/11 victims hope newly uncovered records will help illuminate Saudis' alleged role
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.77
25 years later, 9/11 victims hope newly uncovered records will help illuminate Saudis' alleged role Victims' families are pressing President Trump to declassify more materials. Twenty-five years after Sept. 11, a trove of newly obtained records is offering what families of the victims characterize in court as compelling evidence of deep Saudi complicity in the attacks. Now, as their decade-old lawsuit against the Saudi kingdom marches toward trial, the families are pressing the Trump administration to declassify more government records they believe could finally deliver justice. The newly revealed records, from a lawsuit involving an alleged Saudi agent, include a video purportedly casing the Capitol two years before the attacks and a sketch that purportedly shows calculations for navigating a plane toward a target on the ground, which one family member called "smoking gun evidence." The decision on whether to declassify additional records ultimately lies with President Donald Trump, whose administration has touted government transparency and who has personally signed executive orders declassifying records ranging from purported UFO sightings to high-profile assassinations. "We've seen him do it for the [President John F. Kennedy] files. Why not the 9/11 files?" Brett Eagleson, whose father Bruce was killed in the World Trade Center's South Tower, said in an interview with ABC News. "Now is the moment, 25 years later, to finally bring resolution," Eagleson said, "and the man that sits in the Oval Office has a historic and a tremendous opportunity to do it." Eagleson has enlisted the support of members of the New York congressional delegation to press the administration to release key records that include phone logs purportedly belonging to Omar al-Bayoumi, who the families allege is a Saudi intelligence asset, as well as two of the hijackers. Among those who cosigned a letter seeking the declassification of those records is Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., a Trump ally who is urging the president take up the matter before the 25th anniversary, less than two weeks away. "This is probably one of the better shots that we have at getting this information out there," Malliotakis said. "And I think that hopefully we'll see this type of transparency coming from this administration." White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told ABC News, "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, and his team is working diligently to identify records that are responsive to these families' request." 'Smoking gun' The families have waged their legal campaign against the Saudis in one form or another since 2003, but only recently uncovered videos, notes and other records they say offer irrefutable evidence of Saudi government complicity -- claims that the Saudis have long denied. Al-Bayoumi lies at the heart of those records. The Saudi national lived in the U.S. for the better part of a decade -- nominally as a student -- prior to the attacks, and provided "essential support" to two hijackers when they arrived in California in early 2000, according to the families' lawsuit, which claims that al-Bayoumi assisted the men by "finding them an apartment in his complex" and "providing funds just below the suspicious activity reporting threshold to help them open a bank account." According to the families, al-Bayoumi also threw a party for the hijackers and "the hijackers stayed at al-Bayoumi's apartment for 1-2 days, before their apartment was ready." "He was the man," Eagleson told ABC News. "Omar al-Bayoumi is coordinating and directing logistical and financial support to the hijackers." In 1999, al-Bayoumi travelled to Washington, D.C., where he filmed what the families called a "chilling" video of al-Bayoumi "'casing' the U.S. Capitol for an attack," according to the suit. The Capitol is believed to be the target of United Flight 93, the hijacked plane that crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. In the video, according to the suit, al-Bayoumi describes to an unidentified audience the security posture inside and outside the Capitol building, highlights its proximity to the nearby Reagan National Airport, and opaquely references a "plan." The families also presented in court a sketch and math equation from al-Bayoumi's notebook showing what they claim to be a "line of sight calculation for navigating a plane to a target on the ground." The Saudis have repeatedly denied having any role in facilitating the attacks and replied in court that they remain "an ally of the United States [and] a sworn enemy of Al Qaeda." Attorneys for the kingdom also fervently disputed the families' characterizations of that evidence in court, dismissing the Capitol "casing" film as a "tourist video that includes footage of artwork, flowerbeds, and a squirrel on the White House lawn." They say the notepad sketch "appears to be a high school math assignment" belonging to al-Bayoumi's child. Al-Bayoumi, who is believed to now live in Saudi Arabia, "became entangled in the 9/11 investigation because he had helped two fellow Saudis he had no reason to suspect of wrongdoing," the Saudi attorneys said -- a sentiment al-Bayoumi shared in a deposition in the case. Al-Bayoumi has also denied any connection to Saudi intelligence. Last year the judge overseeing the case ruled that the evidence presented by the families was compelling enough to proceed to trial, dealing a major setback to the Saudis and granting the families what they called "the most consequential step yet" in two decades of litigation. The judge noted that the Saudis' exculpatory explanations "are either self-contradictory or [are] not strong enough to overcome the inference that [the Saudis] had employed al-Bayoumi ... to assist the hijackers." And while there remains no evidence that Saudi leaders at the top of its government were likely aware of plans for the attack, "the total evidence creates a high probability as to al-Bayoumi's ... [role] in the hijackers' plans," the judge concluded, "and the related role of [his] employer," the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. An 'extraordinary irony' For Eagleson, the material amounts to "smoking gun evidence" that should not have taken nearly a quarter-century to unearth. "That information never saw the light of day until 25 years later," Eagleson said. "And what was found in those files should blow everyone's mind. Everyone should be outraged." The families presented this new body of evidence in court last year after retrieving it from British authorities, who first gathered it as part of a raid on al-Bayoumi's home in the U.K. just 10 days after the attacks in New York and Washington. The evidence was turned over to the FBI, Eagleson said, but what became of it later remains murky. Crucially, according to attorneys for the families, much of this evidence was not made available to the 9/11 Commission, which released its report in 2004 absolving the Saudi governing of "knowingly" supporting Al Qaeda. Experts suggest this evidence could reshape the public's understanding not only of the attack on Sept. 11, but also the United States' subsequent geopolitical and military decisions in the Middle East. Daniel Benjamin, a counterterrorism official during the Clinton and Obama administrations, said the al-Bayoumi records and other materials "force us to think that our entire theory of what 9-11 was about -- what the whole war on terrorism was about -- was largely mistaken." "The Bush administration insisted that no non-state actor could have done something as complicated as the 9/11 attacks, and that was a major reason that it turned the focus on Iraq and on Saddam Hussein," said Benjamin, now the president of the American Academy in Berlin. "And it is an extraordinary irony that they may have been right about the need for state support -- but they got the state completely wrong." The Saudi lawsuit is far from the last remaining question mark regarding culpability for the attacks. Last week, a military judge ruled that after spending two decades at Guantanamo Bay, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the self-proclaimed "mastermind" of the attack, would finally face trial in June 2028. 'Repeated obstacles' In July, Rep. Malliotakis, the New York Republican, joined Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Jerry Nadler in writing a letter to a little-known but powerful advisory panel called the Public Interest Declassification Board, housed within the National Archives, which carries the power to consider requests for sensitive government secrets and make recommendations to the president about whether to declassify them. The lawmakers' request, sent at the behest of the families, bemoaned the "repeated obstacles" attorneys for the families have faced "in obtaining access to these materials from U.S. law enforcement and intelligence agencies." In the letter, lawmakers requested the declassification of "various phone records and analyses directly relevant to al-Bayoumi's role" in 9/11, including records for a cell phone purportedly belonging to al-Bayoumi that he, according to the letter, "lent ... to the hijackers to keep in touch with his associates such as Anwar Aulaqi," the high-profile American al-Qaeda follower who in 2011 was killed by a U.S. drone strike. Attorneys for the families believe those records could help them better understand the timing and nature of al-Bayoumi's and the hijackers' communications and key events in the hijackers' planning of the attacks. The board responded weeks later, writing that it was "actively engaged in interagency consultations to determine what equities, if any, may remain in relation to these records." It urged patience as "those discussions continue." The White House said last week that President Trump would attend a ceremony at the Pentagon to commemorate the 25th anniversary. Vice President JD Vance will travel to New York to be at Ground Zero.

item.title: FBI official warns 9/11 is still inspiring terrorists inside America 25 years later
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.48
Top FBI official warns 9/11 is still inspiring terrorists inside America 25 years later Foreign terrorist groups are "adaptable" and "agile," an FBI officials says. Twenty five years after al-Qaeda struck inside the U.S. homeland in shocking and tragic ways, federal authorities are warning that the threat from foreign terrorist organizations has hardly gone away, and in some ways is more challenging to stop now than it was two decades ago. "We see people getting radicalized from the comforts of their own home, through social media, the internet," the FBI's co-deputy director, Chris Raia, told ABC News. "Those are the folks that keep me up at night because it's just so much harder for us to detect those." According to Raia, the FBI is better positioned now to stop a large-scale, sophisticated plot like al-Qaeda's attack in 2001, which killed nearly 3,000 people. "Way better postured now in 2026, based on legislation, based on how far we've come in the [FBI] bureau, based on how far we've come in the U.S. intelligence community," Raia said. But he said foreign terrorist organizations have shown themselves to be "adaptable" and "agile," so al-Qaeda and other major terrorist groups like ISIS are now relentlessly seeking to develop what Raia called "lone offenders" inside the United States. In the past year and a half, the FBI has arrested at least 16 people inside the U.S. homeland for allegedly plotting or supporting plots to kill Americans on behalf of al-Qaeda or ISIS, officials say. In March, the U.S. intelligence community released a report on the state of worldwide threats and noted that, while ISIS and al-Qaeda may be largely relying on social media to reach America, their numbers are actually growing overseas, with ISIS now boasting up to 18,000 members worldwide and al-Qaeda's ranks reaching up to 28,000 members. Raia said that 25 years later, 9/11 continues to be a motivating factor for people radicalized online. "That is their Super Bowl," Raia said. "Every time you start digging into their media, digging into their communications, there's always, always references to 9/11." Just three weeks ago, the FBI arrested 35-year-old Jessica Bowie of Albany, New York, for allegedly plotting to bomb the state capitol there. Charging documents said that in the weeks before her arrest, she wrote on social media: "Praise be to Allah for September 11th." At a press conference after her arrest, the head of the FBI's field office in Albany, Craig Tremaroli, noted that Bowie allegedly "went from a little girl waving the American flag after 9/11 to now having stickers of the fallen towers." "Let that sink in," he said. Bowie has not yet entered a plea in her case. In his interview with ABC News, Raia rejected criticism that the FBI has been distracted by immigration enforcement and other priorities of the Trump administration. "Our footprint when it comes to the immigration policy or immigration is very minimal," he said. Raia said that while the FBI always wants more resources, he can assure Americans that fighting terrorism is among the FBI's top priorities and that the FBI has the resources they need to do that. Raia said it's an ongoing chess match with the FBI trying to predict what terrorists may come up with next. "Drones has really been forefront of my priorities," he said. "You would be silly to think that that's not coming to the United States at some point, and we are trying to stay ahead of that." Nevertheless, Raia said that to truly protect the U.S. homeland, the FBI needs help from the public. "See something, say something," he said. "That campaign that started 20-something years ago, that is just as important today in 2026, if not more important than it was in 2001." ABC News' Luke Barr contributed to this report.

item.title: AI agents are poised to be the next hacking victims, cyber CEO predicts
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 6.81
In a world of AI-enabled cyberattacks , the victims of hacks will no longer just be humans — they'll also be AI agents themselves, Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios. Why it matters: Cyber defenses are tailored toward predicting and defending humans. Now, companies need to start treating the agents roaming their systems as both potential adversaries and the targets. Driving the news: Gerry's prediction during an interview at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last month came after OpenAI disclosed that its agentic system hacked Hugging Face but before the AI lab released its technical deep dive into how its agents carried out that attack. What he's saying: "We're going to see agents as the victim," Gerry told Axios. "You're going to start to see agents getting hacked, not people." The big picture : Gerry's prediction comes as AI labs continue to grapple with the long-tail impact of their agents taking unauthorized actions during pre-deployment security testing. But many of those cases involve AI agents acting in unintended ways, not hacking each other as a way to break into an organization. Zoom in: Gerry fully anticipates that the growing number of hacks against AI agents are going to take place in the enterprise, rather than on consumer-owned and operated agents, since that's where the bulk of AI agents are currently deployed. "It's going to become the No. 1 attack vector that we're going to see," he said. "To make our lives easier as humans, we've given [AI agents] the crown jewels to everything." He noted that many tools that companies have long relied on now also have agents themselves, making it harder to keep track of what's on a company network. "You have all of these enterprise-approved tools that now magically got AI turned on," he said. "Now, there's a backlog of all of this tech debt of things that I approved that I no longer approve." Between the lines: The cybersecurity industry has been trying to raise awareness about securing AI agents' identities for more than a year, warning that AI agents are now the latest example of insider threats. Those insider agents could be leveraged to provide hackers with unfettered access to sensitive systems, exfiltrate data and break into other parts of an organization. "To me, that's inevitable," Gerry said. Zoom out: Even before AI agents started to proliferate in enterprise networks, poor identity controls were one of the top vectors for malicious hackers. Identity-based cyberattacks accounted for 60% of all of Cisco's incident response cases in 2024, for example. The intrigue: Visibility of the actions that AI agents are taking and their chain of thought is becoming more obfuscated as frontier models advance, making it more difficult for security teams to attribute attacks. What we're watching: "It's new attacks. It's moving faster. It's moving at a bigger scale," Gerry said. "But ultimately, this comes back to good cyber hygiene and understanding what exists and how do you put controls around it." Go deeper: AI models are becoming unknowable

item.title: Historic first: Older adults now outnumber the youngest children for the first time
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 6.51
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, International Database ; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios People 65 and older now outnumber children ages 5 and younger worldwide for the first time in recorded history, according to a new report by the U.S. Census. Why it matters: A global plunge in fertility — demographers' term for the number of children being born — and increased longevity are creating a demographic inversion that's projected to deepen for decades. It's a trend that's shifting the historic balance between working-age people and older adults . By the numbers: The scale and speed of the shift as the youngest Baby Boomers move toward their mid-60s are striking. They reflect the scope of the challenge in caring for the elderly and maintaining programs such as Social Security in the U.S., an Axios analysis of the Census data found. More than 71% of the world's population lived in countries with fertility rates at or below the roughly 2.1-births-per-woman replacement level in 2023. That's up from 45% in 2013. The Census says the world reached that tipping point much earlier than demographers expected just a decade ago. The population of those 65+ is projected to grow from 852 million in 2025 to 2 billion in 2060. Stunning stat: That increase would account for about 55% of all net global population growth over that period, according to an Axios calculation using Census projections. The world's total population is projected to rise from 8.13 billion to 10.23 billion by 2060. State of play: The low-birth era has spread far beyond wealthy countries. China and India — the world's two most populous countries — now have fertility rates below the roughly 2.1-births-per-woman replacement level, the Census report says. Bangladesh, Mexico and Vietnam are among the most populous countries to fall below replacement-level births since 2013. Zoom in: In many countries with low birth rates, the decline creates what the report calls a "fertility trap." Smaller younger generations follow larger older ones, accelerating the overall aging of a population and, in some places, eventual population decline. That means fewer potential workers and caregivers supporting growing older populations — putting pressure on pensions, health systems and long-term care. The intrigue: The U.S. ranked as the 48th-oldest country out of 227 in 2025, with 18.9% of its population age 65 or older. By 2060, the U.S. share of older adults is projected to climb to 23.4%, but its global aging rank is predicted to fall to 110th because other countries are aging much faster. Data: U.S. Census Bureau, International Database, 2023 , Axios calculations; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Zoom out: Europe remains the world's oldest region, but the biggest numerical shift in aging is elsewhere. Asia's 65+ population is projected to surge from 487 million to 1.24 billion from 2025 to 2060 — accounting for roughly two-thirds of the global increase. Africa remains by far the youngest region, but its older population is projected to more than quadruple from 60 million to 249 million — surpassing Europe's 214 million by 2060. Globally, the share of people 65+ is projected to nearly double from 10.5% to 19.6% by 2060. Yes, but: A nation's rising percentage of seniors isn't necessarily a catastrophe. Longer lives represent one of the great achievements of the past century: fewer deaths in infancy and midlife, and more people surviving into old age. Older people are less likely to commit crime and many can remain in the workforce, help fill labor shortages and contribute through caregiving and volunteering. Between the lines: The demographic shift could force societies to rethink old age as an economic asset rather than simply a cost, Census report contributor Andrew Scott said. He argues in the report that preventive health, longer working lives and age-friendly jobs could turn longer lifespans into healthier, more economically engaged years.

item.title: "Welcome to the AGI era," OpenAI says as GPT-6 Astra debuts
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 5.43
OpenAI on Thursday released GPT-6 Astra , which president Greg Brockman called a "generational leap" and said could eventually be seen as the arrival of artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Why it matters: Astra pushes AI agents closer to doing complex professional work on their own — while also raising questions about how safely they can be deployed. Driving the news: Brockman says he personally believes OpenAI has reached AGI, while leaving users to decide whether Astra meets that definition. "I think it might be about this model," Brockman said in a briefing with reporters about whether Astra could mark the arrival of AGI. He ended the briefing by saying: "Welcome to the AGI era." Between the lines: OpenAI said that Astra was built on its largest-ever training run, using more than 100,000 GPUs at its Stargate site in Texas. The company also said this is its first model to use other models in a significant role in supervising Astra's training. GPT-6 Astra will first be available to a limited set of organizations in OpenAI's Daybreak Access program and will be available "in the coming days" for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise customers and API developers. Catch-up quick: OpenAI said earlier this week that Astra would be released soon, but that its most powerful cybersecurity capabilities would remain limited to a small group of trusted testers. Astra is the first model OpenAI has designated as reaching its "critical" cybersecurity threshold under its preparedness framework — meaning it can potentially find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities across well-protected systems without step-by-step human guidance. OpenAI previously slowed Astra's release to add safety testing after determining that its cyber capabilities could reach the critical threshold. Zoom in: Astra is designed to work directly inside software, rather than just recommending what a person should do next. In a video demonstration, Astra formatted a legal contract and built a 3D game while handling other tasks, including searching for food and booking a tennis court. OpenAI says Astra can lay out a printed circuit board in KiCad, build a 3D city scene in Unity, create an animated automobile transmission in FreeCAD and Blender, and fill out a tax-return draft from a W-2. In scientific work, the model helped improve a mathematical result on gaps between prime numbers and set new marks on several biology, chemistry, medical and physics evaluations. Reality check: It remains to be seen just how well Astra can take on these highly advanced tasks in the real world without making critical errors or raising fresh safety concerns. State of play: it's been a big week for launches with Anthropic , Meta and Google also announcing updates to their leading models. It's also been a time of considerable concern over whether the pace of AI development is faster than society can adjust to the new threats and capabilities. Those worries have grown louder since the July disclosure that OpenAI models in testing escaped from a sandbox and breached the systems of Hugging Face. "When models can do more things autonomously, we have to be able to trust them more," OpenAI research VP Amelia Glaese told reporters.
