"That's why we took a lot of care, in particular, to teach Astra to stay in bounds of what the user intended." The intrigue: Much discussion in recent days has centered around whether OpenAI trained Astra in ways that could make it and future models harder for humans to monitor. OpenAI acknowledged that Astra was harder to monitor in evaluations designed to test whether it could evade oversight. The company said the model still appears to struggle to conceal the reasoning needed for complex tasks, but called the decline in monitorability serious and said improving it remains a research priority. "We will need to strengthen our ability to to monitor these models either via extending chain-of-thought monitoring, integrating other ideas like activation monitoring, or finding more specific ways to get the models to be more verbose in their chain of thought," OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters. This story is developing.

item.title: Widespread AI outage underway
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 5.22
OpenAI's ChatGPT , Anthropic's Claude, and xAI's Grok are all down Thursday morning, according to the outage company Downdetector. Why it matters: Outages are common, but it's unusual for all three to go down at once, especially as the world increasingly relies on AI models. There have also been reported issues with Google's Gemini, but the company has not issued a confirmed outage notice. Driving the news: Anthropic's Claude dashboard is experiencing outages across Opus 4.8 and Opus 5, and says all other models "have recovered to baseline error rate." ChatGPT and Codex are actively experiencing "elevated errors," according to OpenAI's dashboard. Grok is "experiencing issues," according to xAI, which says it's working on the problem. The intrigue: Microsoft Azure, which provides cloud services for all three models, is also experiencing outages, and some tech outlets have suggested Microsoft's problem may be contributing to the AI model outages. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Brain implants fuel U.S.-China bioscience rivalry
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 4.26
Brain implants like those being developed by Elon Musk's Neuralink are becoming the latest friction point in the intensifying U.S.-China rivalry in the life sciences. Why it matters: The devices are bringing new hope to patients with strokes, Parkinson's disease and other neurological conditions. And tech billionaires have fueled advances by pouring billions into biotech startups focused on linking the brain with computers. But a new national security analysis says U.S. development efforts are being overtaken by Beijing's full-court press around manufacturing, data and commercialization. The consequences could extend beyond health care, affecting U.S. military capabilities and the ability to train the next generation of AI models, according to the analysis. The report was produced by the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology, which was created by Congress to review how biotechnology can affect national security. State of play: Brain-computer interfaces, or BCIs, are going mainstream. Companies like Neuralink, Precision Neuroscience, Paradromics and Synchron are testing new applications, like helping to restore communication for people who have lost the ability to speak. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are reducing the time it takes to calibrate a device to a patient's brain signals and use them for functions like controlling a prosthetic part. And China leveled up the field this spring, when its National Medical Products Administration issued what's thought to be the world's first commercial approval of a BCI designed to revive hand movement in people with spinal cord injuries. The approval was part of a strategy that designated BCIs as a national "future industry," alongside quantum computing and 6G wireless communications systems. The commission analysis says regulatory bottlenecks and funding concerns are drying up the U.S. pipeline for BCIs and shifting the playing field in China's favor, noting that new treatments for neurological conditions take an average of more than 11 years to reach approval. It calls for the Food and Drug Administration to develop a clearer pathway for bringing implants to market, and for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to come up with a way to pay for devices once they're through regulatory approvals. "China is moving strategic technologies like BCI faster than the United States can," Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.), the chair of the national security commission, tells Axios. "Our government needs a coordinated biotechnology strategy to promote U.S. innovation and commercialization of what promises to be a truly revolutionary platform technology for health and national security." Between the lines: BCIs are another example of how technology is outpacing regulation — and posing thorny ethical and privacy issues. There's the basic question of who controls the device and data, and whether privacy laws like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act even apply. Giving patients more control over their data may require new laws or regulations that could limit developers' ability to improve algorithms that decode brain signals, the Government Accountability Office has noted . But more consumer autonomy could provide safeguards that extend beyond medical settings and protect against data being accessed to make insurance or workplace decisions, or to study how people subconsciously respond to advertising or other messages. China currently has no neural-data-specific privacy or security regulations, per the commission analysis. Reality check: Brain implants remain a work in progress. Many fail within their first year, and experts say manufacturing improvements like new materials, coatings and batteries could address signal degradation and extend power life. It's also difficult to recruit patients for clinical trials who have profound disabilities but still are healthy enough to withstand brain surgery. What we're watching: Whether brain implants are included in the Trump administration's RAPID program — a joint effort between FDA and CMS to expedite Medicare coverage of certain "breakthrough" devices. Longer term, BCIs could be adapted for nonmedical purposes, like controlling swarms of drones through operators' thoughts.

item.title: Historic NYT v. OpenAI copyright battle heats up
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 4.18
A landmark copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 moved into a critical new phase Friday, as all three parties presented their official arguments to a judge, with hopes of a favorable ruling ahead of a possible trial. Why it matters: A ruling in favor of the Times could wreak havoc on the lucrative business models underpinning the AI industry. A ruling in favor of OpenAI and Microsoft would serve as a massive blow to the publishing industry, potentially undermining its ability to control and monetize how content is scraped and used by AI giants. Zoom in: In its motion for summary judgment, the Times argued OpenAI and Microsoft copied its works at scale to build commercial substitutes, which it believes violates the law. OpenAI argued existing copyright laws and legal precedents allow tech giants to scrape publicly available works to train their large language models, and that reported facts are not protected by copyright law. It cited studies that suggest outputs to queries via ChatGPT do not create commercial substitutes of the Times' work. Microsoft made similar claims for its Copilot AI product. How it works: In its filing, OpenAI cites two recent California federal court decisions, Kadrey v. Meta and Bartz v. Anthropic, which found using copyrighted works to train AI models constituted as "fair use" in both of those cases because the training was considered transformative. The Times doesn't dispute those findings, but says those cases are different and can't be applied to this suit because those plaintiffs didn't show that AI outputs competed with their products, creating market substitutions for their journalism. The Times also argues that the case, which it filed in a New York federal court, should be evaluated against binding copyright precedents established by higher courts — the Supreme Court and the Second Circuit — rather than those recent lower court rulings. Zoom out: Around the world, the case is being closely watched as a groundbreaking legal precedent that could shape the future of the AI industry. This is especially true for the Trump administration, which has publicly tied its national security and economic goals to the development of AI infrastructure. On Thursday, the Justice Department filed a brief supporting OpenAI in the case, arguing training large language models from millions of digital works delivers a transformative public benefit that offsets any competitive harm to the publishing industry. What to watch: District Judge Sidney Stein is expected to rule in the coming months whether the case, or key portions of it, should move to trial next year. Disclosure: Axios and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement that allows OpenAI to access part of Axios' story archives while helping fund the launch of Axios into several local cities and providing some AI tools. Axios has editorial independence.

item.title: America's jobs scare recedes
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.87
The labor market looks considerably healthier than it did at the start of the summer. Why it matters: Friday morning's jobs report recast the last two months as a period of modest job growth rather than of outright deterioration, capped by a gain last month that was more than triple what economists expected. The labor market is weathering the Iran conflict and an AI-driven transformation of the economy with surprisingly little damage, at least for now. For the Federal Reserve, the report puts inflation even more squarely in focus — with less evidence that the labor market is too fragile to hold up in the event of higher interest rates. What they're saying: "August turned the heat back up on the job market," Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao wrote Friday morning. But Zhao noted that "the data has swung hard from month to month, and revisions keep rewriting what we thought we knew, so the underlying trend is tough to read." Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Driving the news: Employers added a surprisingly strong 162,000 jobs in August, the biggest gain since March. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.1%. Paired with positive revisions to June and July numbers, the release lifts three-month average job gains to 71,000, from just 20,000. June and July payrolls were revised up by a combined 55,000, a revision that flipped July from a 23,000-job loss to a 21,000-job gain . Between the lines: What looked like a labor market shedding jobs this summer now looks like one that slowed but kept expanding. August's headline was boosted by 42,000 jobs added in local government education, which largely reversed July's decline. That suggests some of the summer's apparent weakness — and August's subsequent rebound — reflected seasonal volatility rather than a sudden shift in labor demand. Zoom in: Bars and restaurants added 59,000 jobs in August, a surprising result considering that the World Cup ended in July and that it seemed plausible there would be a falloff in the sector's employment. Manufacturing added another 16,000 jobs, continuing an upward trend in employment that started late last year. The jobs contraction in the information sector — which includes tech infrastructure, publishing and media jobs — deepened, shedding 23,000 jobs in August and 115,000 over the past year. By the numbers: The unemployment rate held at 4.1% (though the unrounded rate edged up to 4.14% from 4.09%). The details of the household survey were promising. The labor force participation rate rebounded to 61.6%, reversing some of a steep two-month slide in which nearly 1 million people had exited the workforce. Still, participation remains 0.7 point below a year ago. The share of prime-age Americans — those aged between 25 and 54 — with a job held at 80.4% in August, still below its recent high of 80.8% in May. What to watch: August may help clarify whether the recent hiring slowdown reflected fewer workers available or less appetite among employers to hire. About 700,000 people entered the labor force last month and most found work, suggesting that employers were able to absorb a sudden influx of workers. That follows a stretch when a shrinking labor force kept unemployment low, obscuring whether weak hiring reflected limited worker supply or weak labor demand. The risk of a sharp labor market downturn looks considerably smaller than it did a month ago. Still unresolved is whether hiring is accelerating again or simply settling into a slower — though still solid — equilibrium. The solid numbers add ammunition for those Fed officials who see an urgent need to raise interest rates to bring inflation down. The big picture: With the labor market hovering at something near full employment but inflation in its sixth year of exceeding the Fed's 2% target, the decision of whether to raise interest rates in less than two weeks comes down to two key August inflation indicators due out next week. The best that can be said of the robust jobs report is that it affirms the preexisting view of the central bank's leaders that the big question now is around inflation. Nothing in the report would act as a caution flag for those who might seek a rate hike, and indeed the data supports the idea that the job market could even be reaccelerating. "August payrolls were strong across the board, including in cyclical sectors like construction and manufacturing," Sonu Varghese, global macro strategist at Carson Group, wrote in a note. "Add in elevated inflation, and the Fed looks well offsides against an economy that's running hot." Yes, but: The jobs report has often been the most important monthly economic data release for parsing what the Fed will do next. Not now. The August numbers don't so much turn the overall economic narrative as affirm chairman Kevin Warsh's statement in a speech last week that "I believe the labor markets are consistent with full employment." What's next: Next week's releases of the August Producer Price Index on Thursday and the Consumer Price Index on Friday have now taken on greater importance for interest rate decisions. Economists can, by combining elements of the two, come up with a quite accurate estimate of where the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, will land when it is released Sept. 30. The bottom line: The jobs numbers bolstered the case for a rate hike, but next week's inflation numbers are more likely to settle the decision one way or the other.

item.title: AI models are becoming unknowable
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.81
AI models may be getting safer while also getting harder to monitor. Which side of that seesaw prevails could determine whether AI is scaled safely or ruins civilization as we know it. Why it matters: Right now both options are running full steam and no one knows who's in charge of making sure the right one wins. State of play: OpenAI on Thursday released GPT-6 Astra , which president Greg Brockman said could eventually be seen as the start of artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Astra performs better, but it's also better at avoiding monitoring, meaning it could be harder to know what it's thinking or doing. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman separately told Axios this week that models are becoming "superhuman" in some capabilities and that "we are just sailing in unknown waters." Between the lines: The top leaders of AI companies are sounding the alarm on their own technology just as it gets harder to understand a model's actions. OpenAI, Anthropic and more than 100 other companies warned that time is running out to prepare for AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure. Altman told Axios that Congress is struggling to figure out how to regulate such a fast moving technology. "We've been talking to some external organizations about potential concrete standards we could put in place" OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters, adding that OpenAI has also been working to strengthen its own processes. Threat level: While awaiting regulation, AI models are becoming unknowable. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said on a call with reporters that it would continue to get harder to monitor the thoughts of AI models over time. The Information reported this week that the latest OpenAI model used a new technique to boost its performance that may have also made its thoughts less transparent (OpenAI disputes that reporting.) In an analysis of a cyber incident in which an OpenAI model broke into the Hugging Face AI library to get the answers to a benchmark test, one researcher said AI agents generate so much activity that humans can't realistically monitor them without the use of more AI . What they're saying: "This is an even bigger deal than Hugging Face," Sydney Von Arx, an AI Safety researcher and founder of the nonprofit Nightingale told Axios regarding lack of insight into model reasoning. The concern is that, over time, a model's thinking could happen in a hidden layer, which means it could do bad stuff without us knowing. OpenAI says this is not the case with Astra: the model doesn't write out its reasoning as often as prior models do, but that was not done intentionally. Regardless, if models do less thinking out loud some researchers worry their behavior will be harder to monitor. The bottom line: AI is getting sneakier and even the executives driving its growth are asking for help monitoring the risks.

item.title: Altman raises stakes on government scrutiny as AI advances
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.73
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called the Trump administration's voluntary review of the company's forthcoming Astra model a "productive process" and said that closer engagement with government officials around the world will matter more as AI capabilities advance. Why it matters: OpenAI is close to releasing Astra, the first model designated at its "critical" cyber capability level that the company says requires stronger safeguards during development and before release. The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release the framework. That leaves much of the government's approach opaque to the public and companies outside the process, even as leading labs participate and more powerful models are released. Altman, in an interview with Axios, confirmed the administration reviewed Astra and noted the process is voluntary : "But we of course did it." "As these models get to a quite significant level of capability, I think the importance of really doing this, closely engaging with the safety institutes in the U.S., the U.K. and elsewhere in the world, will become more important." Altman called Astra "a significant step forward." Context: Altman flew to the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Wednesday to speak with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick before an audience of commerce and technology ministers, who over two days heard the U.S. pitch on lead the world in AI. During a fireside chat with Lutnick at the summit lunch, Altman said he sees OpenAI as "the pragmatic centrists … We think people need to be at the center of the economy and society and global decision-making, and that people should run the future, not AI." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, talking with Lutnick at the summit breakfast, warned against fear-driven AI messaging. "The worst outcome," he told the foreign leader, "is that you don't take advantage of it [AI], that you are left behind." Huang's message prompted nods from many of the ministers in the room. Altman, speaking with Axios, called for a "realistic" and "accurate" approach. "I think doomerism — for the sake of trying to have more power, control or enforce a worldview — is really bad," he said. "I think blind optimism without an acknowledgment of the risks is also bad." Between the lines: OpenAI and Anthropic have faced criticism that their support for some AI regulation could advantage the leading labs and make it harder for smaller competitors to keep up. The big picture: Altman said he expected Congress to establish a "basic framework" for advanced AI after he first testified before lawmakers in 2023, but that hasn't happened. "I thought at that time that Congress was going to do something," Altman told Axios. He said the inaction is likely due to the pace of the technology: "People have a hard time knowing how to regulate the right things and not slow down innovation," adding that "it appears to be very hard to get Congress to do big things." What's next: Expect OpenAI to continue releasing its models as nations grapple with safety questions. "Take our word for it that we have much, much, much more capable models coming soon, and try to think about what all the impacts of that on society could be and then need to get that right," Altman said.

item.title: EU tech chief: AI guardrails inevitable for U.S.
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.33
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — The Trump administration used this week's G20 innovation summit to draw a bright line between U.S. and European approaches to AI regulation. The bloc's top tech official says the U.S. is ending up with many of the same guardrails anyway. Why it matters: The U.S. is urging countries to avoid Europe's sweeping approach to AI regulation, but the fight is shifting to which guardrails advanced AI needs and how governments put them in place. What they're saying: European Commission tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Axios that the two sides often end up addressing the same safety concerns, even if U.S. safeguards are starting to emerge through state laws and court cases rather than something broad like the EU AI Act. "We see when it comes to technologies that in the USA the culture is different. So often it's coming via court cases, but often very similar things anyway, very similar concerns." "I don't see that this is so like black and white," Virkkunen said. ChatGPT is officially facing strict rules under the Digital Services Act, for instance, and Virkkunen said it's important for the EU to simplify the bloc's rules and make the region "easier, simpler, faster" for businesses. The big picture: The U.S. hasn't adopted sweeping federal AI rules, but Washington is still shaping how companies develop and deploy advanced models through executive actions, voluntary frameworks, national security restrictions and other policy. Meanwhile, states are moving ahead with varying degrees of AI regulation, and product changes are being forced on companies through lawsuits. Zoom in: The EU is working on a framework for pre-deployment testing and trusted partner access, Virkkunen noted, another area where the EU is working through similar AI policy questions facing the U.S. "So in [the] European Union, we are also working for that blueprint, and we are continuing to discuss also under G7, especially with our partners, how we should work on this topic." The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release this framework. OpenAI's Sam Altman confirmed this week to Axios that the administration reviewed its Astra model and noted the process is voluntary: "But we of course did it." Industry leaders at the G20 innovation summit knocked the EU approach to regulation in remarks before Virkkunen as well as representatives from Germany, France and Italy. In response to White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios' question about what foreign governments should and should not do, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said an approach that's "relatively free of regulation" is the way to go. It's "pretty straightforward," Musk said. "You have to have an environment that's relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal." "In the EU, for example, we find that the regulation level is extraordinarily high, and things are generally default illegal, and this inhibits progress with new technologies. It slows it down." The bottom line: As AI has grown more powerful, Washington has increasingly gotten involved with model releases.

item.title: U.S. military reviewing deadly strike on Iranian wedding
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.28
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) is conducting an internal review of a civilian casualty incident at a wedding during the strikes in Iran on Tuesday, U.S. officials say. Why it matters: While it still hasn't been confirmed that the incident was caused by the U.S. strike , it is one of the more significant civilian casualty incidents since the war began six months ago. The most significant civilian casualty incident happened on the first day of the war when a U.S. strike hit a school, killing 150 people, most of them children. The U.S. military investigation into that incident is expected to be finalized soon, according to a U.S. official. Driving the news: According to the Iranian Red Crescent, a humanitarian network, five people were killed and 67 wounded in the blast that hit the home where the wedding was happening. Iranian officials accused the U.S. of striking the building and killing civilians. On Wednesday, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper ordered an internal review of the strike, U.S. officials said. "We're aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said. What they're saying: "We're investigating it because obviously we care," Vice President JD Vance said Thursday during a White House press briefing. "We want to know, and if we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran. When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them. So we're investigating it very fully." Behind the scenes: U.S. officials said the strike in the area targeted a communication tower used for both civilian and military communications. As part of the preliminary investigation, CENTCOM is reviewing footage from drones that monitored the area during the strike and the procedures used to identify the target, U.S. officials said. A U.S. official said that in addition to checking whether munitions fired by the U.S. hit the wedding, the investigation will also look at the possibility that an errant Iranian munition fell near the home.

item.title: Axios interview: Altman sees revenge of "idea guy"
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.27
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says this era is bringing the revenge of the "idea guy" — the once-annoying aspiring entrepreneur burbling about their brainstorm with no technical chops to pull it off. Altman says it would be like saying: "I have a great idea for a song. I just need that guy with the guitar to make it for me." "It really did strike me as ridiculous," Altman told me in Chapel Hill, N.C. "But now we're watching a whole generation of people iterate on ideas faster than they ever could. The economics have been reset for what it means to make a new small business or large business." Why it matters: Polls show most Americans think the risks of AI outweigh the benefits , with data-center rage as a bipartisan bonfire in the midterms. Altman — who's trying to sell AI into a massive backlash — wants to remind Americans that amid all the real risks , AI can equal opportunity. "This is gonna be the best time in the world to do a startup," Altman said recently . Reality check: These new tools are great for idea people. But most people are doers, not dreamers, and don't feel they have the time or AI skills to spin up a startup in their spare time. Our experience is that AI is a real unlock for a very small percentage of people who are idea generators or problem solvers, and in a position to put that into action. By the numbers: An American startup boom ignited during COVID and continued through this summer . Filings of new-business applications have continued to set records in the chatbot era. The number of new U.S. businesses formed in the first half of this year, over 3 million, is the most for a January-June stretch in Census Bureau data going back to 2005. The backstory: I first heard Altman's "idea guy" riff last spring , when he was talking onstage with Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, who asked how traits of successful founders were changing in this era. "We would make fun of these [idea] people," Altman said. "They weren't that successful. And it was kind of always personally annoying to me. All of a sudden it's like the revenge of the idea guys." "For a long time, the most important ingredient ... in a founding team was technical talent, and that's still very important. But now people who just really deeply understand their users and can't code at all, I want to fund those people. And that's a big turnaround." That stuck in my mind. So when I sat down with Altman, 41, last week at the Carolina Inn in a bilateral meeting room during the G20 Innovation Ministerial, I asked him how that notion could be useful for today's AI users, or for people who should be wielding AI but are skeptics. With GPT-6 Astra , OpenAI's powerful new model, Altman said, "you can start and run a small business effectively. ... It's like anyone who wants to have a company now has genius-level employees in every area of expertise." Zoom in: AI makes many ideas monetizable that never would have penciled out in the past. "I met this guy recently who had used [GPT-]5.6 to make a piece of software that he had sold to 50 people for, like, $500 a month ... He was so happy." "This would have cost you millions of dollars if you had to pay for software engineers," Altman told me. "All of a sudden you had an idea, you had this tiny corner of this tiny industry, there's one particular kind of task, and you were able to get software written for it. And of course people will pay for that." "With the new model [Astra], someone made a computer game ... probably only fun or funny to people that work at OpenAI. There is real economic value in this to a few thousand people. The economics of making a full computer game for a few thousand people never possibly made sense before. And now they do." The bottom line: "Whether it's a little thing to make your own life more convenient or a big thing that can create a business that adds huge value to other people," Altman said, "the space of viability has increased dramatically." Disclosure: Axios and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement that allows OpenAI to access part of Axios' story archives while helping fund the launch of Axios into four local cities and providing some AI tools. Axios has editorial independence.

item.title: The body image battle is real in 2026, but the bodies may not be
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.13
A societal spotlight on extreme thinness is stripping body diversity from screens, just as fashion magazines did in the early aughts, mental health experts tell Axios. The big picture: Fake content creators are introducing unattainable, AI-generated body images that prey on human nature and exacerbate the struggle for many to reach self-acceptance for their bodies. When shrunken celebrities "become the ideal ... because of their status, then the virtual influencers are going to be emulating that," Katy Bruchmann, who leads Santa Clara University's Social Cognition and Comparison Lab, says. "Then, the more really thin, super beautiful virtual influencers you have, the target changes for all the real people again. It's a really scary cycle." Driving the news: Some are posing as influencers selling wellness products or services, while others are sharing body transitions or beauty advice. Axios reviewed dozens of social media posts that include clear AI-generated body transformations or fitness influencers , while online sleuths have uncovered content that appears fake. Zoom in: Some were labeled as AI. Many were not. But research from Brooke Bennett, the director of the Body image, Eating, Access, and Media Lab at the University of Clemson, and her colleagues found that it essentially doesn't matter. Even when people know the image they're viewing is AI, it still hurts their body satisfaction. "I think it's this expectation management piece," Bennett says. "We might... say, 'OK, I know that person's AI, but that doesn't mean that everyone else knows, and people are going to expect me to look like that too.'" Zoom out: The striving for thinness has been fueled by a GLP-1 boom and pushed to extremes with dangerous internet trends. While "SkinnyTok" was banned by TikTok, the messages are still slipping through. Coupled with images of flawless women wearing a size 00, social media can be a body image minefield. "In the clinical space, we're seeing patients coming in really struggling to deal with some of this AI and ... social media pressures in general," Bennett says. Follow the money: Tech and media companies have flooded the zone with a host of cyber stars that are accessible and low-cost . "You can hire an AI influencer for cheap, and they can be in Brazil tonight selling a beverage, and in Tokyo tomorrow selling a T-shirt," Bruchmann says. Our thought bubble: Beyond the completely virtual vixens, it's easier than ever to edit images using AI. I tried it myself, asking ChatGPT to slim me down. I still looked like myself, with no immediate signs that the photo had been altered, like garbled text or extra fingers. The fine print : When organic AI content is posted to Meta products, users can opt in to identify it, or Meta's system may. TikTok "encourage[s]" creators to label content generated or significantly edited by AI. The platform may also label it. But the rules aren't foolproof, and likely AI-generated content still appears unlabeled. Reality check: Zoë Bisbing, founding director of Body-Positive Therapy NYC, tells Axios that body diversity (yes, real bodies) is still online. "It's true — the thin ideal is getting thinner," she says. "At the same time, it's not hard to find size diversity on the street, at the beach and [in] your algorithm." Start simple by searching terms like body acceptance, body positive or body liberation, she says. Go deeper: TikTok glorifies weight loss among teens, young adults: Study

item.title: A record 47% want stronger unions. Labor's challenge is turning support into power.
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.05
For only the second time in a quarter century, a majority of Republicans — 52% — approve of labor unions , according to a new Gallup poll . Why it matters: Despite Americans' rising approval , union membership remains near a modern low. Congress has repeatedly blocked labor's biggest priorities, and House Republicans are now investigating unions, even as their own voters approve of them. Republicans' warmer feelings toward unions don't translate into wanting them to wield more power: 49% of Republicans want unions to have less influence, compared with just 19% who want them to have more. Data: Gallup Poll Social Series; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios By the numbers: Overall, 71% of Americans approved of unions, tying the 2022 level. Gallup last recorded higher approval in 1959 at 73%. Approval stands at 89% among Democrats, 70% among independents and 52% among Republicans. The only other time since 2001 that Gallup found majority Republican approval was in 2022. A record 47% of Americans want unions to have more influence, more than double the 23% who want less influence. Another 26% want their influence to remain the same. The big picture: The latest numbers mark a reversal from the Great Recession. In 2009, union approval bottomed out at 48%, and 42% of Americans wanted unions to have less influence while just 25% wanted them to have more. Reality check: Americans are embracing unions at a time when few workers belong to one. Just 11% of U.S. workers — 16.5 million — were represented by unions in 2025, compared with 23% and 20.5 million workers in 1983, the first year of comparable data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics . The most recent year included union representation for less than 7% of private-sector workers. State of play: Workers have been trying to make up for lost time. Union election petitions filed with the National Labor Relations Board more than doubled from 2021 to 3,286 in 2024. The agency received 2,633 election petitions last year , down from the prior year's peak but still well above earlier years. Americans are skeptical that today's goodwill will translate into greater strength. Just 27% expect unions to become stronger, while 39% expect them to weaken and 29% expect little change, according to the Gallup polling. Data: Gallup Poll Social Series; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Zoom in: Organized labor has repeatedly failed to turn Democratic control of Washington into its biggest legislative prize: rewriting federal law to make it easier for workers to join unions and to win contracts. The Employee Free Choice Act, a signature priority at the start of the Obama administration, would have made it easier for workers to unionize when a majority of workers signed cards. Despite overwhelming Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, it never became law. In 2021, the House passed the Protecting the Right to Organize Act, the next sweeping attempt to rewrite federal labor law, with five Republicans joining Democrats. But it stalled in the Senate where Republicans and even Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly, Mark Warner and Kyrsten Sinema withheld their support. Between the lines: President Biden leaned on executive action and appointments, creating a task force to promote organizing and pushing the NLRB to favor unionizing workers. In 2023, he became the first president to join striking workers on a picket line, standing with autoworkers in Michigan. The environment has swung sharply. President Trump has used executive orders to remove collective bargaining rights for broad swaths of the federal workforce and to fire the labor board's pro-union general counsel and a Democratic board member. The latest: House Republicans have also intensified scrutiny of union leadership, launching investigations into the United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, the American Federation of Teachers and three railroad unions, demanding records about political activity. The bottom line: Labor has won back popularity it lost during decades of decline, but its harder fight is turning that goodwill into bargaining power and growing its membership. The fine print: Gallup surveyed 1,200 U.S. adults by cellphone and landline Aug. 3–24. The overall margin of error is 4 percentage points.

item.title: Not so fast on rate hikes, some Fed officials say
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.04
After Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh's speech in Jackson Hole , the markets penciled in an interest rate hike for the central bank's mid-September meeting. Comments from two influential officials now throw those expectations into question. The big picture: With August jobs and inflation data due out before a policy meeting in two weeks, the decision of whether to tighten policy appears to be on a knife-edge. A meaningful contingent of Fed leadership is eager to raise interest rates to address stubbornly high inflation, while another, as Fed governor Christopher Waller put it Thursday morning, channeling John Lennon , is willing to "give disinflation a chance." It's a close enough call that Warsh will likely be able to steer a decision whichever way he prefers. Driving the news: At a Reuters newsmaker event Thursday, Waller noted two consecutive months of improving inflation data. If it continues in August reports over the coming days, he said, "I would be inclined to support" holding rates steady. But if the incoming data shows "improvement has been fleeting," he is open to a rate hike, Waller added. On Wednesday, New York Fed president John Williams told CNBC that "I think we have to wait and see" whether an interest rate increase is needed. "There's no clear signs right now whether monetary policy is currently sufficient to make sure we bring inflation back to target in the next year or two, or whether you need to see further action to do that." State of play: Their comments come after Warsh said that the Fed "must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed," or else they "have work to do." That leaves room for a judgment call on whether that bar has been reached. Warsh has resisted hanging policy decisions on the fine details of each incoming data release, as Waller seems inclined to do. CME's FedWatch tool now puts the odds of a rate hike at the meeting concluding Sept. 16 as essentially a coin flip, whereas on Wednesday, the futures market-based odds favored an increase. Zoom in: The New York Fed president is vice chair of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee and has traditionally acted as part of a leadership troika, with the chairman and vice chair of the Board of Governors. Traditionally, governors like Waller are reluctant to dissent from policy decisions, though that norm has dissolved in the last couple of years. Three reserve bank presidents, meanwhile, dissented at the late July meeting favoring a rate hike, implying that Warsh will face internal disagreement — the "good family fight" he often speaks of — no matter which way he ultimately leans. Of note: Waller has offered none-too-subtle criticisms of Warsh's reticent communication style. Warsh has said he wants markets to react to "the ball" of incoming data, not "the ref," or how the Fed may react to it. On Thursday morning, Waller made his own addendum to that metaphor. "I view myself as a home plate umpire in baseball," he said . Both the pitcher and the batter "want to play the ball, but they cannot do that until they know the umpire's strike zone," which is essentially the umpire's reaction function. "If the ball goes here, it's a strike; if it goes there, it's a ball. The players don't expect the umpire to have a perfect strike zone — they just need a rough idea of its parameters and some guarantee that it won't change much on every pitch."

item.title: Alaska seeks oil revival while grappling with a warming future
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 2.55
EXIT GLACIER, Alaska — America's 49th state is a study in contrasts: Rapidly melting glaciers like this one attract tourists, while the oil industry underpinning its economy is getting a fresh boost from Washington after decades of decline. Why it matters: Few places put the causes and consequences of global warming in such proximity, making Alaska a vivid window into the world's reliance on fossil fuels as climate impacts mount. Driving the news: "Alaska is a powerhouse," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week in Anchorage at the state oil and gas trade group's annual conference, according to Alaska News Source. "I think you could have an incredible several years, several decades coming with just some common sense policies to set Alaskans free." State of play: Alaska has emerged as perhaps the Trump administration's biggest geographic focus for expanding U.S. oil and gas development, with the government pushing new leasing , easier permitting , Arctic drilling and a massive natural gas pipeline. A major new North Slope oil field started producing in May, and another is expected to begin producing in 2029 . Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) told Axios this moment is a "second wind" for the state's oil industry. The big picture: No offense to Texas, but everything is actually bigger in Alaska. It's more than double the size of Texas and has more coastline than all other states combined. It ranks near the top for both proven oil and gas reserves in the nation, and it has the largest icefield wholly contained in the U.S., the Harding Icefield, which feeds Exit Glacier. Reality check: Alaska's heyday as a top oil powerhouse is likely behind it. Its oil production has been declining since the late 1980s, and projects underway aren't expected to restore anything close to that. Friction point: Some of Washington's efforts are facing hurdles. The Interior Department's June lease sale in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, a vast wilderness home to polar bears, caribou and hundreds of bird species, generated little industry interest . A separate sale for new drilling in Cook Inlet near Anchorage received zero bids. An Interior Department spokesperson described the wildlife refuge auction as "a success for this frontier area," and pointed to a record-breaking March lease sale elsewhere in Alaska's North Slope. Zoom in: The roughly $50 billion effort to pipe natural gas 800 miles from the North Slope to the Kenai Peninsula for export to Asian markets is struggling to move forward. Wright called it his "number one" energy infrastructure priority earlier this year. But last week, he said: "I'm disappointed that I'm sitting here right now and we're not talking about shovels in the ground," Alaska News reported. Jason Bordoff, founding director of Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who recently visited Alaska's northernmost regions, called the economics of the project "terrible." Inside the room: Or more aptly: next to the glacier. Signs along the hiking trail at Exit Glacier tell visitors how much this glacier has retreated dating back to the late 1880s; the most recent sign is from 2010. Its retreat has accelerated in recent decades due to human-caused warming, according to Albin Wells, who researches the topic at the University of Zurich. The seven glaciers near the ski town of Girdwood are all likely to vanish or be vastly reduced within 75 years, Wells said. One of our guides near Girdwood, describing how dramatically the glaciers had changed during his lifetime, said he avoids the term "climate change" because of its polarizing politics. Axios' Amy Harder, on Aug. 16, standing at the most recent sign showing where the Exit Glacier, pictured in the foreground, reached in 2010. Photo courtesy of Amy Harder/Axios Between the lines: The changes go far beyond glaciers: Thawing permafrost and disappearing sea ice are destabilizing land and accelerating erosion along parts of Alaska's coast. Follow the money: One of the nation's fastest-warming states remains deeply reliant on oil and gas. Decades of oil wealth helped build the Alaska Permanent Fund, which now provides more unrestricted state revenue than current oil and gas revenues do — as well as an annual dividend for residents. What we're watching: With energy security demanding attention amid the ongoing Iran war, climate change may be on the back burner, Bordoff said, "but it is going to come back in a nonlinear way because of the impacts we're seeing." Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: A growing movement wants AI out of schools
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 2.38
America's two largest school districts both imposed sweeping AI bans this past week, hitting the brakes on a technology that's rapidly making its way into classrooms around the country. Why it matters: Research on AI's educational value is mixed. Some studies have found personalized AI tutors can improve learning, while other research has linked AI-assisted essay writing to weaker critical thinking. Driving the news: New York City's public school district blocked AI use for roughly 600,000 students in Pre-K through 8th grade, restricting it to specific uses for high school students. Hours later, Los Angeles Unified imposed a districtwide moratorium on AI use on school devices for the 2026-27 school year, following a separate screen-time crackdown. And Chicago school board candidates are lining up to sign a pledge demanding a three-year moratorium on generative AI in its schools. What they're saying: Nicki Petrossi, a mother and co-founder of the Tech-Safe Learning Coalition, tells Axios one parent called today's kids "the guinea pig generation," adding, "you won't find a parent who's not concerned about this." Another parent told her that their "five-year-old, who still believes in the Tooth Fairy, [is] being asked to interact with chatbots. What could go wrong?" Between the lines: Bans may be hard to enforce because AI is already embedded in classroom technology. Google's Gemini, for example, can appear when students search on school Chromebooks. The other side: Some educators warn sweeping bans could eliminate useful tools. "If you're working with students with special needs or English language [learning] students...there are a lot of benefits to using technology that allow us to augment the lessons," Janice Jackson, executive director of the Aspen Institute Education & Society Program and former Chicago Public Schools CEO, tells Axios. "We shouldn't throw that out." "The jury is still out on the quality of each policy, and that is not an indictment on any of these policies. It's more related to the fact that this is still very new," she says. By the numbers: Teachers are worried AI is becoming an easy out for students, according to a recent NPR/Ipsos poll . 55% say students mostly use it as a shortcut to avoid work, 54% say it makes critical thinking skills harder to build, and 57% say it makes it harder to gauge what students actually know. More than half say their school hasn't given them guidance on how to handle AI. The bottom line: "The ed tech industry has a reckoning coming," Brendan Bouffard, associate general counsel at Fairplay, adding that multiple states are considering strong legislative guardrails. "It's going to be good to see some real standards put in place to help make sure that these tools are being used safely and effectively for students, and that these tech companies are actually held accountable for what they're selling." Go deeper: Schools adopting AI could see benefits (and more work) - Axios Kansas City

item.title: Nepal observes national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.33
- Published Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period. While flags were flown at half mast, commemorations were scaled back as rescue teams continue to search for survivors. Candlelight vigils were planned for Monday evening. At least 1,287 people are known to have died after a flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through villages in a Himalayan valley along the border between Nepal and Tibet. Almost two weeks later, more than 5,000 people are still missing. Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency that there would be "no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas." Nepal's president, Ram Chandra Paudel, toured areas devastated by the floods on Monday, an aide told Reuters. The home ministry said that government offices, as well as missions abroad, would fly the national flag at half mast to mark the final day of the mourning period. Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the BBC that rescue efforts were "intensifying" in hydropower tunnels, with rescuers "continuously conducting search and rescue operations". Rescue operations were also continuing on the ground and by air, he told news agency Agence France-Presse. "We are making sure that no one is still stranded." Among the few places where rescuers still see a chance of finding survivors is in tunnels that form part of the region's hydropower stations, with hundreds of workers among the missing. Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said in an update on X that the operation meant facing "multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved." Four people have been rescued in recent days, three at hydropower stations or tunnels. On Saturday, a 64-year-old Nepali woman was pulled from her buried house on Saturday, more than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud partially buried her house in the Nuwakot district. She was discovered alive on the fourth floor of the building by Nepal's Armed Police Force and airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment. On Sunday rescue workers in China recovered twelve bodies in the Nepal-Tibet border, using excavators, shovels and ground penetrating radar at the site. At least 5,083 people are still missing in Nepal. On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.

item.title: Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.30
- Published Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has attacked energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia with dozens of drones and missiles, injuring 73 people, Saudi authorities say. Tuesday's attacks hit four south-western cities, causing fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that its forces would respond to the "dangerous escalation". The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi strikes on areas of north-western Yemen that they control. On Monday, they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of al-Hazm and killing at least 11 people. Twenty inmates are reportedly missing under the rubble. The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured. An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted. The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added. Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes". He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage". A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500. The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

item.title: Four Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.16
- Published Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France. Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said. The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight. One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen. CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said. The alarm went off at 05:48 (03:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms. He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed". They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added. Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects. The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered. The two paintings that are still missing are: - Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) - Jeune fille au puits (1886) And the two pieces that were recovered are: - Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895) - Coco Lisant (1905) "Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," the mayor told reporters at the museum. "It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," he said. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Last month, four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily. "Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," the local French mayor warned. Masson called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals".

item.title: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.05
- Published The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes. Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future. Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres. However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future. Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe. Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history. Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer. "Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. "However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI. Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it. He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples. "It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements. "That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients." Job losses 'overstated' In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade. "With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do." Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities. He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI. Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said. This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March. Big Boss Interview: Arm Holdings Rene Haas The CEO of chip design company Arm tells the BBC AI will help cure cancer, lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but says its rapid growth is being held up by a shortage of chips needed in data centres. There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres. He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space. "We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space." But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here. "I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those." As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London. But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

item.title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.84
- Published Grindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties. The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information. The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants. According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability. Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun. The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September. "While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing. The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027. 'Significant distress' The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws. It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users. People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices. Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent. She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised". Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data. The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users. It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers. Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies. It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices. The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community". "Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

item.title: Five killed as Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.39
Five killed as Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport Video footage from Miami shows an Amazon Air cargo plane overshoot the runway while attempting to land at the city's international airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five more. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft crashed just before 14:00 local time (19:00 GMT) after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The flight also hit several vehicles on the ground.

item.title: Asbestos 'nearly everywhere' after 9/11 - new documents reveal air-quality concerns
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.81
- Published Toxic air quality was being recorded in Manhattan soon after the 9/11 attacks even as officials played down health risks to the public, according to a trove of newly released files. Asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" tested near Ground Zero, where the World Trade Center towers collapsed in 2001, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," he said, announcing the release of 170,000 documents related to the attacks. Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have claimed more lives than the nearly 3,000 who died in the attacks, US health officials say. Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants after the Twin Towers collapsed. Speaking alongside Mamdani at Tuesday's news conference, TV host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart said the new files show the city knew by October 2001 - a month after the terrorist attacks - that the air in Manhattan was toxic. "So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically. The records show asbestos was found near Ground Zero for months after the attacks at the same time people were being advised it was safe to go there. The files, which include air-quality reports and communications among city officials, include October 2001 correspondence known as the "Harding Memo". In it, an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks. The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)". City officials also told citizens to clean up dust and debris with "wet mops and rags" despite the presence of asbestos, which is only supposed to be cleaned by licensed professionals, according to another memo documenting the concerns of congressman Jerry Nadler. The memo pointed to testimony from the city's top health official at the time saying a study had found "no elevated levels of asbestos in indoor air", but that tests showed dust had "low levels of asbestos in some samples". The memo, attributed to Ester Fuchs, a special adviser at the time to Mayor Michael Bloomberg, acknowledged "potential problems for City Hall". Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe. Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had". Tuesday's release of documents resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued after officials said they did not have the records. City officials found 68 boxes of documents last year. The pages of air quality reports and other records were released through an online portal timed for this Friday's 25th anniversary of the attacks. More documents are to be shared over the next year. Karen Klingon, who was involved in the 9/11 Health Watch lawsuit, told the BBC on Tuesday her brother lived five minutes away from Ground Zero. He developed asthma, was later diagnosed with cancer and died at 61 of a related brain tumor. "There's a lot of research, probably, that can be done about what was in the air, and the kind of illnesses that derived of those toxins that were in the air, like what happened to my brother," she said. "Hopefully it helps people that were sick know and in the future." Phil Alvarez, whose brother Luis Alvarez died of cancer in 2019 after exposure to Ground Zero toxins, told the BBC that people "continue to get sick every single day, continue to die".

item.title: Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.23
- Published Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of government figures. Most air attacks used to come at night but Russia's new tactic of striking Ukraine's capital during the day is causing huge disruption to schools and businesses. The round the clock attacks have forced people to head for shelter as many as 13 times a day, with air raid alerts lasting from a few minutes to nearly four and a half hours. Residents in Kyiv are struggling to adapt to this new reality, adding to existing stress and anxiety. The alerts force pupils to leave their classrooms and workers their offices and leave commuters struggling to get home as overland trains stop. This has forced the government to plan a new, two-tier warning system that allows people to carry on working, travelling and studying depending on the scale of the threat. There was a brief pause in attacks on Kyiv over the weekend while US envoys were in town for talks about trying to end the war. But analysis of figures from the state-owned app Kyiv digital shows that since the round-the-clock Russian attacks began at the end of August, air raid sirens have sounded across Kyiv's skies on average 10 times a day. In the seven days from Thursday 27 August, Kyiv endured 76 air raid alerts. The largest comparable number in 2022 was the week beginning 27 February when there were around 66 alerts. Absolute comparisons are not possible because data gathered in the first few days of the invasion was sometimes incomplete. But the trend shown by the numbers is clear. From the BBC's office, we hear the near constant rumble of air defences and drone explosions. The more frequent Russian strikes are exacerbated by a second development, the use of newer and faster attack drones powered by jet engines. Some of these fly almost 370 mph (595 km/h), three times as fast the older Shahed drones driven by propellers, and are harder to shoot down. Ukraine's air force says Russia launched 2,800 fast drones in August, almost twice as many as in July. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has held an emergency meeting with ministers and commanders to work out how to produce new high-speed missiles that can intercept the faster Russian drones. "You can all see that the Russians have changed the tactics of their strikes against Ukraine and, since August, have been terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely," the president said. Diplomats say the risk is that Russia will manufacture its fast attack drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop a new generation of interceptors. Some military sources say this threat could become far greater than Russia's ballistic missiles which have largely overcome Ukraine's depleted Patriot defences. Ukraine uses warplanes, anti-aircraft guns and shoulder-launched missiles to try to bring down the jet-powered drones. But Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said only about 60 percent of the drones were being shot down and they needed new interceptors to tackle the threat. "The task now is to make them faster and equip them with specialised guidance systems so that they can shoot down jet-powered UAVs, the jet-powered Shaheds," he said. "The key issue really is having guidance systems, because that is one of the crucial elements. It is not enough for the interceptor simply to fly fast — it has to hit the target. That is very important." Analysts say Russia's aim is not only to weaken Kyiv's morale but also damage Ukraine's economy by targeting businesses and warehouses. The alerts are also disrupting the start of the new academic year and forcing school children to leave their classrooms throughout the day. When another air raid began, some students at the Drahomanov Ukrainian State University in central Kyiv headed underground; others stayed chatting on the street, such is the normality of these alerts. Diana, a student teacher, said she did not sleep well at night and her schedule was disrupted during the day. "Sometimes it is hard because most of the day I need to go to safe places, like the metro or somewhere underground," she said. "It's a terrible time, but thank God we are alive. We go day by day." Ihor, studying to become a chemistry teacher, said he was used to the alerts after many years of war but life was still hard. "We are annoyed by the sirens because they are constant," he said. "It destroys the quality of our education… We cannot study normally." After a drone attack in a residential part of central Kyiv, students from a nearby school were evacuated for fear of explosions or a secondary, so-called "double-tap" attack. Sophia, 17, told us it was very sad but this is what life was like now. "It's a little bit scary to live here in Kyiv," she said. "It's very difficult." The interview was then interrupted by another siren. "We need to go," she said. "It is very dangerous for you to stand in the streets. Maybe we can have a second detonation." The constant air raids are a huge problem for businesses, many of which have to shut their doors every time a siren wails. We saw crowds of shop workers from Kyiv's biggest department store hanging around the streets during an alert, forced to leave their work place but not fearful enough to seek shelter. There is also disruption to public transport. Some metro trains have to stop during an alert because they travel overground across the Dnipro river that bisects the city. This causes chaos for commuters who are forced to get on replacement buses. To minimise this disruption, the government has agreed a new air-raid warning system with two different threat levels. A yellow warning to indicate a drone attack with less threat and fewer restrictions on work and travel. A red warning to indicate a more dangerous missile attack with more severe constraints on activity. As ever, Ukraine is adapting to a yet another new threat. But the fear is that Russia's constant attacks now may leave the country and its capital less prepared for what many expect to be a tough winter as Russia shifts its attack back to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

item.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.20
- Published Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities. "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details. Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance. The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful".
