item.title: Vintage photos show how the role of women in the workforce has evolved in the last 100 years
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.74
From factory floors to corner offices, women's roles in the workplace have undergone many reinventions over the past century. By the 1920s, decades of industrialization had drawn growing numbers of women into the workforce. Then, as men were sent off to war, more women entered the wartime effort in factories and other professions previously dominated by men. Women's equality movements throughout the 1960s and 1970s gave working women more opportunities, and in recent years, the gap between men and women in the workforce has been closing, according to data released by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. These vintage photos show how women's roles in the workforce have evolved over the last 100 years. In the wake of the Industrial Revolution, more women than ever began to leave the household and go out to work. Jobs commonly held by women included postal clerks, who sorted letters and packages. While it wasn't uncommon for women to work in post offices, very few women actually delivered mail. The US Postal Service reported that in 1920, only 5% of the nation's 943 village carriers were women. As local postal delivery was gradually phased out in favor of larger city delivery, most of the remaining women village carriers either resigned or were transferred to clerk positions. Many women also began working in factories. The US Department of Labor reported that in 1920, women made up about 20% of the labor force, an increase from previous generations. Many of them were involved in the production and manufacturing of clothing, food products, and tobacco products. Women of color, on the other hand, were largely employed in agriculture and domestic service work for much of the early 20th century. During World War I, women held occupations in domestic and personal service, clerical occupations, and factory work. Many women took typing courses to secure higher-paying jobs as secretaries or typists in clerical offices rather than working in factories. The Encyclopedia of Chicago reported that working conditions, wages, and hours in clerical work were seen as the best at the time. Clerical work attracted young, literate, mostly white women who would work as typists until they were married, only to be replaced by other young unmarried women when they left their jobs to raise their families. The government also began paying greater attention to women's working conditions. In 1920, Congress established the Women's Bureau. As the popularity of silent films began to rise, women also found work behind the scenes on movie sets. The Women Film Pioneers Project wrote that a 1923 edition of "Business Woman" published a list of 29 different jobs that women held in the film industry, apart from actresses. Job positions included those of a typist, secretary to the stars, executive secretary, costume designer, seamstress, telephone operator, hairdresser, script girl, film retoucher, title writer, publicity writer, musician, film editor, director, and producer, among others. Women also held jobs as blacksmiths and worked on vehicles. However, most occupations were seen solely as a precursor to marriage. Among married white women of both native and immigrant backgrounds, only around 10% were in the workforce, History reported. It was more common for married women of color to hold jobs outside the home, however. Unemployed women during the Great Depression could join "SheSheShe" camps. Inspired by the Civilian Conservation Corps, which only allowed men to join in exchange for free room and board, Eleanor Roosevelt campaigned for so-called "SheSheShe" camps to help women gain employment in environmental conservation, The Corps Network reported. Many families during the Great Depression were able to achieve middle-class status by adding another working member to the household — in many cases, a woman. Many women during the Great Depression found work as secretaries, teachers, telephone operators, and nurses. Women also earned incomes by sewing clothes in Works Progress Administration (WPA) sewing rooms. The rooms manufactured products such as men's trousers, boys' coveralls, baby clothes, women's dresses, and diapers. In the 1930s, women made 25% less than men for some government jobs. A 1933 law called the National Industrial Recovery Act established the National Recovery Administration, which oversaw industry codes that set standards including minimum wages and maximum hours. Just over a quarter of the codes set lower minimum wage rates for women than for men. In 1942, during wartime, the War Labor Board ruled that women would be paid the same as male workers who were now away at war. However, the war ended before they could receive equal pay. With no laws to protect female workers from pay inequality, female workers in the 1940s earned around 60% of what their male counterparts made, MarketWatch reported. By 1943, women made up 65% of the US aircraft industry's workforce. Before the war, women were largely in traditionally "female" fields such as nursing and teaching. After Pearl Harbor, many women entered the armed forces at astonishing rates. In 1943, more than 310,000 women worked in the US aircraft industry, making up 65% of the industry's total workforce, History reported. Before the war began, women made up just 1% of the industry. By 1945, one in every four married women worked in jobs outside the home. During World War II, women assisted in manufacturing wartime necessities like gas masks. Forbes reported that between 1940 and 1945, women's participation in the US workforce increased from 27% to nearly 37%. Women were largely seen as "supplemental" workers in the 1950s, meaning their income was secondary to their husbands'. Even though there were technically more women in the workforce in 1952 than during the war, women were often paid less and given jobs with less upward mobility than their male counterparts. After the war, women returned to stereotypically "feminine" jobs. In some cases, jobs were advertised for women only. Many women were forced to give up the jobs they had worked in during wartime, giving them to male soldiers returning home. The most popular jobs for women during the 1950s were secretaries, bank tellers or clerical workers, sales clerks, private household workers, and teachers, The Week reported. Female secretaries in the 1950s gained a reputation for being young and attractive. In fact, a 1959 quiz from a secretarial training program in Waco, Texas, reposted by The Atlantic, asked women if they have what it takes to be a secretary, including "smiling readily and naturally" and being "usually cheerful" among its requirements. The 1950s marked the beginning of the "jet age," and many young women found work as flight attendants, then called "stewardesses." Flight attendants during the 1950s became symbols of the golden age of flying — when traveling by air was seen as the height of sophistication and glamour. However, with this "glamorous" career also came a host of sexist protocols. Condé Nast Traveler reported that women were not allowed to work as flight attendants after they reached the ages of 32 to 35, while male flight attendants could work well into their 60s. In 1957, Trans World Airlines dropped its no-marriage rule for female flight attendants. However, many airlines continued to only hire non-married female flight attendants. While many women joined the workforce, they were nevertheless expected to fulfill their duties at home, in what would be coined "the second shift." After women returned home from their secretarial or office jobs, they had another job to do: caring for the children, doing the housekeeping, and, of course, putting a hot dinner in front of their husbands. This became known as the "second shift." If women didn't hold office or other jobs during the day, they were relegated to being "housewives." In the 1950s and 1960s, women found creative ways to make their own incomes from their homes. Many suburban women began selling Tupperware out of their own homes in what became known as "Tupperware parties." "Tupperware ... took those moms out of the kitchen where they were 'supposed to be' and let them enter the workforce, and let them have something outside the home," Lorna Boyd, whose mother Sylvia was an at-home Tupperware seller in the 1960s, told the Smithsonian Institution. Women were also making history in their careers. In the 1960s, Barbara Walters was a broadcast journalist working in New York City. In 1976, she would become the first woman to anchor a nightly newscast, Variety reported. Many other women were also joining the journalism field as coverage of the Vietnam War became increasingly widespread. While technology-based and other computer programming jobs may now be dominated by men, they were considered "women's work" in the 1960s. Smithsonian Magazine reported that "computer girls" became a term for "savvy young women" pursuing careers in computer programming. Computer programming was seen as "easy" work similar to typing or filing, so many women ended up building the field that would come to be known as software development. From the '40s to the '60s, women played a major role in the development of computer programming. Women were among the earliest computer programmers in the US, working on projects including the ENIAC computer during World War II, but programming was often treated as routine work. "Women were seen as an easy, tractable labor force for jobs that were critical and yet simultaneously devalued," technology historian Marie Hicks said in her book "Programmed Inequality," which detailed a similar phenomenon in Britain, The Guardian reported. But as computing became more prestigious and lucrative, the field became increasingly male-dominated. By the mid-1980s, the share of computer science bachelor's degrees earned by women in the US had begun to decline. In the 1960s, multiple pieces of legislation were passed to protect women in the workplace from discrimination. Title VII was added to the Civil Rights Act of 1964, protecting workers from employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. In 1963, the Equal Pay Act of 1963 was passed in order to protect men and women who perform "substantially equal work in the same establishment" from sex-based wage discrimination. These measures were especially beneficial to women of color. Up until the 1970s, women of color could be openly discriminated against in the hiring process and were often assigned to providing "domestic service work" to white families, The Economic Policy Institute reported. During the 1970s, computing work gained more prestige as the industry realized how valuable computers would become. It meant women were no longer welcome in many computer programming offices. "They weren't going to put women workers – seen as low-level drones – in charge of computers," Hicks told The Guardian. Female computer workers, or "computer girls," were gradually phased out and replaced with men, who received higher salaries and more prestigious job titles. By the 1970s, many women were still fighting for better workplace conditions, equal pay, and more job opportunities. The Atlantic reported that from 1972 to 1985, the number of women working "professional" jobs increased from 44% to 49%. The number of women working "management" jobs nearly doubled, rising from 20% to 36%. However, in 1970, women still did not earn equal wages to men holding the same positions. In the 1970s, education became more important than ever for securing a well-paying job. After measures were passed that prevented universities and institutions from discriminating against students on the basis of sex, more women were admitted into medical school than in past generations, according to a study published by the British Medical Bulletin. Other strides were made for women in the late 1970s. In 1978, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act was passed as an amendment to Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibited pregnancy-based employment discrimination. Women in the workforce in the 1980s continued to make strides, but there was still a way to go. The Atlantic reported that, in 1985, half of all college graduates were women. However, only 41% of women between the ages of 25 and 44 held full-time year-round jobs. Even in the mid-1980s, women themselves saw their own careers as inferior to their husbands'. The Atlantic also cited a 1985 Roper survey that showed only 10% of women said that a husband should turn down a "very good job" in another city "so the wife can continue her job." However, women of the 1980s made history in their fields. Dr. Mae Jemison was among 15 new astronauts named by NASA and became the first Black female shuttle flyer. In 1984, at the Democratic National Convention held in San Francisco's Moscone Center, Geraldine Ferraro became the first woman nominated as vice president by a major political party. Women were encouraged to "do it all" — meaning, hold a successful job as well as maintain a happy and healthy marriage and raise children. In the 1990s, women overwhelmingly began to be employed in offices and earned higher salaries than before. Computers became increasingly prevalent, reducing the need for secretaries, bank tellers, and retail workers. Some women were also postponing marriage and children until later in life. For most earlier decades, women would be married between the ages of 20 and 22, Time reported. The median age for women to get married rose to 24 in 1990, and by 1997, it was 25. In 1995, nearly half of all women surveyed for a report by the National Center for Education Statistics said they earned half or more of their total family income. In recent years, women have held more jobs than men in the US. Fortune reported that at the start of 2020, 109,000 more women were working than men, and women in the US made up 50.4% of the labor force. Sectors that traditionally hire women, like healthcare and education, were growing, and other industries previously dominated by men were also hiring more women than ever before. Forbes reported that 13.8% of mining and logging jobs were held by women, and more women were employed in manufacturing and transportation than in years past. The COVID-19 pandemic caused the women's labor force participation rate to hit a 33-year low, with 2.3 million women in the US leaving the labor force between February 2020 and January 2021. By 2025, however, nearly half of all US employees were women, some of whom chose to start their own businesses and chose entrepreneurship over traditional careers. Between July 2025 and July 2026, women's labor-force participation fell from 57.6% to 56.4%.

item.title: Inside Jackie Kennedy Onassis' luxurious homes, from sprawling estates to full-floor apartments
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.23
Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis grew up in spacious New York apartments and several-acre estates, and, after her marriage, spent summers at the famed Kennedy Compound and winters on the family's estate in Palm Beach. Still, she said her family's "happiest years" were those spent with her husband, President John F. Kennedy, in the White House. Before they moved there, the couple lived in a 19th-century red-brick home in Georgetown, Washington, DC, which recently sold for $6.125 million, Mansion Global reported. The Kennedys bought the home in 1957 for $82,000. While most of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis' former homes can only be admired from the outside, one of her final properties is open to visitors. Parts of what was once known as Red Gate Farm on Martha's Vineyard opened to the public last summer, The Vineyard Gazette reported in 2025. Five miles of public trails meander through the land, which the Kennedy family sold to two nonprofits in 2020 and is now known as Squibnocket Pond Reservation. Here are all of the impressive places she lived in and owned in her lifetime. Before she was a Kennedy or an Onassis, Jacqueline Lee Bouvier spent her early years in New York City. In 1932, the Bouviers moved into an apartment on the sixth and seventh floors of 740 Park Avenue. The apartment building was developed by her grandfather, James T. Lee, The New York Times reported. At least for a period, her father couldn't afford to furnish it so Jackie and her sister could roller skate from room to room, The Wall Street Journal reported. The apartment building later became a home for billionaires and was once considered one of the most iconic apartment buildings in the city. In 2017, her old apartment sold for $25.25 million. In the 1940s, Bouvier's mother remarried, and they left New York. They moved into a Georgian-style mansion called "Merrywood" in McLean, Virginia, near Washington, DC. The home sits on the edge of the Potomac River and has an extensive garden. Bouvier wrote fondly about the house in her diary, saying, "I always love it so at Merrywood — so peaceful … with the river and those great steep hills." Bouvier spent her summers at her paternal grandfather's East Hampton estate. The 8,500-square-foot home, which was built in 1917, is called "Lasata," which means "place of peace," in the native Algonquian language. In 2023, fashion designer Tom Ford bought it for $52 million, The Wall Street Journal reported. She also spent some of her summers at her maternal grandfather's house in East Hampton called "Wildmoor." The 18th-century home, covering about 5,700 square feet, was a shingle-and-clapboard wooden house with a view of fields, a swamp, and the sea, per the WSJ. In 2021, the house was sold for $6.8 million. Her next notable property was the Kennedy family's summer home in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts. Joseph Kennedy Sr., John F. Kennedy's father, bought a white-shingled cottage in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, in 1928 for $25,000, or about $470,000 today. The coastal Massachusetts cottage became the Kennedy family's home base for years to come. Before they married, Bouvier and John F. Kennedy spent time together there. It later became known as the "Kennedy Compound." In 1953, Bouvier became a Kennedy when the couple married in Newport, Rhode Island. They had the wedding reception at her mother's husband's sprawling estate, known as "Hammersmith Farm," anchored by a grand, 28-room Victorian-era mansion. The property was last sold in 1999 for just over $8 million. The estate became a part-time summer home for the Kennedys, along with the Kennedy Compound. Jackie Kennedy spent summers on the estate during her childhood, and the Kennedys later vacationed there in the summer of 1961. In 1953, not long after the Kennedys were married, they rented a four-story, four-bedroom house in Washington, DC. The Kennedys lived there for almost two years. They enjoyed throwing dinner parties and spending time in the back gardens. The house, which was built in the 1940s, is about 3,000 square feet. It last sold for $4 million in April 2025. Two years later, in 1955, the Kennedys moved to "Hickory Hill," another Georgian-style house. The home was built in 1815 and had a tennis court, a pool, and 12 fireplaces on a 5.6-acre plot in McLean, Virginia. They bought it from Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson, The Washington Post reported. Two years later, the Kennedys sold it for $125,000 to John's brother, Robert, who would end up raising his own family there. Jackie didn't want to go back after her daughter was stillborn. The couple sold it to Robert Kennedy for the same price they'd paid, The Washington Post reported. Robert Kennedy was at the house when he heard John had been assassinated, the Baltimore Sun reported. He spent an hour alone, walking around the estate. In 1956, the Kennedys bought a summer home in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, right beside the original Kennedy summer home. The 4,484-square-foot clapboarded home sat on less than an acre of land and soon became part of the "Kennedy Compound." They spent $45,948 on the house, The Wall Street Journal reported. In 1957, the Kennedys bought an 18th-century brick row house in Georgetown for $82,000. Jackie spent about $18,000 on remodeling the home, called Marbury House for William Marbury (you might remember his name from social studies class), which was built in 1811, and she decorated it with armchairs and fine porcelain. Her husband campaigned and was elected president during their years here, Architectural Digest reported. They lived in the home between 1957 and 1961, selling it soon after. In 2026, the 5,215-square-foot, five-bedroom home sold for $6.125 million. Though not a property she owned, Jackie lived in the White House with her family during her husband's presidency from 1961 to 1963. While they were living in the White House, they spent winters at her father-in-law Joseph Kennedy's Palm Beach estate. The Palm Beach estate became known as the Kennedys' "winter White House." In 2020, the house sold for $70 million and underwent extensive renovations by the new owner. In 1963, after her husband was assassinated, Jackie and her children left the White House and moved into an 18th-century home in DC. She paid around $175,000 for the five-bedroom house but only lived there for about a year. It was too public, and she reportedly became overwhelmed with all of the tourists. In 2017, it was purchased for $5.25 million. In 1964, they returned to New York after she bought a 5,300-square-foot apartment on Fifth Avenue. The then-$200,000 apartment had five bathrooms, three fireplaces, two terraces, and a library. It also had a view of Central Park. Jackie Kennedy owned the apartment until she died in 1994. In 1974, she purchased a country home, a converted barn on almost 10 acres, for $200,000 in Peapack, New Jersey. She liked the area for its natural beauty and space for horse riding, The New York Times reported. She knew the area well because she had previously rented a farmhouse described by The Times as a "badly made-over barn" in Bernardsville since 1965. After she bought the property, she painted it yellow with white trim. After her death, a neighbor and friend bought the property for $1.47 million in 1997. The neighbor, Marjorie McDonnell Walsh, told The Wall Street Journal they tore the house down. "It doesn't matter," she said when declining to share details about the new house. "The much more important thing is we both love the property. It's a private valley. It's beautiful." In 1979, after her second husband died, Jackie decided to build a new house called "Red Gate Farm" on 340 acres of Martha's Vineyard land. She reportedly spent a little more than $1 million on the land, and then another $3.1 million on building the house, which was finished in 1981. The main building covers 6,456 square feet. There's also a four-bedroom guest house, a pool, and a tennis court. The property stretches across a mile of beach. Starting in 2020, parts of the estate were sold for $37 million. The land opened as a public park in 2025. Two nonprofits, the Martha's Vineyard Land Bank and Sheriff's Meadow Foundation, bought 304 acres of the land for $27 million, the Vineyard Gazette reported, and the Land Bank later bought an additional 32 acres for $10 million. It is now known as Squibnocket Pond Reservation, and members of the public can walk on trails that cut through the land. But it's not easy — in the summer, just 10 parking spaces are open to the public, and you need an online reservation to get them. The Kennedy family still owns 65 acres of the estate, including the home, the Vineyard Gazette reported in 2025. This land is out of view from the public area, meaning you're unlikely to see any Kennedys running around, The New York Times reported. Editor's note: This story was first published in September 2023 and was most recently updated in September 2026 with additional information.

item.title: The Amazon cargo plane that crashed in Miami nearly hit a parking lot full of Tesla Cybercabs
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.93
Sunday's Amazon plane crash almost destroyed a bunch of Elon Musk's latest invention. At least five people died, and five more were injured, after the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport. Images showed the airplane came to a halt next to a parking lot that appeared to contain a few dozen Tesla Cybercabs. The gold-colored robotaxis have no steering wheel or pedals, and feature distinctive gold wheel hubs. Tesla officially launched the cabs in Austin last week to great fanfare. The launch has prompted an inquiry from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to check that Tesla has followed all the rules. On Sunday, when the Boeing 767 passed the end of the runway in Miami, it appeared to strike multiple vehicles but stopped short of the parking lot full of Cybercabs. Tesla has not officially confirmed that it is testing or planning to roll out Cybercabs in Miami, but its robotaxis, which use modified Tesla Model Ys, have been available in the city since July. Teslarati, a Tesla blog, shared a photo of about 40 Cybercabs at Miami Airport three days before the crash. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider, though Musk wrote "Weird" on X in response to a post from financial blog Zero Hedge about the presence of Cybercabs. According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue radio transmissions recorded on Broadcastify, the plane crossed 67th Avenue, a nearby road, before it struck a truck. "We have a patient trapped," a first responder said, according to the recordings. The airplane was operated by 21 Air, a charter firm, and had flown to Miami from Puerto Rico. Weather data shows there were thunderstorms and gusting winds at the time of the crash. It was not immediately clear on Sunday how many people were on the plane, and whether those killed were people on the ground. This was the second 767 cargo plane to crash from Amazon's Prime Air network. In 2019, an Atlas Air freighter flying on behalf of Amazon crashed into Trinity Bay near Houston, killing the three people on board.

item.title: 'There's no accountability': AI startups keep claiming huge revenue. VCs say the math is getting 'murky.'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.60
Few metrics thrill Silicon Valley investors more than surging annual recurring revenue (ARR). In the AI boom, however, VCs are increasingly skeptical of what that number actually represents. "The amount of VC-backed AI companies lying about their ARR publicly is absolutely unsettling," Greg Isenberg, CEO of Late Checkout, wrote in a post that went viral for saying something out loud that has been whispered about, but rarely said publicly in tech circles. ARR was a metric that came into vogue during the software era, intended to estimate the yearly sales a company can expect from paying customers, a quick way for investors to judge a startup's valuation. Now, venture capitalists and founders who spoke with Business Insider said ARR has become so loosely used that it can blur the line between contracted subscriptions, future deals, token consumption, hardware sales, and a single strong month of revenue. In short, recurring revenue is often not recurring. "It's ARR inflation," said Shruti Gandhi, a general partner at Array Ventures. "There's no accountability right now." Gandhi says she has called out founders for exaggerating revenue. Their defense: "Everybody else is doing it." To Alexander Niehenke, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, the current trend of padding ARR reflects a top-of-the-bubble mentality when founders have all the leverage. "It feels like we're at the tail end of 2021 again, given some of the behavior I'm seeing in the venture ecosystem," he said. "Anytime you get deeper into a bull cycle, everybody has more tolerance for risk." Founders know how excited VCs get about ARR, according to Niehenke. "The smart and brilliant entrepreneurs use it like catnip on us," he said. Cluely CEO Roy Lee raised eyebrows earlier this year when he admitted to misstating his startup's ARR to a TechCrunch reporter. But that was very much the exception. With startups under much less regulatory scrutiny than public companies, revenue claims are rarely verified. it’s genuinely crazy tech has so isolated itself from regulatory forces that you can just admit to securities violations on the internet — Will Manidis (@WillManidis) March 5, 2026 More startups are using run rate, but is it better? Before AI, Silicon Valley was in love with software-as-a-service companies, where ARR was much more dependable. SaaS companies like Salesforce or Workday often sell annual or multiyear deals, making it fairly straightforward to tally the value of subscriptions likely to recur. "When you have ARR, you have a signed contract, and you know what you've signed up for for the year," said Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo Ventures. AI has proven less predictable. Many AI companies no longer sell a simple per-seat license that costs the same every month. They charge customers based on how much they use, often measured in tokens. Someone may use a product aggressively, then pull back, or switch to a cheaper model. The startup's own costs vary widely, too, because it may have to pay a model provider or cloud company every time a customer uses its product. AI startups have increasingly shifted to describing run rate, which extrapolates a month of revenue over a full year and does not purport to be recurring, according to Murphy. "Venture does this from time to time, which is that there's a new metric that shows up," he said. Pocket, which makes an AI recording device, is one of those companies, having recently said it crossed the $100 million run rate threshold. Founder Akshay Narisetti said he avoids ARR because tokens make revenue too unpredictable to expect it to be recurring. Run rate can come with its own problem in that a gangbusters month does not necessarily translate to a year, but Narisetti said he avoids doing that. "We never annualize one large month with a spike," Narisetti said. The biggest AI labs have used both metrics. OpenAI has described subscription sales as ARR while calling its newer advertising business an annualized revenue run rate. Anthropic has generally described its overall sales as run-rate revenue. Linear, which is an increasingly rare breed of SaaS startups, recently said it crossed $100 million in ARR. Cofounder and CEO Karri Saarinen said he stands by the metric because Linear sells multiyear contracts and has been in business since 2019. "Since we've been operating longer, we can better forecast the actual ARR," he said, adding that for newer AI startups, it is a different story. "It's gotten really murky," he said.

item.title: 19 surreal photos show the mud, chaos, and glamour of Burning Man
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.97
Every year, the question returns: Has Burning Man lost its edge? First tech billionaires turned the desert oasis into their playground. Then the festival's younger crowd began to thin. Burning Man has been deemed uncool by Gen Z: In 2025, 10% of surveyed attendees were in their 20s, down from more than 30% in 2015. And still, an estimated 70,000 made the pilgrimage to Black Rock City this year, braving dust storms and the logistical gymnastics of surviving for a week in the desert. Maybe Burning Man is no longer the cutting-edge counterculture experiment it once was. But the art cars still rolled, the costumes still glittered, and the playa still became home to a group of revelers unlike any other. These photos offer a glimpse of what it looked like in 2026. Additional reporting by Katherine Li. For decades, a city has risen at summer's end on a remote stretch of Nevada desert. Burners call this temporary metropolis 'Black Rock City.' Roughly 70,000 people were expected to attend the art and music festival this year. They hauled the food, water, shelter, and supplies needed to survive a week. The 'mutant vehicles' were a sight to see. Rain and heavy winds forced the gates closed on the first day. Mud has dogged the festival in recent years. These resourceful burners got creative with their footwear. The weather didn't appear to dampen the mood. Some of the fashion channeled 'Dune.' Goggles were a practical accessory. The Man structure rose above the Cryptomeria, a treehouse-like pavilion at the center. Art installations took shape across the playa. 'Titantic's End' showed two halves of a massive ocean liner sinking into the dry lake bed. Gazelle Dasti's artwork, 'Zarvan,' links Persian culture and the idea of endless time. Burners escaped the heat under an acre-wide canopy at the festival's center. Organizers issued a new rule this year. Smart glasses were allowed. But wearers needed to ask permission from anyone who might appear in the recording. A Burning Man Project spokesperson told Business Insider that its privacy and consent rules are not new, but that it recently updated its guidance to explicitly include smart eyewear as the technology has evolved.

item.title: Andrew Garfield says one spot in his house is his antidote to burnout
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.82
Andrew Garfield, 43, said his ideal day off involves a lot of lying down and looking out the window. Speaking on Monday's episode of the "Smartless" podcast, the actor said he was happy to do very little after nearly a year of nonstop work. "I can do it for a couple of months. I really can," Garfield said. He spent 11 months moving between dramatically different roles: Sam Altman in "Artificial," a grieving farmer who leads a rebellion against King Richard II in "The Uprising," and magician Roy Horn in the upcoming Apple TV+ series "Wild Things." Constantly switching between the characters felt disorienting, he said. "You get to the point sometimes where you're so deeply resentful of the work that you love to do so much, and that's kind of where I'm at," Garfield said. By the end of it, Garfield said he was ready to take a break, adding that some of his favorite ways to unwind include reading books, watching "dumb TV," and "literally looking out" the window. "I have a lovely window in my house, and there's a beautiful tree that I just stare at," he said. "Again, it's like the most valuable commodity outside of live performance is quiet, and time, and space, and not having our attention snatched by the things that are always snatching our attention," he said. Garfield said he also values time with friends and family, who help keep him grounded. "One of the gifts of being raised the way I was is that it was made very, very clear to me by osmosis that there was no way that I could ever allow myself to drink my own Kool-Aid enough to lose myself," he said. That perspective has also made him more conscious of the personal cost of spending months away from home for a job. "I'm thinking about that more as I get older. In my 20s and 30s, it was like, I'll go anywhere any time, and I'll devote myself to this in a way that's probably a little unhealthy," Garfield said. But now, he feels that "time is ticking" and has become more aware that "it's not forever," he said. Other celebrities have also spoken about how they enjoy their downtime. Hilary Swank has said that exercise helps her decompress when she's stressed. "Ultimately, working out for me is about stress relief. I really like resistance training, and I try to do it twice a week. It really helps me cope with stress and I find it also makes me sleep better," she told Business Insider in 2024. Keke Palmer has said some of her favorite ways to unwind involve "doing things solo." "I love journaling, prayer, and any type of fitness, such as Pilates, yoga, and hiking. All of that stuff brings me immense joy," she told Business Insider in 2025. "I love bingeing comfort TV. It doesn't even have to be the most interesting thing."

item.title: People ask how I manage 6 kids and caring for 3 relatives. I work a second job and barely get time to myself.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.47
This story is based on an interview with Kaitlin Manns, 33, a home health aide and server from Granite City, Illinois. It has been edited for length and clarity. My grandpa employed a carer before he died at 76. And my grandma, 76, mom, and stepdad, both 56 — all of whom have chronic medical conditions — had them, too. They were wonderful, but they ended up leaving for better-paid jobs. I didn't blame them, but it left our family struggling to find cover. So I decided to step in and do the job myself. It made sense because I've got a nurturing personality, and it felt like the right thing to do. I work 2 jobs I qualified as a home health aide, a role that still requires monthly virtual training, and combined it with working as a server at a restaurant on weekends. My days are pretty hectic, particularly because I have six kids aged between 2 and 13. Two of my siblings — both 9 — also live in my five-bedroom house, along with Mom and my stepdad. Grandma lives in her own home, about a 15-minute drive away. Thankfully, my husband, Justice, 28, is wonderful and really helps out. Still, he works mornings at a furniture rental company, so he's busy, too. Our schedule begins with him walking the oldest child two blocks to the school bus around 6:45 a.m. The others leave for their school, and I drop off Justice at his job. The state pays my salary Then I drive to the toddlers' day care before starting my caregiving around 9:30 a.m. I look after the three adults at separate times, helping them with things like showering, laundry, and doctors' appointments. On Mondays, I'll take care of Grandma and my stepdad. Tuesdays, it's my mom and stepdad. Wednesday is only my stepdad, Thursday is my grandma again, and I work for Mom on Friday morning. I usually put in 38 hours a week, earning $18.50 an hour, which is paid for by the state. On weekends, I work at least 23 hours as a server at a bar and grill, earning $7.50 an hour. But my pay is mostly tips. I can earn as much as $300 per shift. I love the job because it's a Mom-and-Pop business, and everybody knows each other. It's like being with friends. People often ask me how I manage to do it all. It's challenging at times, particularly because my grandma and stepdad have mobility and memory issues. I have little time to myself There's a lot of paperwork, too, such as getting Grandma approved for a scooter and a ramp. It takes a mixture of patience and organizational skills. It's very rewarding because I get to be with my loved ones all day. My job as a carer, big sister, and mom, plus the server work, leaves me little time for myself. However, I enjoy movies and reading on my Kindle before bed. I rest easy knowing I'm doing my very best for everyone. I'm paying my folks back for raising me while giving my kids a similar, loving childhood.

item.title: An Anthropic researcher just quit, saying OpenAI and Anthropic are 'gambling with our lives'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.21
An Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI just quit. He's the latest insider who's warned that the AI race has become dangerously reckless. Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday, saying he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at the two AI giants. "Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon wrote on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Coxon was a member of OpenAI's technical staff from 2023 until July 2026, when he moved to Anthropic as a researcher. His research at OpenAI included work on GPT-4o. In Tuesday's post, Coxon said the two labs have not been transparent about their fears regarding AI. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt," he wrote. "If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately." There is one difference between the two companies, he said. "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes," Coxon wrote. "At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk." Evan Hubinger, a current Anthropic employee who leads the alignment stress testing team at the lab, agreed with Coxon in a reply to his post. "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," he wrote. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Safety has taken a 'backseat to shiny products' Coxon is the latest among staffers walking away from frontier labs while sounding the alarm, a trend that appears peculiar to the AI boom. While the dot-com and smartphone explosion era had their own set of concerns regarding a digital divide and bubbles, they did not draw as much scrutiny about safety from people closest to the action. OpenAI has lost a string of safety researchers in recent years, and Anthropic is increasingly facing the same phenomenon. In February, Anthropic safeguards researcher Mrinank Sharma left the company, writing in a resignation letter that he wants to contribute toward something that fully aligns with his "integrity." "Throughout my time here, I've repeatedly seen how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions," he wrote in the letter he shared publicly. "I've seen this within myself, within the organization, where we constantly face pressures to set aside what matters most, and throughout broader society too." In February, OpenAI researcher Hieu Pham said that he could "finally feel the existential threat that AI is posing." Later that month, he announced he was leaving the company, citing burnout. In 2024, former alignment chief Jan Leike quit OpenAI after saying he reached a "breaking point" with leadership. "OpenAI is shouldering an enormous responsibility on behalf of all of humanity," he wrote. "But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products." Recent incidents have added fuel to those fears. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models escaped a test environment and hacked into Hugging Face's systems. OpenAI called the incident a "warning shot" and paused its largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning run. Later that month, Anthropic said it found three cases of Claude models gaining unauthorized access to other organizations' systems. The company also amended a key safety pledge this year, dropping a commitment not to train more powerful models without adequate safeguards in place and replacing it with safety roadmaps and risk reports.

item.title: I used to see countries I'd visited as places I'd 'done.' Slow travel changed that.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.02
Earlier this year, as I set foot in country number 50, I expected the milestone to feel significant. Instead, I realized how little the number actually meant. As a teenager, I became obsessed with seeing the world. My first purchase on Amazon was a set of 50 mini flags to study each day. I turned to quiz websites like Sporcle to learn country capitals and populations when I should have been solving math equations for school. At 14, I'd already developed my first major travel goal: visit every country in Europe. Later that year, after a trip to Greece, Italy, and France, I was every bit as enamored with Europe as I'd imagined I'd be. Unfortunately, I wouldn't visit again for seven whole years. By then, I was 21, in college, and finally had the freedom to start traveling on my own. Visiting Paris, Amsterdam, and Barcelona reignited the obsession I'd developed years earlier. I began traveling during every school break These trips were far from relaxing. I planned jam-packed itineraries to see as much as I could within a one- or two-week window. There was one trip in particular that still makes me anxious to think about. In June of 2019, my friend and I crammed Greece, Croatia, Czechia, Hungary, and Germany into 10 days. We didn't have time to visit the Acropolis in Athens. We spent less than 48 hours in each place and were constantly rushing to catch the next flight. After checking off the main attractions, there was little time to experience the culture and history of each place. I remember spending more time in Split's airport than I did exploring the city. It went like this for my first year of traveling. At most, I would spend three days in each country, sticking mostly to capital cities. At one point, I tried to justify a two-hour layover in Keflavik as a trip to Iceland. Social media made travel feel like a competition Seeing people list the number of countries they'd visited in their bios reinforced my own urge to keep score. Looking back, I was using my number in much the same way: as proof that I was well-traveled. At the same time, part of my rushed travel style stemmed from necessity. Between being a busy college student and later a full-time employee, I only had so much time to travel. But when I was laid off at the end of 2023 and decided to spend most of 2024 traveling in Asia and Australia, those time parameters became obsolete. I was able to prioritize slow travel instead of seeing how many countries I could squeeze into a week or two. On that eight-month trip, I generally spent three weeks in each place, sometimes longer. The longer I stayed, the more I felt like I was actually traveling. Instead of only crossing off must-see attractions, I actually had the time to learn local history and customs, visit lesser-known areas, and experience everyday life. In the end, I felt a deeper appreciation for the countries I traveled through slowly than the ones I raced through. Staying longer made room for experiences that would have never fit into my early itineraries. In Malaysian Borneo, I spent three days exploring the Kinabatangan River deep in the jungle, observing orangutans, crocodiles, and native birds along the way. I took a sailing trip through the Komodo Islands in eastern Indonesia and earned my advanced diving certification on Gili Air, a small tropical island near Lombok. Those two months I spent traveling across Indonesia showed me how culturally and geographically diverse a single country could be. From Java to Flores, each island I visited had its own dialect, religious traditions, crafts, and local delicacies. It's not just about the numbers I stopped viewing the countries I had already visited as places I'd "done." The destinations I know best are the ones I've returned to over and over again, and I still discover something new with each visit. I first traveled to Italy at 14 and returned to live there 10 years later. A trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina in the summer of 2025 led me to establish Sarajevo as my current home base. Those returns didn't increase my country count. Still, they have given me things that a number could never reflect — meaningful relationships, new perspectives, language skills, and a genuine connection to each place. Nowadays, I like planning my trips so I begin or end in a familiar location. I'm always just as excited to return to the places I love as I am to visit somewhere new. There's always comfort in being back in a place where I know my way around, have friends and favorite spots, and can pick up where I left off. I haven't completely stopped counting. My goal to visit every country in Europe is still alive and well — there are 12 left on my bucket list. Admittedly, I still get satisfaction from adding a new country to my Been app, and every milestone is still exciting. The biggest difference is that the number is now something I track instead of something I chase.

item.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.54
The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums. The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters. Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026. Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August. "It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery." "The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," said Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research. However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said. Where has the good news come from? The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up. Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds. This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards. Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war. Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year. Brzeski told DW that many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefited from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil. "There was a bit of a rechanneling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he said. The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identified this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks." It said that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains. "Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added. Can the German government take some credit? Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026. "It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," said Fuest. The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness. It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," said Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy." Germany's structural problems remain Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain. The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined. "Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" said Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist. "Chinese competition is still there," he said. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse. Tentative optimism among Germany's businesses Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands. In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums. For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable. "It could hardly have gotten much worse," said Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder ["economic miracle"] 3.0, we have to keep that in mind." He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve. "They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he said. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival." For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He said three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows. "It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he said. Edited by: Rob Mudge

item.title: Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.20
A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people. Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative "reset" in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support. Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots. Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken. Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued. There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective. More provinces, better governance? Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution. "Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people," Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW. Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan's four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized. Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services. Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan's growing population. But there is disagreement over the solution. "Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level," Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW. He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies. Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively. Altering the political balance "Pakistan's history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services," Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW. The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens. Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country. New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources. Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources. The political resistance has already begun, with Sindh's provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories. A risky strategy? Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time. "Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge," he said. "Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus," he added. The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power. Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh. He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option. "We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services," Ismail said. Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units. "In Pakistan's case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions," he said. For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15. It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions. Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Australia targets big tech with algorithm opt-out bill
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.36
The Australian government announced planned new rules for social media platforms on Tuesday that would give users greater control over their social media algorithms. Under the "My Feed, My Way" initiative, social media platforms would have to allow users to opt out of content recommended by an algorithm in their feeds. What is in Australia's social media algorithm bill? Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled draft legislation that would impose a "duty of care" on major social media platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram. Users would only see content from accounts they choose to follow. "It's not about giving government control. It's about giving people control," Albanese said. The bill is expected to be approved by the Australian Parliament and introduced later this year. Companies that do not comply could be fined up to AU$100 million ($72 million, €62 million). Social media bans for children Anika Wells, Australia's Minister for Communications, said the measure would help ensure children's safety on social media. Australia became the first country to restrict social media access for under-16s in 2025. Several countries, including Germany, Spain, France, Denmark, and New Zealand, followed Australia's lead and drafted plans to introduce similar age restrictions. Some big tech companies have opposed such new regulations. They argue it could encourage young users to move to unregulated online spaces. Edited by: Rob Turner If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.36
Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014. Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday. Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions. Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded? The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023. Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead. "Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko. Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived. The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard. "The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement. Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo. "Russia can demand that the district court reassess the case," the Justice Ministry said. How did Russia respond? Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. "We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said. The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint. The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them. "The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website. He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case. What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement? Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people. It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century. The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions. The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades. Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: India news: Hindu group apologizes over Eiffel Tower row
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.34
What you need to know These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us. Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India from Tuesday, September 8. - Hindu group apologizes after Eiffel Tower strike over alleged discrimination - Manipuri musician killed in Delhi - Iran hails longstanding India relationship ahead of Pezeshkian's visit Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. WATCH — Can we turn household gardens into food systems? In the southern Indian state of Kerala, the village of Kanjikuzhy has built a remarkable community-led food system. Nearly all 9,000 families grow their own vegetables organically — turning homes, backyards and small plots into productive gardens. Find out more: eBay to investigate how banned gender-test kits were sold in India — report US e-commerce platform eBay is conducting an internal review of its platform's safeguards after news agency Reuters found that several gender-prediction kits were listed for delivery to India. New Delhi has banned the use of such kits under a law aimed at preventing sex-selective abortion. Reuters identified nine listings, including kits from brands SneakPeek and Peekaboo, which were being offered by third-party sellers with shipping to India. The platform removed the listings after being notified last week. "These listings violated local regulations and eBay's policies, and we are reviewing these controls, including the relevant shipping and checkout experience, to determine whether further enhancements are appropriate," eBay told Reuters in a statement. "eBay has controls in place intended to prevent certain gender-prediction products from being visible in India," it added. While eBay does not have a dedicated Indian shopping site, the company does ship to India, functioning purely as a marketplace for third-party sellers. India has a strict prenatal gender determination law dating back to 1994, which followed a steep decline in the ratio of girls born after ultrasound technology spread. With patrilineal inheritance being the norm, people misused the technology to abort female fetuses. Under the law, violations carry prison terms of up to three years, with repeat offenses being hit with harsher penalties. Separately, India's Health Ministry has pressed Google to remove search results linking to Peekaboo's website, according to notices reviewed by the news agency.
Manipur singer killed after confronting group drinking outside Delhi home A group of men has been apprehended for beating Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh to death outside his apartment in Southeast Delhi, local media reported. The 54-year-old lived in Kilokari village, where he was allegedly assaulted by a group of delivery workers and local eatery staff after he confronted them for drinking and creating a nuisance outside his residence, police said. Seven people have been arrested, and a juvenile has been detained in relation to the assault. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi slammed local authorities and Home Minister Amit Shah, raising concerns over the safety of people from the northeastern states of India in Delhi. "A father, killed outside his own home, in his own country's capital. After many such incidents, every Northeast family in Delhi is asking the same question today - are we safe here?" he wrote on X. Chief Minister of Manipur, N Biren Singh, also offered condolences to his family, urging Delhi Police to take swift action on the matter. He also shared CCTV footage that claimed to show the accused heading downstairs after assaulting Singh. The incident has raised concerns among New Delhi's Northeast community. The area that comes under the Sunlight Colony police station is known to have a sizeable population from the region, the Telegraph newspaper reported. In 2023, a group of men assaulted a Manipuri family in the area. Iran hails 'civilizational' relationship with India ahead of BRICS summit Iran highlighted its "long-standing, historic and civilizational relationship" with India ahead of President Masoud Pezeshkian's visit to New Delhi for the upcoming BRICS summit. Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei emphasized the importance Tehran places on its ties with New Delhi during a press conference. He highlighted President Pezeshkian's bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to reaffirm Iran's plans to engage diplomatically with India to deepen economic collaboration. Referring to the upcoming BRICS summit, he added: "We will certainly make use of the opportunity provided by the BRICS Summit to continue our discussions and consultations with India in areas of mutual interest." The 18th BRICS summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital. BAPS apologizes over Eiffel Tower row, denies preventing access A Hindu religious group has apologized after the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by the organization. The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), however, reiterated that their tour was pre-coordinated with the tower's team, adding that no person was denied access. BAPS also offered apologies to anyone hurt or inconvenienced. "We understand the concerns raised and take them very seriously. Given the size of our delegation, the visit was organised in coordination with the Eiffel Tower team at the beginning of normal opening hours to minimise any inconvenience to other visitors," BAPS said in a statement on social media. "To our knowledge, at no point was anyone denied access to the Eiffel Tower. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation," the statement added. Around 100 men from BAPS were visiting the landmark. The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited. SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake: "These conditions should not have been accepted." On Sunday, BAPS conducted the consecration ceremony of France’s first traditional Hindu temple in Bussy-Saint-Georges, near Paris. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi virtually addressed the inauguration gathering, adding that "India and France’s relations have reached new heights." Read more about the controversy here. Welcome to our coverage Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from across India. If you tried to go up the Eiffel Tower in Paris yesterday, you may have been in for a rude shock, as the tourist hotspot was closed over alleged discrimination during a visit by a Hindu group. The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) has apologized for any inconvenience caused, but with a small caveat. In Delhi, a Manipuri musician was killed after he objected to a group of men drinking raucously outside his apartment. Finally, Iran has hailed its longstanding ties with India ahead of President Masoud Pezeshkian's visit to New Delhi for the 18th BRICS Summit from September 11 to 13. For this and more, follow our live blog.

item.title: Hungary orders 10 Russian diplomats to leave
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
Hungary has ordered 10 members of Russia's diplomatic mission to leave the country over activities it said were incompatible with their diplomatic status, Foreign Minister Anita Orban said on Tuesday. The move marks a significant step by Budapest against Moscow, with Orban saying it was intended to protect Hungary's "security and sovereignty." Why is Hungary expelling the diplomats? Orban said a Hungarian Foreign Ministry official had informed the Russian ambassador that the 10 individuals had engaged in activities deemed "unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention." She did not specify what the individuals were accused of doing. Hungary's authorities had made the assessment before the government called on them to leave, Orban said. "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote. Does this mean a break with Russia? Orban stressed that Hungary was not severing diplomatic relations with Moscow. "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia," she said, adding that Budapest intended to maintain "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules." Orban has served as Hungary's foreign minister and deputy prime minister since May, following the change of government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar. The expulsion is nevertheless a notable deterioration in relations with Moscow, particularly given Hungary's previously close relationship with Russia under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
