item.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.31
It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike. The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now. The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death. Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him. Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus. Seeking German cooperation Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg. One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group. Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi. A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats." "It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there. Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation. Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human. "This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained. Patients require intensive care, isolation He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes. Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever. "If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure. Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious. Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo. The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible. Successful tick tactics Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus. Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area. In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been. Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen. Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there. "Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored." This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Russia announces it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.95
The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg. The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 at the latest, according to the Foreign Ministry. "It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences. Russia also earlier ordered the closure of all Goethe-Institut branches on Russian territory, with Goethe-Institut staff having to leave the country by September 13. Goethe-Institut is a center that promotes German language and culture. Goethe-Institut is largely financed by the German government. Germany, Russia trade barbs over Leipzig drone attack The moves are a direct response to Germany's decision to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin, a decision Russia labeled "unfriendly." Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. The EU, too, said the incident had all the signs of "state sponsored terrorism." The Leipzig airport is an important international freight hub, also used for providing support to Ukraine. Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected Germany's allegations, calling them "the beginning of a real war." Edited by: Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.94
Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare. "The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman. Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage. "A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency. Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point. Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days. Berlin: BER operations remain restricted Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening. "Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman. She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport. "Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays. "Regular operations will resume on Friday." What did the airport say about departures and arrivals? The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land. Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said. Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website. An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2. Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains. BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year. The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal. item.title: Japan's empty temples seek new ways to survive
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.86
The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar. Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan, the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million, US3.01 million). The estate agent's pitch says the price includes dismantling by "expert heritage craftsmen" and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a "stunning" two- or three-bedroom home. The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan. There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll. That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly. A temple brought back to life Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation. "The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track," he told DW. "Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard," he said. "In the countryside, it is much more difficult." Iwayama's biggest problem is the country's shrinking population: fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple's upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard. One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple's "smart graveyard," where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative's ashes from the columbarium. Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said. "Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back," he said. "Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on." Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing. But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades. Demand for Buddhism remains "I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism," he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking. "Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person," he said. "A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer." Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockermans, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service. "We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available," he said. Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan's religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo's Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot. "I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline, and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation," he said. "Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects," he said. The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adelstein explained. Young people shun religious careers "Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside," he said. Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said. As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open. "The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation," he said. Edited by: Karl Sexton

item.title: India news: Rescue efforts underway in deadly Delhi building collapse
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.61
What you need to know - At least seven people have died after a building collapsed in Delhi - The building was located in South Delhi's Satya Niketan, popular among Delhi University students - Rescue operations are underway - India and Pakistan are exchanging barbs after UN map vote - Amritsar airport was closed briefly after drones were spotted at the border airport This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India on Monday, September 7. Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. Thank you for reading Thank you for reading our India blog. We'll be back with a fresh blog on Tuesday. See you then! WATCH — As AI data centers cause a surge in water usage, can India adapt? AI is driving a boom in data centers and a surge in water use. In India, where water is already scarce in many places, campaigners say that cost must count when new infrastructure is planned. Find out more: India, Pakistan trade barbs over Kashmir claims after UN map vote Pakistan's Foreign Office on Monday rejected India's position on Kashmir's status, after New Delhi invoked the disputed territory while commenting on a newly adopted UN resolution on map projections. The dispute comes after Friday's UN General Assembly vote backed "Correct the Map," an African-led resolution promoting more accurate cartographic representations that shrink Europe and North America while enlarging Africa. India was among 164 countries voting in favor. Later, Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India's support did not endorse any specific map or boundary depiction, adding that India's "sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India's official map," calling deviations "unacceptable." Both India and Pakistan claim Kashmir in full but rule it in part, creating a decadeslong flashpoint between the nuclear-armed neighbors. Pakistan's Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan responded Monday, saying Pakistan "categorically rejects India's baseless assertions" on Kashmir, according to Pakistan's Dawn newspaper. He said India's "illegal occupation cannot alter the internationally recognized disputed status" of the territory, calling it one of the UN Security Council's oldest unresolved disputes requiring resolution through "a free and impartial plebiscite under UN auspices." The US, the sole nation to vote against the UN resolution, separately criticized the map, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility." India's food warning labels challenged in court Indian health activists have filed the first formal court objection to the government's proposed food warning labels, calling the plan an "industry-friendly loophole" that lets many unhealthy products avoid scrutiny. The Indian government has proposed that a red hexagonal label be added if a food exceeds limits in at least two of three concerning nutrients: added sugar, salt or saturated fat. Nonprofit group 3S And Our Health told the Supreme Court the proposal would let high-risk items slip through, as a product high in just one nutrient would not be flagged, the filing, as accessed by Reuters new agency, said. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also drawn criticism over exemptions for foods like honey and jaggery. Health activists have been pushing for front-of-pack warning labels for years, but it remains unclear how effective they will be in their current form. "After years of advocacy, and after the Supreme Court pushed the issue, FSSAI has accepted a front-of-pack warning. That fight is won. The next fight is not whether there will be a label, but whether the label will tell the truth," Dr Arun Gupta, paediatrician and Convenor, Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi) told Firstpost. The Indian government intends to make rules stricter by having warning labels for each concerning nutrient in the second phase of the plan, a source told The Telegraph newspaper. According to a study published in The Lancet journal, India had 180 million adults who were overweight or obese in 2021. The number is projected to rise to 450 million by 2050. The case will be heard on September 10. Drone scare at Amritsar airport prompts flight diversions: reports Multiple suspected drones were spotted around the operational area of Amritsar's international airport Sunday night, Indian news agency ANI reported, prompting authorities to divert seven flights. Airport Director Anirudh Kumar said the Air Traffic Control (ATC) unit received information from the Indian Air Force at around 9.45 pm local time regarding suspected drone activity over the airfield. This prompted all flight operations to be suspended for 90 minutes. "Two of the flights were diverted to Chandigarh and five of them were diverted to Delhi," a Delhi airport official told the Hindustan Times. Malaysia Airlines, Air India, Air India Express and IndiGo flights were among those diverted, local news agencies reported. Amritsar's Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport is located about 30 kilometers (~18 miles) from India's border with Pakistan. Reports suggested that the drones may have been flown locally, but the sensitive nature of the airport’s location prompted swift security action from all agencies involved. Amritsar police told the Indian Express that the drones were flown during a sports tournament in a nearby village. "These drones originated from the video recording of a sports tournament. Drones were used for this purpose without permission. It is not allowed to fly drones in 8 kilometres radius of the airport. We will take legal action in this matter," said Raja Sansi Station House Officer Gurpreet Singh. At least 7 people killed as rescue efforts continue The death toll has risen to seven after rescue personnel recovered another body amid the rubble of a five-story building in India's capital city Monday, a day after the nearly 50-year-old structure came crashing down. The building was located in Satya Niketan, a popular student hub that houses hundreds of university students often living in crowded conditions. It is situated in close proximity to Delhi University's South Campus, making it a popular destination for students. Local media reported that the building housed a private hostel. In its latest update, Delhi Police said a total of 12 people had been rescued during the operation. Emergency crews say more people may be trapped in the rubble. Rescue teams, including personnel from disaster agencies as well as fire and police teams, were using heavy machinery and sniffer dogs to locate those trapped. Earlier, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), which is treating victims of the collapse, said its trauma center received 10 people: "Out of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while one patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to his injuries." Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta addressed the potential cause of the collapse, saying: "It is certain that there was water in the building's basement, and due to accumulation of water, due to ongoing repair work, the old building collapsed." The police have registered a First Information Report (FIR) under Sections 105, 290 and 125(a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (the official criminal code of India) against the building owners, local media reported. The specific sections relate to culpable homicide, negligence in the construction or repair of buildings as well as acts that endanger human life. Welcome to our coverage Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest from across India. We are back, reporting on the building collapse in an area frequented by Delhi University students, including me (albeit over 10 years ago). Rescue operations are underway, putting the lack of infrastructure, which forces students to opt for private housing options amid a severe lack of college hostels, into the spotlight. For this and more, follow our live blog.

item.title: EU's von der Leyen pledges $232 million Greenland investment
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.18
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has pledged €200 million ($232 million) investment package for Greenland as the EU seeks closer relations with the Arctic territory. Von der Leyen has been visiting Nuuk, the capital of thje Danish autonomous island, for the past two days where she met with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic counterpart Jens-Frederik Nielsen. Von der Leyen's visit comes after threats of US annexation earlier this year by President Donald Trump. What von der Leyen said? "Territorial integrity sovereignty, the inviolability of borders, these are fundamental principles of international law," von der Leyen told a joint press conference. The EU chief announced the "EU-Greenland Partnership Package," focusing on three priorities: connectivity, clean energy and critical raw materials. "This is 200 million euros of new investments for Greenland for this year and the next," von der Leyen said. She emphasized that "Greenland's future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide, no one else." The European Commission head arrived in Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Nielsen and Frederiksen. "We’re deepening our cooperation across the board. Connectivity, clean energy, critical raw materials. And of course, more opportunities for the people of Greenland," Von der Leyen said in a post on X. What does the EU investment package include? The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in: - critical minerals - satellite communications - renewable energy Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU. The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship. Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland? Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources. Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place." Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia. His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.00
Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems. In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection — a local green space known for its rapeseed blossoms — was rezoned in 2024 to make way for a five-building data center campus. The damage often extends beyond the site itself. Gas pipelines and power plants built to supply these facilities require their own land, fragmenting habitats and eroding soil along their routes. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.84
Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday. On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet. German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied. What did Dobrindt say about the shield? Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves." The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units. The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks. Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices. The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage. Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by and large, the start of a real war." He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats. "All these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again — they are being put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti. He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn. New tech planned to boost cyber security Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks. The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs. The newspaper said the government also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks. Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025 The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year. These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks. Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub. The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion. Edited by: Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
