item.title: A Great Rebalancing Is Coming
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.90
The trade imbalances that have come to characterize the global economy are fundamentally untenable. China, Germany, and a handful of other economies run large, persistent trade surpluses, while the United States absorbs much of these surpluses by running the world’s largest trade deficit. Sooner or later, something must give. For an advanced, capital-rich economy such as that of the United States, an enduring trade deficit will bring with it either rising unemployment or rising debt, neither of which is sustainable. In theory, the major surplus and deficit economies could agree on a coordinated adjustment in which surplus countries would expand domestic demand and deficit countries would gradually reduce their dependence on debt-fueled consumption, allowing the imbalances to shrink without a sharp contraction in global demand. That would be the sensible solution. But because the major players disagree about the causes of the imbalances, they are unlikely to come to such a solution. China attributes them to excessive U.S. consumption and fiscal deficits; the United States blames foreign industrial, trade, and currency policies; and Europe has yet to settle on a coherent diagnosis. As a result, they all have proposed remedies that are at odds with one another. Beijing wants deficit countries to save more and prefers not to change China’s growth model. Washington wants surplus countries to reduce their surpluses by redistributing income to the household sector. European leaders continue to advocate for multilateral cooperation and rules-based trade. This makes the chances of a coordinated response slim. And as the economic analyst Martin Wolf wrote in the Financial Times earlier this year, if there is little prospect of preemptive action, “the second-best option is to prepare for a crisis.” Individual economies are now doing just that. History shows that trade imbalances of this scale almost always end painfully—and that the pain of the adjustment is not distributed evenly. High levels of debt combined with low productivity makes a country more likely to bear the burden of a trade adjustment, but economic and political power can also give it the tools to pass the burden off to others. Among the three main economic players today, China is the most vulnerable, the United States has the most capacity to reduce its exposure, and Europe possesses latent power but a dubious ability to use it. None of their maneuvers to protect themselves are likely to reduce the risk or overall cost of a crisis. The question is only who will feel the brunt of the losses when it arrives. HISTORY REPEATS ITSELF Large, persistent trade imbalances have cropped up periodically over the past century, and they are rarely benign. One such episode occurred during the 1920s, when a surge in American productivity was not accompanied by rising wages. Production soared past consumption, and the United States ran enormous trade surpluses. Europe ran the corresponding deficits, as many countries borrowed heavily abroad to rebuild economies devastated by war. Germany in particular borrowed extensively to finance both domestic growth and its reparations payments. American domestic debt also rose rapidly, much of it to fund consumption and asset speculation. As the imbalances persisted and U.S. manufacturing expanded at the expense of European manufacturing, protectionist pressures intensified. France devalued its currency in 1927, the United Kingdom abandoned the gold standard in 1931, and the same year Germany imposed import restrictions and rationed access to foreign currency. Even the United States, whose manufacturers and farmers complained that weak demand was threatening domestic production and employment, passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act in 1930. The adjustment came in the form of a collapse in global trade during the Great Depression of the early and mid-1930s. Nearly every major economy suffered from the contraction, but they did not suffer equally. Those with large deficits, such as the United Kingdom, recovered more quickly and suffered less severe financial distress than the United States, which absorbed a disproportionate share of the costs. American exports fell faster than imports, domestic investment imploded, banks failed, and bankruptcies surged. Trade imbalances on a large scale almost always end painfully. The next major episode of persistent trade imbalances was the rare case in which the imbalances faded away without causing major disruption. During the 1950s and 1960s, the United States again ran very large surpluses while Europe and Japan ran corresponding deficits. Similar to the situation in the 1920s, these deficits financed the reconstruction of postwar economies as resources poured into infrastructure and manufacturing. But unlike in the earlier period, governments maintained strict controls over capital flows and imported capital mostly to fund investments that generated enough future income to service the associated liabilities. Because the investments were so productive, debt rose little relative to GDP. There was also minimal protectionist pressure, largely because Europe and Japan urgently needed imports and the United States actively encouraged reconstruction in both places. As a result of these unusual conditions, trade imbalances disappeared gradually without any countries bearing severe costs. Four more episodes of trade imbalances would follow, all of them ending in pain for the countries involved. One happened in Latin America during the 1970s. The oil shocks of that period, in which the global price of oil soared from roughly $2 per barrel at the beginning of the decade to around $30 per barrel by the end, generated massive petrodollar surpluses in the oil-exporting economies of the Middle East and other members of OPEC. Much of this was deposited in major international banks that, eager to find new customers, loaned the funds to Latin American and other developing economies, eventually leading to overvalued currencies and large trade deficits. By the early 1980s, rising global interest rates made their debt unsustainable. Debt crises resolved the trade imbalances but left the deficit countries with the overwhelming share of the adjustment costs: recession, inflation, austerity, and lost decades of growth. The next case developed during the late 1970s and 1980s. Japanese productivity growth outpaced Japanese wages during this period, and the country began running enormous trade surpluses. The same happened in Germany, allowing the country’s manufacturing sector to become increasingly competitive internationally. The United Kingdom and the United States ran deficits that accommodated both Japan’s and Germany’s surpluses. Japan in particular saw a spectacular surge in domestic debt during the 1980s, as extremely high levels of investment flowed into projects whose returns fell far below expectations. China has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can. Protectionist pressures rose steadily, culminating in the Plaza Accord of 1985, in which the world’s major economies agreed to appreciate the yen and the deutsche mark against the dollar in an effort to reduce trade imbalances. Yet a real resolution of the imbalances did not come until Japan’s economic downturn in the 1990s, which brought collapsing asset prices, persistent deflation, and years of stagnation. It is difficult to compare this to Germany’s experience, however, given that the 1990 unification of East and West Germany fundamentally altered the economy at precisely the same time. The Asian financial crisis of the 1990s in some ways resembled the Latin American trade imbalances of the 1970s. In the early part of the decade, foreign capital poured into a group of East Asian economies. These economies developed large trade deficits, which were balanced by surpluses in Japan, European countries, and, increasingly, China. Although their domestic and external debt rose rapidly, protectionism remained limited. Even so, when investor confidence broke in 1997, the adjustment was swift and brutal. Currency collapses, banking crises, and deep recessions struck the East Asian deficit countries, while the surplus countries bore few costs. Finally, between roughly 2002 and 2008, Germany accumulated large surpluses after implementing labor reforms that pushed wage growth down relative to productivity growth and caused huge increases in saving. It exported more and more to Greece, Portugal, Spain, and several other eurozone economies, which in turn accumulated deficits financed by rapidly rising debt. Because this dynamic emerged within the eurozone, where most members shared a common currency, countries could not impose protectionist measures and exchange-rate adjustment was impossible. When the 2008 global financial crisis triggered the eurozone crisis, the deficit countries experienced sovereign debt crises, unemployment, austerity, and prolonged stagnation that unwound the imbalances. COST ANALYSIS These events demonstrate that trade imbalances become dangerous when they are accompanied by rapidly rising debt and growing financial fragility in either surplus or deficit economies. If a country with a surplus uses its high savings to finance productive investment at home or abroad, the imbalance can persist for many years without causing serious economic disruption. But if instead its excess savings finance unproductive investment at home or drive high household consumption, asset bubbles, or persistent fiscal deficits in the economies of its trading partners, the whole system becomes increasingly shaky. Protectionism is generally not the cause of trade conflicts, but rather a symptom of imbalances that have endured for too long. Its absence does not make the eventual adjustment less painful. Yet when countries adopt protectionist policies, they can influence where the adjustment occurs and who bears the costs. Whether it is surplus or deficit economies that take on those costs may also depend on which side has the greater ability to use trade, financial, or exchange-rate policies to compel the other to adjust. Deficit countries more often bear the costs when they are politically weak and unable to finance themselves independently, defend their currencies, or restrict capital and trade flows without triggering a financial crisis—as Latin American countries were in the early 1980s, much of East Asia was in 1997, and southern Europe was after 2008. Surplus countries are at risk, meanwhile, when deficit countries have sufficiently strong economies and political systems to reduce their own deficits by restricting imports, limiting capital inflows, depreciating their currencies, or otherwise preventing the surplus countries from exporting their excess savings. This is what happened to the United States in the early 1930s and to Japan beginning in the 1990s. Their trade partners reduced their deficits by intervening to reduce imports and increase exports, forcing the U.S. and Japanese surplus-based growth models to unravel as investment collapsed and exports, profits, and asset prices fell. The main takeaway for governments today is twofold. First, the place where debt has risen furthest without a corresponding rise in productive capacity is most at risk when an adjustment to a trade imbalance eventually arrives. Second, the countries involved in imbalanced trade can take action to push adjustment costs onto others, but their success depends largely on economic power and their ability to wield it. THE CRISIS TO COME Today’s global trade imbalances are unusually large, and the coming adjustment is likely to be especially difficult. China looks most vulnerable. Its debt burden is already among the world’s highest; the country has experienced perhaps the fastest increase in debt relative to GDP in history. Much of this debt has funded investment that has generated progressively lower—even negative—economic returns, including excess residential real estate, underutilized infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity that far outstrips demand. This huge and growing debt burden creates enormous pressure on Beijing to take any steps necessary to avoid absorbing the bulk of the adjustment costs. China will almost certainly try to push as much of this burden as possible onto its trade partners. It has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can, allowing excess production to be absorbed abroad rather than forcing a sharp contraction in domestic production and employment. In doing so, China can spread the adjustment over many years as it gradually works down its debt, while its trading partners endure greater costs in the form of larger trade deficits, rising debt, deindustrialization, or weaker growth. If foreign protectionist measures or weaker external demand make this strategy impossible, however, China’s economy would face some combination of slower growth, rising unemployment, falling investment, and financial distress. Whether Beijing can offload the costs of adjustment depends on the willingness of the rest of the world to absorb them. Washington has little reason to continue allowing large, persistent trade deficits. As the world’s largest economy and by far its largest source of demand, the United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit and stop acting as the world’s consumer of last resort. And because U.S. trade policy is centralized within the executive branch—with the president able to impose tariffs, investment restrictions, and export controls under broad statutory authority—Washington has the political ability to exercise this power. If the United States uses industrial policy to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and, more important, takes greater control over its trade and capital flows using tariffs and other restrictive measures, China and other major surplus economies will not be able to maintain their surpluses with corresponding U.S. deficits. They will have to either reduce those surpluses with a painful contraction in domestic production or find new importers among countries that remain both willing and able to absorb them. The United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit. This leaves Europe in perhaps the most difficult position. The eurozone is the world’s third-largest economy and its second-largest source of demand, so Europe has economic power at its disposal. What is much less clear is whether it has the political ability to exercise this power, given its fragmented policymaking institutions and the often divergent interests of its member states. If the United States is able to reduce its trade deficit and expand its share of global manufacturing while China resists an equivalent contraction in its surpluses, a politically divided Europe could be forced to take on larger deficits almost by default. The costs could include deindustrialization, rising debt, and weaker growth. This process may have begun already. Once the major economies stop asking how to minimize the global costs of adjustment and begin asking instead how to minimize their own risk, the opportunity to find a relatively painless solution to the global trade imbalance will have passed. Beijing seems set on trying to preserve its surpluses for as long as possible. Washington is just as intent on reducing its deficits. If Europe can develop the political capacity to do the same, the burden of adjustment will increasingly fall onto the surplus economies, which would have to rely more on domestic demand and less on exports. If it cannot, Europe will absorb more and more of the global surpluses, and what appears today to be a trade conflict mainly between China and the United States may become a conflict between China and Europe—and a struggle between the two of them to avoid bearing steeper costs down the road. History makes clear that trade imbalances are always resolved eventually. What remains uncertain is how damaging the resolution will be—and for whom. item.title: The Emerging U.S.-China Détente
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.37
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump met in Beijing, in May, they agreed that their two countries should build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Although many observers in Washington responded skeptically to this new framework, dismissing it as empty words, it marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize. Strategic stability does not refer to nuclear détente; rather, it suggests a new equilibrium in which both sides can avoid further deterioration of the relationship and even expand cooperation where interests align. Leaders in Beijing do not expect that this new framework can resolve most of the differences between China and the United States or that it can stop new frictions from emerging. In June, for example, the U.S. Department of Defense placed more Chinese companies—including private-sector giants Alibaba, Baidu, and BYD—on its list of firms involved in civil-military fusion activities, barring the Pentagon from contracting with them. In retaliation, China placed ten U.S. entities on its dual-use export control list, which prevents any company from supplying them with items that have the potential for both military and civilian use. But Beijing hopes that a consensus built around strategic stability can help China and the United States manage their differences more effectively and that it will prevent the worst outcomes: military conflict or a new cold war. So far, ongoing friction has not derailed the overarching consensus established in May. By keeping sanctions and countermeasures relatively limited, Beijing and Washington have avoided dangerous escalation and kept the relationship moving forward. The goal of the new diplomatic framework between Beijing and Washington is a pragmatic one. It aims to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations rather than try to achieve an unlikely grand bargain that would resolve all conflict. It also represents a changing approach in Beijing to dealing with the United States. Unlike in the past, when China rejected U.S. frameworks focused on competition, it is now willing to recognize that the fundamental nature of U.S.-Chinese relations is competitive. Allies or partners, after all, would not set strategic stability as the overarching goal of their relationship; only competitors, or even adversaries, need to do so. Beijing’s willingness to accept a formulation to manage, rather than exclude, competition shows that it is gaining confidence and seeing itself more as an equal to Washington. Adopting this confident mindset could lead China to act with more restraint in its dealings with the United States—which could in turn bring a further degree of calm to the relationship. It now appears plausible that bilateral relations have turned a corner and entered a more stable phase. Although fundamental challenges remain that could cause new turbulence, the peak tensions of the past eight years may well be receding. The upcoming leaders’ summit in late September, when Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet in Washington, is a chance to further move the relationship forward. The two leaders can now add more concrete measures to support this new framework of strategic stability, including taking steps to reduce economic friction, increase military-to-military communications, improve crisis management mechanisms, expand citizen exchanges, and offer reassurances about Taiwan, thereby defusing tensions that could escalate into potentially catastrophic military conflict. With Xi and Trump likely to meet again multiple times in the next few months, the new framework is the first chance in years to lay the groundwork for enduring stability in bilateral ties. BEYOND STRATEGIC COMPETITION For a long time, leaders in both Beijing and Washington sought to define the bilateral relationship in terms of some kind of partnership. In 1997, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin visited the United States, Beijing and Washington announced aims of “a constructive strategic partnership oriented toward the twenty-first century.” In 2005, the George W. Bush administration urged China “to become a responsible stakeholder” in the international system; Chinese leader Hu Jintao responded in 2006 that the two countries were not only stakeholders but “should also be constructive partners.” But between 2009, when President Barack Obama and Hu agreed to “steadily grow a partnership” to address common challenges, and the Trump-Xi summit earlier this year, the countries’ leaders were unable to reach a new consensus on how to position the relationship. The United States moved away from seeing the relationship as a partnership earlier than China did. During Trump’s first term, the United States began to define U.S.-Chinese relations in terms of “strategic competition.” At first, China tried to accept the competitive element in bilateral relations. Beijing acknowledged that some competition was inevitable while hoping that the relationship could remain positive overall. But as U.S.-Chinese relations deteriorated sharply in the final year of Trump’s first term and continued to worsen into the Biden administration, Beijing began to see “strategic competition” as a narrative designed to foreclose China’s rise. It felt that the U.S. approach threatened its development prospects, leading Beijing to push back more forcefully against the concept. In July 2022, during a phone call with President Joe Biden, Xi told his counterpart that it was a mistake to make competition the defining feature of the relationship. To policymakers and analysts in China, the framework of strategic competition turned all U.S.-Chinese interactions into something akin to the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. They saw the United States’ actions such as export controls on semiconductors as concrete manifestations that the United States was trying to suppress China, to undercut its political system, and to constrain its development. Although official statements from Washington discussed bilateral ties in terms of cooperation, competition, and confrontation, in practice competition and confrontation snuffed out any potential for cooperation. After almost a decade in which China rejected and criticized strategic competition, transitioning to a relationship of constructive strategic stability reflects Beijing’s recalibrated assessment of both countries’ positions and roles in the international system, as well as the new realities of U.S.-Chinese relations. China is looking at bilateral relations from a position of greater equality and with more confidence, and it is less anxious that competition will undermine its national development prospects. Instead, Beijing believes that competition can be effectively managed without presenting an existential threat. MORE THAN ONE MAN Whether strategic stability succeeds as the basis of a new phase in U.S.-Chinese relations depends on whether it is rooted in the personal wills and agendas of Trump and Xi or it arises from structural forces that are more powerful than any individual leader. Many observers in both Beijing and Washington view the emerging consensus as a contingent result of the interests of the two men currently in charge. Trump, for instance, has taken it upon himself to change the direction of U.S. policy. His unexpected turn toward embracing a more stable relationship with China coincides with other unexpected turns in his second-term agenda, including adopting a cold and even hostile attitude toward European allies and launching a war against Iran despite frequently decrying U.S. military involvement overseas. But these shifts also obscure more durable structural factors in the U.S.-Chinese relationship that have pushed the two countries toward more stability, and which make it more likely that the new diplomatic framework can survive. The current rapprochement is the fourth time in the past eight years that a period of tension between China and the United States has given way to an announcement of some kind of stable state. Ongoing friction has not derailed the consensus established in May. After China and the United States first aggressively confronted each other on trade and technology, culminating in the trade war in 2018, the two countries reached the Phase One trade agreement, in January 2020, which stabilized ties. The COVID-19 pandemic, which broke out soon afterward, severely inflamed tensions, sending the relationship to its lowest point since before U.S. President Richard Nixon first visited China, in 1972. In November 2022, Biden and Xi met in Bali and announced that they wanted to restabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, but just months later, in February 2023, recriminations over a Chinese object floating over the United States—described by Beijing as a civilian meteorological airship and by Washington as a spy balloon—interrupted such efforts. That November, Biden and Xi smoothed over ties for a third time at their San Francisco summit. This set the tenor of relations until April 2025, when Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs spawned a new trade war. Across this period, the United States went through three different presidential terms under both Democratic and Republican administrations, yet U.S.-Chinese relations repeatedly swung back to a stable state. Structural factors independent of any individual leader’s views encourage stability in the relationship. This includes the prohibitive cost of total economic decoupling and the catastrophic consequences of potential military conflict. Put differently, since the beginning of Trump’s second term, it has become clear to both sides that the bilateral relationship is simply too big to fail. The two sides occupy such important positions in global and international affairs, each with enough power to cause enormous damage, that neither wants to see the other become an enemy. The intense clashes between China and the United States over tariffs and rare earths in 2025 revealed that each side could exploit the other’s vulnerabilities, reminding them both that the two countries are highly interdependent and need to act prudently in an economic confrontation. Moreover, as nuclear powers, Beijing and Washington are aware that they cannot afford the prospect of a steadily deteriorating relationship that increases the risk of military conflict. If U.S.-Chinese relations again become more volatile after the next U.S. president takes office, it will test the resilience of the relationship. Yet the structural forces at play are unlikely to have changed. Even if future American leaders announce a new approach to the U.S.-Chinese relationship, therefore, in the end it is likely that they will come to the same realizations as their predecessors and seek stability. TANGLED UP IN RED Other critics argue that the consensus on strategic stability is, at most, a temporary truce. In their view, both sides will use this time to shore up their weaknesses, seek new sources of leverage, and prepare for a future confrontation. The United States could find alternate suppliers for the rare-earth elements it needs, for instance, and China could find new sources of semiconductors or develop its own advanced chips. But despite intense trade and geopolitical frictions, global supply chains have proved more resilient—and more deeply intertwined—than most observers anticipated. U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology have fragmented global supply chains, but they have not severed them. Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit U.S. battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on U.S. soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence will make it particularly difficult for either the United States or China to eliminate the other’s sources of leverage. New technologies create new vulnerabilities. With the possibility of artificial general intelligence on the horizon, the frictions in the U.S.-Chinese relationship are unlikely to be concentrated in the same fields and to manifest themselves in the same ways as today. The likelihood of either China or the United States creating what Chinese martial arts novels call an “iron shirt”—a training regimen that makes someone impervious to blades and bullets—is very low. As both countries acquire more powerful, faster, and less predictable technological capabilities, what is needed to preserve stability is likely to change. Attempts by either side to achieve an overwhelming advantage or to ensure absolute security could instead heighten the other’s insecurity and intensify bilateral competition, ultimately forcing both countries to accept some mutual vulnerability and a different strategic equilibrium. The two countries are already realizing that they will have to manage the enormous challenges that AI presents, especially safety risks, whether through joint action or parallel efforts. U.S.-Chinese relations have stabilized four times over the past eight years; this also means that, viewed from the opposite perspective, the relationship has repeatedly devolved into confrontation. With each successive clash producing renewed grievances and hostility, a palpable fatigue has set in on both sides. Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways. THE EAST IS RISING One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more. But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive. Structural factors have pushed the two countries toward more stability. China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States. Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea. In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition. A NEW BALLAST The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities. Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries. Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result. The goal is to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations. As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible. Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead. A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement. item.title: 25 Years After 9/11, What Are We Failing to Imagine Now?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.27
25 Years After 9/11, What Are We Failing to Imagine Now? The counterterrorism community struggles with how technology might be applied to novel use cases. In the aftermath of the al Qaeda terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 on Sept. 11, 2001, the 9/11 Commission Report lamented a “failure of imagination” on the part of the U.S. government and intelligence community. After all, the primary weapons used in the simultaneous attacks were boxcutters, knives, and ultimately, passenger jets. Terrorists hijacking planes was certainly conceivable. Between 1968 and 1972, there were more than 130 attempted hijackings in the United States, most bound for Havana. Abroad, there were spectacular hijackings across Europe and the Middle East, often conducted by Palestinian terror groups primarily motivated by nationalism. And while these hijackings did not result in terrorists flying planes into buildings, the idea that they could had been discussed at length for decades. In fact, legendary terrorism scholar Brian Michael Jenkins warned about exactly that in 1989 at an international conference on aviation security in Israel: “The nightmare of governments is that suicidal terrorists will hijack a commercial airliner and, by killing or replacing its crew, crash into a city or some vital facility.” In the aftermath of the al Qaeda terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 on Sept. 11, 2001, the 9/11 Commission Report lamented a “failure of imagination” on the part of the U.S. government and intelligence community. After all, the primary weapons used in the simultaneous attacks were boxcutters, knives, and ultimately, passenger jets. Terrorists hijacking planes was certainly conceivable. Between 1968 and 1972, there were more than 130 attempted hijackings in the United States, most bound for Havana. Abroad, there were spectacular hijackings across Europe and the Middle East, often conducted by Palestinian terror groups primarily motivated by nationalism. And while these hijackings did not result in terrorists flying planes into buildings, the idea that they could had been discussed at length for decades. In fact, legendary terrorism scholar Brian Michael Jenkins warned about exactly that in 1989 at an international conference on aviation security in Israel: “The nightmare of governments is that suicidal terrorists will hijack a commercial airliner and, by killing or replacing its crew, crash into a city or some vital facility.” Twenty-five years after 9/11, airports can no longer be considered soft targets for terrorists. However, terrorists and violent extremists have access to a range of technologies today that either didn’t exist or were in their infancy two and a half decades ago. The internet has been most consequential for terrorists, allowing them, through websites and social media platforms, to spread their message widely; to make contact with aggrieved individuals; and to radicalize and recruit. But advances in encrypted communications, 3D printing, unmanned aerial systems (drones), virtual currencies, and artificial intelligence (AI) also can serve as force multipliers for lone actors and terrorist organizations planning attacks. Over the last decade, barriers to entry for engaging with these technologies have been appreciably lowered, and access has been commercialized, meaning everyday citizens can now acquire and master tools once obtainable only by states. In late 2026, a failure of imagination persists, though its form has evolved. While the counterterrorism community today is aware of emerging technologies in the hands of terrorists, it continues to struggle with creatively thinking through how these can be combined or applied to novel use cases. While it is beyond the scope of this essay to assess every possible tool terrorist groups could misuse, it makes sense to consider what adoption and use patterns can tell us about the potential misuse of current technologies. We tend to avoid publishing terror-attack scenarios—we’re not in the business of giving bad people good ideas. Our intent is instead to describe existing vulnerabilities so that policymakers, intelligence officials, and law enforcement agencies might pay attention and prepare accordingly, and never again suffer such a consequential failure of imagination as in the lead-up to 9/11. Terrorist groups have already used drones successfully in combat and to commit attacks on the battlefield. Twenty years ago, in 2006, Hezbollah launched multiple drones into Israeli airspace, loaded with explosives. Although most of the drones were shot down, the combination of capability and intent was foreboding. Since then, a number of terrorist groups have weaponized drones, including Hamas, the Houthis, the Islamic State, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, Iraqi Shia militias, and violent non-state actors in Pakistan, Syria, and Venezuela. Drones are now used not just in sporadic attacks, but in combined arms warfare and maneuvers by a range of violent non-state actors. However, though there have been several high-profile plots that have been disrupted, there has yet to be a spectacular terrorist attack in the West perpetrated by a group using drones. Upon closer inspection, some of these plots were nearing fruition and would likely have struck their intended targets if they had proceeded as planned. Individuals, acting independently (rather than as part of the rank-and-file of designated terrorist groups), have been experimenting with drones too. Instructional guides by Islamic State supporters have given detailed, incremental instructions to others on how to weaponize drones; these resources also make clear that drone weaponization is seen as more accessible following the advent of widely available generative AI tools. Conflicts where drones loom large—such as the Russia-Ukraine War—have also expanded the boundaries of what is possible. Although only recently commercialized, generative AI has featured in several recent terrorist plots and attacks, including on U.S. soil. AI has also been used at the organizational level by terrorist groups, including for propaganda purposes (as the Islamic State Khorasan Province has demonstrated over the past several years) and operational purposes (as seen with Boko Haram). There have been myriad examples of AI being used by lone terrorists for operational purposes as well, including assisting extremists with instructions to build bombs; providing tips on practicing exquisite operational security; and red teaming (that is, simulating the actions of adversaries looking for weaknesses) by prompting AI chatbots to have back-and-forth conversations about how to refine tactics, techniques, and procedures. While the AI safety community predominantly focuses on existential risks, violent non-state actors’ exploitation deserves serious resources and interventions too—especially as open-weight AI models become more capable and can be used by terrorists and violent extremists with no leakage. In general, agentic and generative AI may let terrorists execute organizational and operational tasks more efficiently, providing additional uplift with minimal effort. When we think about terrorists’ using emerging technologies, the reality is not “either/or”—it’s “and.” In other words, terrorists can use encrypted platforms to communicate and fund their operations with virtual currencies, and use 3D-printed components that will augment drones, and have AI assist with target selection and even pre-program the drone’s attack route. Back in 2018, conflict analyst Daveed Gartenstein-Ross openly mused about this possibility in an op-ed for Defense One, writing: “What of the next generation of terror drones? Will they use AI-enabled swarming to become more powerful and deadlier? Or think bigger: will terrorists use self-driving vehicles for their next car bombs and ramming attacks? How about assassinations?” Orchestrating a terror attack using a drone targeting a dense urban environment in the West is not a difficult feat. Indeed, it is surprising we have not yet seen a successful attack along these lines. Whether an outdoor farmer’s market or a summer concert in a park, crashing an explosive-laden drone into a crowd of civilians would be a devastating attack that, in addition to killing and injuring people, would have immense psychological impact. The internet is the pervasive facilitator that allows these technologies to be adopted by terrorist groups, their supporters, and acolytes. Without ecosystems of social media platforms, websites, self-hosted servers, messaging applications, and forums in which individuals are presented with engaging media from terrorists and violent extremists—ranging from propaganda, doctrinal essays, lifestyle content, and instructional manuals on everything from drones to operations security to AI—many of these technologies would not be readily used. Not only has the internet democratized access to information about technology, but it has also facilitated connections between terrorists and their supporters separated by vast distances. At the peak of the Islamic State’s caliphate, British hacker turned Islamic State member Junaid Hussain became the group’s “chief terror cybercoach,” remotely directing jihadist recruits in other countries on how to carry out violent attacks. Today, the Salafi jihadist terrorist threat landscape in the West is largely driven by individuals who have never set foot in a conflict theater. Nor have they received sustained guidance from terrorist rank-and-file in attack planning. Virtual currencies are used as terrorist groups solicit donations in propaganda magazines distributed online; drone weaponization manuals can be accessed in supporter forums. Even the benign internet—from online hobbyist communities to the social platforms and AI models we all use—can be misused to engineer explosives. Terrorist use of the internet is the leitmotif in terrorists adopting technology. Without access to information online, terrorists would have little choice but to travel directly to training camps, as the al Qaeda militants who perpetrated the 9/11 attacks did, congregating under the protection of the Taliban in Afghanistan. But in 2026, particularly after the foreign fighter phenomenon that saw tens of thousands of militants from dozens of countries travel to Iraq and Syria, there are far more counterterrorism measures in place to detect and disrupt terrorist travel. Perhaps most effectively, a technical infrastructure has integrated different data streams to significantly narrow the mobility of any terrorist: Fingerprinting and iris scans, forensic innovations able to identify latent prints on bomb fragments, machine-readable passports, and harmonized passenger name records have proven effective in denying travel to terrorists. Engineering marvels, specifically precision guidance, have made ultra-precise strikes possible. Perceptual hashing has made it harder for terrorists to propagate their propaganda online and has been cheap to implement. Disrupting terrorists’ use of the internet is not about preventing it entirely—which is rather unrealistic—and more about raising the costs and effort of using it to finance, recruit, radicalize, spread propaganda, and plot attacks. This requires robust cooperation between the public and private sector, with governments, law enforcement, and tech platforms working hand in glove to identify threats and prevent terrorists from exploiting the internet. Advances in artificial intelligence could prove promising for improving content moderation and removal. Machine learning has been used to identify potential terrorist propaganda for hashing. Text, speech, and vision classifiers filter millions of posts across languages, and ranking models can demote borderline content. AIs are also used to apply content policy directly. This infrastructure has been used across counterterrorism—for object detection in CCTV footage, to spot anomalies in financial flows, or to rapidly search freshly seized documents from terrorist groups. Beware shiny object syndrome, though. While terrorists openly discuss how new technologies and modes of war can be used for their purposes, attacks and disrupted plots in the West in recent years reveal reliance on simple methods. As terrorism and political violence have atomized—and perhaps because they primarily feature lone actors—stabbings, vehicle ramming, and shootings have become the most commonly executed attacks. These are predominantly perpetrated by individuals who are largely radicalized through online pathways. This does not mean that these simple methods cannot be optimized through tech-facilitated operational planning. The man who attacked New Orleans on New Year’s Day 2025 used smart glasses for reconnaissance months earlier but used vehicle ramming and a firearm during his attack; recent Islamic State-inspired individuals in Italy used a chatbot to gain information on where to strike someone optimally to paralyze them. Shiny object syndrome also plagues the counterterrorism apparatus at times: While technology has demonstrably been useful in counterterrorism, community interventions and deep human cultural knowledge have proven effective as well and should not be supplanted by technology when not appropriate. Twenty-five years after 9/11, the day that planes, the all-American invention of the Wright brothers, were turned into a weapon against Americans, a similar affliction befalls the West: Its innovations are continuously misused by terrorists against it. To prevent the next strategic surprise, serious consideration must be given to how technologies can be used in new creative ways by terrorists in order to optimize casualties, and—as is always a consideration for such actors—cause a violent spectacle. And technology is a two-way street. While it provides some advantages to terrorists and violent extremists, technology can also be harnessed by actors combating them to recognize patterns in large volumes of data and to enhance structured analytic techniques that fuse myriad streams of intelligence. Moreover, it appears that terrorists’ use of chatbots for operational planning has already become a method of intelligence gathering and, ultimately, plot disruption by law enforcement. Governments are not destined to suffer from a failure of imagination. But to ensure that the past is not prologue, it is crucial to avoid a creeping sense of complacency 25 years after the most devastating attack on U.S. soil. item.title: Turkey’s Kurdish Peace Process Is Not About Erdogan
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.28
Turkey’s Kurdish Peace Process Is Not About Erdogan The government’s negotiations with the PKK will succeed because they are driven by geopolitical threats rather than domestic concerns. In August, Turkey’s parliament passed a law that will allow thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) to lay down their weapons and thousands more political prisoners and exiles to return to normal life. Over the coming months, hundreds of PKK members are expected to travel to Turkey to take advantage of the new law and reintegrate into a country that they left behind to take up arms against. This was unimaginable only a few years ago, when Turkey and the PKK were locked in a conflict that stretched across Turkey, Iraq, and Syria. Now, for the first time in 30 years of on-and-off negotiations between the PKK and the Turkish state, a legal basis for the end of armed conflict exists. For decades, a peaceful resolution to the Kurdish conflict was long seen as vital for Turkey’s full democratization. Yet last month’s development was met with widespread criticism from some of the most outspoken supporters of Turkish democracy. Their concern, which has been voiced widely in Turkey, is that the agreement is a cynical ploy by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to win Kurdish support for perpetuating his authoritarian rule. Moreover, many question whether the government will actually follow through and provide real political concessions to the country’s Kurds. In August, Turkey’s parliament passed a law that will allow thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) to lay down their weapons and thousands more political prisoners and exiles to return to normal life. Over the coming months, hundreds of PKK members are expected to travel to Turkey to take advantage of the new law and reintegrate into a country that they left behind to take up arms against. This was unimaginable only a few years ago, when Turkey and the PKK were locked in a conflict that stretched across Turkey, Iraq, and Syria. Now, for the first time in 30 years of on-and-off negotiations between the PKK and the Turkish state, a legal basis for the end of armed conflict exists. For decades, a peaceful resolution to the Kurdish conflict was long seen as vital for Turkey’s full democratization. Yet last month’s development was met with widespread criticism from some of the most outspoken supporters of Turkish democracy. Their concern, which has been voiced widely in Turkey, is that the agreement is a cynical ploy by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to win Kurdish support for perpetuating his authoritarian rule. Moreover, many question whether the government will actually follow through and provide real political concessions to the country’s Kurds. When it comes to Erdogan, suspicion is always prudent, and the concerns raised about the peace process are hardly unreasonable. It is true that Erdogan faces constitutional constraints on securing a third term that require him to navigate significant parliamentary hurdles. It is also true that he will seek to extract domestic political benefit from this process, as he does from most political developments. Yet this is not the full story. The government’s willingness to make peace with the PKK is also driven by important national security concerns. Understanding the agreement on foreign-policy terms is crucial to appreciating why it will likely succeed—and ultimately prove beneficial for Turkey. The primary drivers of this peace process have always lain beyond Turkey’s borders, in a cascading series of events that began with Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and led through the destruction of Hezbollah, fall of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, and the current war with Iran. The fall of the Assad regime “is a direct result of the blows we have inflicted on Iran and Hezbollah,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed at the time. He was not wrong, and in Turkey, Devlet Bahceli, the leader of the ultranationalist Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) and Erdogan’s coalition partner, agreed with him: “The fire that began in Gaza spread to Lebanon, extended its shadow over Syria, reached Iraq, and ultimately produced a shock wave that penetrated the heart of Iran.” In October of 2024, shortly before the rebel assault that brought down Assad, Erdogan spoke at the opening of the Turkish parliament. In his speech, he warned that “Israel’s next target will be Turkey” and called for the “strengthening of the home front.” The very same day, Bahceli shook hands with pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party representatives in parliament—something that he had previously refrained from doing with members of a party that he had called to be banned on multiple occasions. This action alone immediately ignited talks of a new peace process between Turkey and the Kurds. Amid these geopolitical dynamics, Erdogan’s domestic political concerns played a more complicated role in the process. While he no doubt ultimately hopes to secure Kurdish support for a new term in office, any concessions to the PKK or the Kurdish movement also risk an intense nationalist backlash. Erdogan has consistently appeared uncertain about how the process would be received by Turkish nationalists and whether the Kurdish support he may be banking on will be sufficient to carry him over the line in the next election. Indeed, it was precisely the same fears that led to the collapse of the last significant peace process between the two sides more than 10 years ago. In this context, Bahceli himself has often taken the lead in publicly promoting the process, working to overcome the delays by pushing for several measures that the government had been slow to implement. Initially, as Turkey’s regional anxieties overrode Erdogan’s political hesitations, the peace process got off to a hectic start. Numan Kurtulmus, the speaker of the Turkish parliament and a senior figure in Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party, framed the urgency of the new peace process through a familiar conspiratorial trope in Turkish nationalist and Islamist traditions: the belief that external powers seek to weaken and ultimately partition Turkey. Warning that “in the so-called ‘Greater Israel’ project, Turkey is seen as the primary force to be absorbed,” he argued that this reality requires Ankara to “fortify its home front.” Since the outset of the process, fortifying the home front against “global imperialist conspiracies and Zionist ambitions” has emerged as a central organizing concept across the Turkish government’s public messaging. While the Palestinian cause is an ideological issue for Erdogan, the widening instability in the region—and its implications for Kurdish aspirations—is a unifying concern for the entire Turkish political and security establishment. With Operation Midnight Hammer in 2025, a major fear for Turkey had become reality. Iran—the country with the second-largest Kurdish population after Turkey—was now in the crosshairs, and, after Iraq in 2003 and Syria in 2011, the Kurds once again appeared to be poised to take center stage. In both Syria and Iran, the most capable forces on the ground are PKK-affiliated groups—the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and the Free Life Party of Kurdistan (PJAK), respectively. In an attempt to get ahead of the curve, the Turkish government turned to negotiating with the person whom both organizations see as their leader: Abdullah Ocalan. Ankara’s main concern was that regional upheaval, especially in Syria and Iran, could strengthen Kurdish autonomy or political leverage in ways that eventually reverberate inside Turkey. A second concern is the prospect of Israel deepening ties with Kurdish actors—again, especially in Syria and Iran. From Ankara’s perspective, closer Israeli-Kurdish relations would not only empower Kurdish movements in ways that complicate Turkey’s own domestic challenges but would also alter the regional balance of power by enhancing Israel’s reach and capabilities in the emerging Turkey-Israel regional rivalry. While it was widely reported last year that Syrian Kurdish officials had met with Israeli counterparts, such contacts remained far removed from the kind of sustained and institutional engagement that Ankara fears. Ankara regularly hosts Hamas, but we remain far from seeing the PKK in Tel Aviv. In effect, the presence and operational capabilities of the SDF and PJAK have given Ocalan more leverage in his negotiations with the Turkish government than the PKK ever possessed within Turkey alone. It is no coincidence, then, that the earliest and most visible outcomes of the negotiations have so far materialized in these two arenas. Ocalan reportedly intervened in Syria to help peacefully resolve the fighting between the SDF and the new government in Damascus at the beginning of this year, leading to the SDF’s integration into the new Syrian state. The Turkey-PKK peace process’s impact on Iran has yet to fully manifest itself, but Turkish columnist Abdulkadir Selvi—widely seen as a conduit for government messaging—recently argued that it prevented the United States from deploying PKK-affiliated groups into Iran during Operation Epic Fury, forcing Washington to instead engage with less-capable Kurdish organizations. The chain of regional events set in motion on Oct. 7, 2023, coupled with a need to transcend Turkey’s historic vulnerabilities, have both energized and unified Turkey’s ruling elites around a new Kurdish policy. Even the main opposition party has backed the peace process, despite its leading presidential contender, Ekrem Imamoglu, being imprisoned in what is widely viewed as a politically motivated trial. This exceptionally rare political consensus reflects a deeper, if paradoxical, reality: No other country has grasped the significance of Kurdish agency in the Middle East quite like Turkey has. In a recent statement, Bahceli characterized the peace process as “not merely a matter of security, but one of strengthening brotherhood, national unity, and solidarity.” In a country where a significant portion of the population has been willing to take up arms in pursuit of ethnic rights, there is a lot to do for true unity to be achieved. It will ultimately require legal and constitutional reforms that allow Kurds to govern their towns and their local economies without the risk of arbitrary intervention by the government. What’s more, it is unrealistic to expect Kurds to feel secure in their rights unless Turkey’s authoritarian downtrend is reversed and members of other political parties are no longer being systematically jailed. That said, the PKK’s immediate expectations are more limited and pragmatic than a wholesale democratization of Turkey. At the outset of negotiations, Ocalan made it clear that he had no cultural or ethnic preconditions for ending the armed struggle. At this stage, the process rests on the PKK’s confidence that it can transition from an armed movement into a legitimate political and civil actor without being dismantled or excluded from public life. The most immediate test for Ankara will be Ocalan’s status. The PKK expects improvements to his working conditions in prison and, crucially, greater access to the outside world so that he can communicate freely with the movement and play an effective role in managing its transition away from armed struggle. None of this necessarily requires Erdogan to stop repressing political opponents or suddenly embrace liberal democracy, and Ocalan’s willingness to bring the process this far without such commitments suggests that he does not regard broader democratization as a prerequisite for taking the first steps. But for the process to advance beyond disarmament, the PKK will need evidence that laying down its weapons creates political space rather than simply eliminating the only leverage that it has possessed for half a century. In that sense, the immediate question is less about whether Erdogan is prepared to democratize Turkey than whether he is prepared to accommodate the PKK’s transformation into a legitimate, exclusively civilian actor. Peace does not guarantee democracy, but it is a prerequisite for it. Pro-democracy critics of the current process should recognize that even while the fate of Turkish democracy will remain dangerously uncertain whatever happens with the Kurds, ending the state’s military conflict with the PKK is an important achievement in its own right. The PKK has now laid down its arms. If Turkey permanently ends its military operations against all Kurdish organizations, including those in Syria, Iraq, and Iran, then the process will have succeeded on geopolitical terms. This will measurably improve the lives of all people in the region and set the stage for the fight for democracy to continue on more favorable terrain. At a moment when the Middle East appears to be poised for prolonged turbulence, stabilizing the Kurdish question at home may prove to be Turkey’s most consequential strategic investment in its own future. Giran Ozcan is the fellow for Kurdish affairs at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription.
