item.title: World Food Programme's Carl Skau discusses Yemen's food insecurity crisis
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.65
World Food Programme's Carl Skau discusses Yemen's food insecurity crisis NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with Carl Skau of the World Food Programme about the food insecurity crisis in Yemen. LEILA FADEL, HOST: Not many people are getting in and out of Yemen these days. Carl Skau did, though. He leads the U.N.'s World Food Programme. And we reached him just hours after he left. CARL SKAU: I spoke to women who were not eating more than once or maybe not even once a day because they're not just getting the assistance they need. You know, we used to provide them food and cash. The food is now gone. And the cash is only every other month. FADEL: Yemen is already in the middle of a civil war that's currently escalating between the Iran-backed Houthis, who control two-thirds of the country, and the internationally recognized government. Now parts of the country are in famine. SKAU: I also spoke to young men who were eager to try to join the conflict because they also didn't have any opportunities. And they weren't able to put food on the table for their families. FADEL: And since the U.S. and Israel started a war with Iran, the Houthis are getting involved in that regional conflict, too. They're threatening to shut down access to a strait in the Red Sea by attacking ships. And overnight, they struck Saudi oil facilities and other civilian infrastructure, injuring dozens. Skau says the consequences could be broad. SKAU: We're extremely concerned that this escalates further - maritime trade, which are important for global food security as well. It has already disrupted the economy inside Yemen, with some 18 million people who are acutely food insecure. And this crisis is now pushing them further onto the brink. We have had severe cuts in our programs because of the cuts in funding over the past few months. So quite a desperate situation. But already these funding cuts are really having a great impact. FADEL: And the funding cuts, are they because of the U.S. government's cuts to USAID and to the U.N.? SKAU: Well, it's across the board. Obviously, in the north, the main issue is that we don't have the basic conditions to operate. FADEL: Because of the Houthis' control there? SKAU: Exactly. Seventy-three U.N. colleagues have been detained, 38 of them from WFP. Our offices are occupied. Our assets are confiscated. So the basic conditions to operate in the north is no longer there. In the south, it's really an impact of funding cuts. And that's across the board for donors. And so we assisted some 3 million people a year ago. We're now down to 1 million. FADEL: What needs to happen so that more humanitarian aid can get to hungry people across Yemen? SKAU: Well, I think, one, there needs to be political attention to this. I know the competition is high now. But this is a very critical situation, and so that there is diplomatic efforts to try to deescalate the situation and ultimately try to find a path towards a peaceful settlement here. Second, of course, we need to fund the humanitarian operations. We are effectively working in the south, and so those operations need to be funded. The people that have been displaced, that are struggling, need to be supported. And, third, there needs to be a solution in the north. The Houthis need to be convinced to allow for principled humanitarian action and for our colleagues to be released. FADEL: You're speaking to the largest radio network in the United States. And there are going to be people who are listening thinking, well, Yemen is so far away - the Houthis are part of the problem. Why should I care about this? Why should my government care about this? What do you say to them? SKAU: Twelve percent of world trade passes outside Yemen. And this conflict is now having a disruption on that trade route. In addition to the Strait of Hormuz that everyone knows about, in addition to the Black Sea, where there is escalation between Ukraine and Russia right now. And so these are three choke points that are really pushing global trade. And it's pushing up prices across not only in the developing world, but also in the U.S. and Europe. And so if this is not brought under control, it's going to have a massive impact on stability across the world. FADEL: And for Yemenis, if something is not done to deescalate now, what does that mean for them? SKAU: They are already struggling. Half the population are struggling to put food on their tables. And of course, further escalation is going to mean more displacement, more economic crisis. And, you know, Yemen is already a country that's importing 90% of its food. So these disruptions to trade route is also hitting hard on the Yemenis. And, you know, I met a lot of desperate people who just cannot take anything more. And children are already malnourished. They will have damage for the rest of their life unless they are being treated and supported urgently. And so we need attention to this situation. We need funding for our operations. And we need to be able to operate across the country. FADEL: Carl Skau is the acting executive director of the World Food Programme. We're speaking just hours after he left Yemen. Thank you so much for speaking with us. SKAU: Thank you for having me. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. item.title: TSA is letting PreCheck members past airport security without a plane ticket
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.82
The Gateside by TSA PreCheck program is active at 13 airports and allows eligible visitors to shop, dine, and meet passengers at the gate Named Gateside by TSA PreCheck, the no-cost program is currently operational at 13 U.S. airports, among them Los Angeles International Airport, Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, and San Diego International Airport. TSA said it plans to expand the program to additional airports in the coming months. Eligible visitors can use the program to walk family members to their gates, greet travelers coming off a flight, or browse the dining and retail options on the secured side of the checkpoint. To qualify, applicants must hold TSA PreCheck benefits and a Known Traveler Number. Children may participate but must be listed on a parent or guardian's application. Applications must be submitted through an online portal no earlier than three days and no later than one day ahead of the intended visit. Once approved, they present an acceptable form of identification at the TSA PreCheck screening lane and may be asked to show their approval status on a mobile device. Screenshots and printouts are not accepted. Passes are valid for one calendar day. The program represents a limited loosening of airport access restrictions that have been in place since the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, according to Newsweek. Before those attacks, people who had no intention of flying were typically free to move through checkpoints and spend time at the gates. In the aftermath, only ticketed passengers and a limited category of authorized individuals — such as adults escorting unaccompanied children or helping travelers with disabilities — were permitted beyond the checkpoint. Receiving a Gateside pass does not exempt visitors from security screening; they must clear the TSA PreCheck lane just as any ticketed traveler would. Gateside passes also do not grant access to TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes, and the program may not be available when airports are operating at high capacity. Airport officials at participating locations have welcomed the program. Columbus Regional Airport Authority president and CEO Daren Griffin said in a statement, according to Newsweek, that the program "helps bring back special moments that many travelers have missed – welcoming loved ones at the gate, enjoying a meal together before a flight, or simply sharing time in the terminal." The other participating airports are Mesa Gateway Airport in Arizona, John Glenn Columbus International Airport in Ohio, Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport in Michigan, Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport in Kansas, Indianapolis International Airport in Indiana, Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport in Arkansas, Will Rogers International Airport in Oklahoma, Eppley Airfield in Nebraska, and Salt Lake City International Airport in Utah. item.title: 10 under-the-radar cities crowned the world's most walkable for 2026
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.58
10 under-the-radar cities crowned the world's most walkable for 2026 Some of the easiest cities to explore on foot never crack the top lists. Skyscanner ranks 10 under-the-radar destinations built for walking in 2026 Getting around a new city usually means picking between a few flawed options. A taxi gets stuck in traffic, a metro system takes explaining nobody has offered yet, or a long walk turns into a slog because two "nearby" landmarks turn out to be 40 minutes apart. Cities that avoid this problem tend to share a few traits. Their historic cores stay compact, their major sights sit within a reasonable stroll of each other, and their streets don't force pedestrians to dodge six lanes of traffic every few blocks. None of that happens by accident. It usually comes down to a city's layout, its elevation, its air quality and even its crime rate, all of which shape whether a place is genuinely pleasant to explore on foot rather than merely survivable. That combination of factors is starting to matter more in how people choose where to go next. Flight-search data increasingly shows travelers drifting away from the handful of famous European capitals that dominate every "best city break" roundup, toward smaller, less congested alternatives that still deliver a full day of sightseeing without ever needing a rental car. Population density and pollution levels play a bigger role in that shift than most travelers realize. A city can have all the right landmarks and still feel exhausting to explore if its sidewalks are narrow, its air is thick with smog, or its crowds turn every street into a scrum. The cities picking up interest for exactly this reason tend to be smaller, quieter and, in more than one case, cities most travelers couldn't have placed on a map a few years ago. Skyscanner built its 2026 walkability index by first mining its own flight-search data to identify 30 rising city-break spots beyond the United States, deliberately skipping over perennial favorites like Berlin and Dubrovnik. From there, it scored each contender across 14 separate factors, among them the walking distance between major attractions, the total steps and time needed to cover that distance, average elevation, the number of walking trails, air quality, pollution levels, crime rates, population density and the sheer number of attractions on offer. The result is a top 10 list of cities most travelers have never seriously considered visiting, let alone walking across. Cordoba, Spain Alex / Unsplash Twenty-six minutes. That's how long it takes to walk between Cordoba's major sights, and it's enough to put the Spanish city at No. 1 on Skyscanner's 2026 walkability index, with the lowest walking distance of any city on the list. Cordoba packs an enormous amount of history into that short stroll. Once a major Roman city and later a center of Islamic learning in medieval Al-Andalus, its historic core carries UNESCO World Heritage status and is built around La Mezquita, the Great Mosque-Cathedral. The building sprawls across 24,000 square meters and rests on 856 columns supporting double-stacked arches, a design the Umayyads began around 785 and expanded for two centuries before Christian rulers added a full Baroque cathedral at its center in the 16th century. The original minaret was converted into the bell tower now known as the Torre Campanario. Getting inside for free is its own small ritual. Monday through Saturday, the Mosque-Cathedral opens without charge between 8:30 and 9:30 a.m., though locals recommend a weekday visit after 4 p.m. instead, when the tour groups have mostly cleared out. The building has 19 gates in total, but only six lead into the Patio de los Naranjos, the orange-tree courtyard that visitors reach first and can enter free at any hour of the day. Beyond the Mezquita, Cordoba's other major stops, the Palacio de Viana, La Juderia and the Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, sit close enough together that walkers rack up just 2,730 steps covering all of them. Around the city, 29 separate walking trails extend the options well past the historic core. Visitors looking to round out the day can catch a traditional flamenco show, walk across the Roman Bridge at sunset, or try oxtail cooked Cordovan style, a slow-braised dish that shows up on nearly every menu in the old town. Nagasaki, Japan Tayawee Supan / Unsplash Built across a working harbor with buildings terraced into the hills around it, Nagasaki claims the No. 2 spot on Skyscanner's 2026 list, helped along by the lowest crime rate of any city in the top 10. The city carries a heavy history that shapes almost every major attraction, starting with the Atomic Bomb Museum and continuing through Peace Park and the man-made island of Dejima. In August 2025, Nagasaki marked 80 years since the atomic bombing, with about 2,600 people, including survivors and representatives from more than 90 countries, gathering for the annual memorial ceremony. That same week, the twin bells of Urakami Cathedral rang together for the first time since 1945, after a second bell, funded by Catholics in the United States, was cast to replace the one destroyed in the blast. Nagasaki has also picked up international attention beyond its wartime history. The New York Times named the city in its 2026 list of places to visit, pointing to a major redevelopment project around the main train station as a reason travelers now have fresh cause to stop there. On the ground, the numbers back up the ease of exploring. There are 531 separate attractions within a city whose average elevation is a gentle 89 meters, flat enough to keep most walks manageable. Local survivors' groups have spent the years since the 80th anniversary digitizing hibakusha testimony for younger generations, translating decades of firsthand accounts into video archives meant to outlast the dwindling number of people who lived through the bombing itself. Beyond the memorial sites, visitors can catch the autumn Sasebo Yosakoi dance festival, ride the cable car up Mount Inasa for a sweeping night view of the harbor, ride the ferry to the beaches of Goto island, or grab a Sasebo burger, a local specialty dating back to the city's decades as a U.S. naval port. Hiroshima, Japan Redd Francisco / Unsplash It takes 41 minutes to walk between Hiroshima's major sites. That pace, combined with a strong safety record both day and night, is enough to land the city at No. 3 on Skyscanner's 2026 walkability ranking. Like Nagasaki, Hiroshima's story can't be separated from the 1945 bombing that defines the city's global reputation, and the Peace Memorial Museum sits at the center of any visit. The museum has now broken its own attendance record three years running, drawing 2.58 million visitors in fiscal 2025 alone. Foreign travelers made up nearly 37% of that total, or 945,618 people, a nearly threefold increase from a decade earlier, as global interest in the site has grown alongside rising tension over nuclear weapons and a 2024 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to the Japanese survivors' organization Nihon Hidankyo. Beyond the museum, the index credits Hiroshima with 771 separate attractions and a total of 3,959 steps between the major ones. The nearby National Peace Memorial Hall for the Atomic Bomb Victims set its own record too, drawing 515,784 visitors, up 10.6% from the year before, as the two sites increasingly draw foreign tourists together rather than as separate stops. Rising visitor numbers have not been entirely smooth. During last year's Obon holiday, one of Japan's busiest travel weeks, crowds grew so dense that staff had to temporarily halt entry to the museum on multiple occasions, prompting organizers to rework the flow of visitors for 2026. The riverside food hall Okonomimura is worth the detour for okonomiyaki, the savory layered pancake that's become the city's signature dish, sold from dozens of small stalls stacked on top of each other. Late March brings its own crowds to the park surrounding the Peace Memorial as the cherry trees bloom, while the floating Torii gate a short ferry ride away on Miyajima island remains one of the most photographed sights in the country. With record visitor numbers still climbing, Hiroshima's museum has started encouraging travelers to book tickets online in advance to avoid the queues that now form daily outside its doors. Reggio Calabria, Italy antonino trimboli / Unsplash Reggio Calabria sits across the Strait of Messina from Sicily, and most travelers rush past it on the way to the ferry port. Skyscanner's 2026 list ranks the city No. 4 anyway, pointing to its small size and clean air as reasons to actually stop. City limits cover just 239 square kilometers, and the walk between its main attractions takes only 25 minutes and 2,321 steps, the kind of distance that makes an afternoon feel unhurried rather than rushed. The waterfront promenade was once called "the most beautiful kilometer in Italy" by the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio, and on a clear day it delivers views straight across the water to Mount Etna. The city's real draw sits inside the Museo Nazionale della Magna Grecia, home to the Riace Bronzes, two nearly life-size Greek warrior statues cast around 450 B.C. A diver named Stefano Mariottini stumbled onto them by chance in 1972, submerged eight meters underwater off Riace Marina, and after years of restoration work in Florence and Reggio Calabria they were finally installed in the museum in 1981. The statues now stand in a climate-controlled room on earthquake-proof pedestals, their eyes made of calcite and glass paste and their lips detailed in copper and silver. The same room holds two bronze heads from the same era, known simply as the Philosopher and the King, and the whole gallery sits behind an airlock designed to keep temperature and humidity from ever fluctuating in a region still prone to earthquakes. Visitors who make the trip can pair the museum with a plate of Fileja Tropeana, a hand-rolled Calabrian pasta usually served with a spicy 'nduja sauce, a fitting reward for a city built to be seen on foot rather than glimpsed from a ferry window. Most tourists still barrel straight through Reggio Calabria on their way to the Sicily ferry without stopping to look around, missing a city built at a scale that rewards a slower pace. Monte Carlo, Monaco Maxime Vandenberge / Unsplash Monte Carlo is better known for supercars and casino chips than sensible walking shoes, but the city still lands at No. 5 on Skyscanner's 2026 walkability index. Part of the reason is sheer scale. Monte Carlo's city limits cover just 0.44 square kilometers, small enough that walkers can cover the 100 attractions packed inside it, including the Oceanographic Museum of Monaco, Casino Square $SQ and the Private Cars Collection of the Prince of Monaco, in a brisk 36-minute loop. The hills can be steep in places, but the compact footprint more than makes up for the incline, and public elevators and escalators built into the hillsides help walkers cut between the harbor and the upper districts without the climb. Monaco's tightly packed streets also mean crowds concentrate fast whenever a major event lands. Timing a visit around the calendar is worth planning ahead. Hotel rates in the principality can multiply several times over during race week alone. Monaco's calendar gives visitors plenty of reasons to plan a walking trip around a specific date. The 2026 Formula 1 Grand Prix ran on June 7, 78 laps around the 3.337-kilometer Circuit de Monaco that doubles as the city's own streets for race weekend, with Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli taking the win and becoming the youngest driver ever to claim the race. A Formula E round followed in May on the same circuit, and the Monte Carlo Rally, the opening round of the World Rally Championship, ran from January 22 to 25 across a mix of tarmac and snow stages in the surrounding mountains. Outside race season, the streets return to their usual mix of designer storefronts and idling supercars, and a walk up to Rue des Remparts still delivers one of the best views in the principality, looking out over the harbor toward the Palais Princier de Monaco. Tartu, Estonia Marek Lumi / Unsplash Estonia's second-largest city, Tartu, rounds out the middle of Skyscanner's 2026 list at No. 6, propelled by the lowest air pollution score of any city in the top 10. Tartu built that reputation deliberately. The city has been shortlisted for the 2026 European Green Pioneer of Smart Tourism competition, and its public buses now run on renewable biomethane. That switch saves an estimated 4,330 tonnes of carbon dioxide every year. A bike-share network of more than 800 bicycles and a set of dedicated cycling lanes connecting tourist sites to residential neighborhoods round out the push toward low-impact transportation. The city earned its cultural credentials well before the sustainability push. Tartu served as a European Capital of Culture in 2024, a year National Geographic Traveller called one of the 30 most exciting destinations to visit, and it followed that up by holding the title of Estonia's Culinary Capital in 2025. The Kissing Students statue near the Town Hall Square $SQ has become the symbol of that cultural run, inspiring an annual one-day festival built around art, music and a mass public kiss. On the ground, the index clocks Tartu's average elevation at a gentle 53 meters across city limits of just 39 square kilometers, flat and compact enough to cover comfortably on foot. The University of Tartu, founded in 1632 and among the oldest in Northern Europe, still gives the city its energy. Roughly one in five residents is a student. Visitors can walk the neoclassical Old Town, tour the Estonian National Museum, wander the Botanical Garden of the University of Tartu, or take in the view from Toome Hill Park before finishing with a food tour through the city's growing restaurant scene. The town hall on Raekoja Plats, completed in 1789 in a mix of neoclassical, Rococo and Baroque styles, anchors the same square as the Kissing Students statue, making the central plaza an easy loop to cover on foot before heading out toward the riverbanks. Bursa, Türkiye Furkan Ataç / Unsplash Long before Istanbul became its capital, the Ottoman Empire ruled from Bursa, and that history helps explain why the city sits at No. 7 on Skyscanner's 2026 walkability list. Bursa and the nearby village of Cumalikizik were jointly named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014 under the title "the Birth of the Ottoman Empire," recognizing the kulliyes, complexes combining a mosque, school, public bath and free kitchen for the poor, that shaped the city's urban plan after Orhan Gazi captured it in 1326. The same index also ranked Bursa the single most accessible city on its separate 2026 wheelchair-friendly list, citing its wide, uncrowded routes and the accessible layout of the Bursa Museum. On foot, Bursa spreads out more than some of the other cities on this list, requiring about an hour and 5,324 steps to cover the main sights, though a low population density of just 306 people per square kilometer keeps the walk from ever feeling crowded. Known historically as the Royal Springs for hot mineral baths that have drawn visitors since Roman and Byzantine times, the city today mixes 406 catalogued attractions with a genuinely modern, industrial pulse. Bursa's role as a Silk Road hub still shows in the Koza Han bazaar, where merchants have traded silkworm cocoons since the 15th century, a trade the medieval traveler Ibn Battuta once described after passing through the city's fine bazaars and wide streets. The Tomb of Osman Gazi and the Bursa Grand Mosque anchor most itineraries today, and the bustling covered markets remain the best place to feel the commercial energy of that history. Visitors shouldn't leave without trying a plate of Iskender kebab, sliced lamb served over pita with tomato sauce and browned butter, a dish invented in the city in the 1860s and still considered its culinary calling card. Bursa and the neighboring village of Cumalikizik together form a serial UNESCO listing of eight component sites, meaning the World Heritage designation covers not just the city's mosques and bazaars but a genuine working village that still shows what rural Ottoman life looked like beyond the palace walls. Bolzano, Italy Riccardo Nestola / Unsplash Bolzano is the gateway to the Dolomites, and most travelers treat it as a fueling stop before heading up into the mountains to ski or climb. Skyscanner's 2026 index puts the city itself at No. 8, citing its compact size and its status as the safest city in the entire top 10. City limits run just 52 square kilometers, and more than 505 separate walking trails wind through the surrounding vineyard-covered hills, giving visitors far more options than the hour it takes to stroll between the main sights in town. The city's biggest single draw is the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, better known locally as the Ötzi Museum, after the 5,300-year-old glacial mummy discovered by German hikers in 1991 near the Austrian border at 3,210 meters above sea level. Ötzi has been on permanent display since 1998 in a specially built chamber kept at a constant minus 6 degrees Celsius and 98% humidity, viewable through a small window, making the museum one of the most visited in the entire Alps despite its single-artifact focus. The exhibition spreads across three floors, moving from the mummy itself on the first level up to the historical context of his Copper Age world and finally to interactive displays exploring how researchers pieced his story together from a Stone Age copper axe, a bearskin cap and a fatal arrow wound. Beyond the mummy, Bolzano's historic center revolves around Walther Plaza and the arcaded Via dei Portici, and the surrounding valleys support a serious wine industry worth exploring on a guided tour through hillside vineyards. After a day on foot, canederli, bread dumplings served in broth, remain the regional dish to order. Plans are already underway to relocate the museum to a larger site elsewhere in Bolzano in the coming years, a move officials say will finally let the collection expand beyond its single-artifact reputation into a fuller picture of South Tyrol's deeper archaeological record. Sarajevo, Bosnia & Herzegovina ADEV / Unsplash Sarajevo's Old Town is a tangle of cobbled streets and Ottoman-era bazaars pressed between the Miljacka River and the Dinaric Alps. Skyscanner ranks the city No. 9 on its 2026 walkability index, thanks in part to how much of that history fits into a compact core, with just 22 minutes needed to walk between the top attractions and a population density of only 328 people per square kilometer. Sarajevo city hall, the Bascarsija bazaar and the Latin Bridge, where the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand set off World War I, all sit within easy reach of each other, alongside 513 catalogued attractions in total. The city's more recent history is just as walkable, if considerably heavier. Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics, welcoming 49 nations and producing Yugoslavia's first-ever Winter medal when skier Jure Franko took silver in the giant slalom. The abandoned bobsled and luge track built for the Games on Mount Trebević, later used as an artillery position during the 1992-1996 siege, is now open to the public and covered in layers of graffiti along its 1,300-meter, 13-turn concrete curve. The cable car up Trebević reopened in 2018 after a 26-year closure caused by war damage, and the roughly seven-minute ride now costs about 15 euros round-trip for foreign visitors, giving them an easy way to reach the track without the hike. Back in the city center, the Museum of Crimes against Humanity and Genocide and the War Childhood Museum offer a sobering counterpoint to the coffee culture and cobbled charm of Bascarsija, while a bowl of Bosanski lonac, a slow-cooked meat and vegetable stew, remains the standard way to end a day of walking through the city's layered history. Few cities anywhere pack Olympic glory, wartime siege and a compact, walkable Ottoman-era core into the same few square kilometers, and that density is a large part of why Sarajevo keeps drawing visitors back for a second look. Victoria, British Columbia Vlad D / Unsplash No city in Skyscanner's 2026 top 10 scores higher for air quality than Victoria, British Columbia, which closes out the list at No. 10. The Canadian capital of British Columbia sits on the southern tip of Vancouver Island, and its Victorian-era architecture has earned it a reputation as one of the most British-feeling cities in the country. More than 457 walking trails wind through and around the city, giving visitors far more options for exploring on foot than the compact downtown core alone would suggest, and city limits cover a manageable 223 square kilometers overall. Victoria's biggest draw outside downtown is Butchart Gardens, roughly 55 acres of themed flowerbeds built inside a converted limestone quarry that now pulls in close to a million visitors a year. Whale-watching tours departing directly from the Inner Harbour report sighting success rates between 95% and 98%, with three-hour trips into the Salish Sea starting around CA$149, or about $110, putting orcas, humpback whales and sea lions within reach of a single afternoon out on the water. The Inner Harbour itself doubles as the city's front door for visitors arriving by BC Ferries from the mainland or by floatplane, a roughly 35-minute hop from downtown Vancouver that lands walkers within a few blocks of the Fairmont Empress Hotel and the British Columbia Parliament Buildings, both dating to the late 19th century. Back on land, the Royal BC Museum is widely considered the best museum in the country, while Craigdarroch Castle, Emily Carr House and Helmcken House each offer a different window into the city's 19th-century origins. A plate of fresh seafood down at the wharf, an afternoon in Beacon Hill Park and a walk along the Inner Harbour round out a visit built almost entirely around exploring on foot. Most visitors from the mainland cross over on BC Ferries from Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay, a roughly 90-minute sailing that turns the approach itself into part of the sightseeing before a single step gets walked in the city.

item.title: America's 10 most walkable cities for 2026, ranked by Walk Score
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.47
America's 10 most walkable cities for 2026, ranked by Walk Score Some U.S. cities let you ditch the car for good, if you pick the right one. Walk Score ranks America's 10 most walkable spots for 2026 Car ownership in the United States is expensive enough that plenty of people would drop it entirely if their city actually let them. A handful of American cities do. In these places, groceries, a doctor's office, a decent bar and a subway stop all sit within a few blocks of nearly everywhere you'd want to live, and a car becomes a weekend convenience rather than a daily necessity. Most American cities aren't built this way. Wide arterial roads, single-use zoning and long blocks turn even a short errand into a drive, which is exactly why the exceptions stand out so clearly on a map of the country. The gap between a walkable city and a car-dependent one shows up in ways beyond convenience. Households that give up a car altogether save somewhere in the neighborhood of $10,000 to $12,000 a year compared with those that keep one, and residents of walkable neighborhoods log 35 to 45 more minutes of exercise every week than people in car-dependent areas, without ever setting foot in a gym. Real estate markets price the difference too. Homes in more walkable neighborhoods tend to carry a meaningful premium over otherwise similar homes in car-dependent ones. Carbon footprints track the same pattern, with dense, walkable metro areas producing dramatically less per-capita emissions than sprawling ones. Residents of walkable neighborhoods also consistently report stronger social ties with the people around them. That kind of connection tends to come from running into a neighbor on the sidewalk rather than passing them in traffic. Walk Score built its ranking around a simple 0-to-100 scale that treats any address the same way. It measures how close a location is, on foot, to the groceries, schools, parks, restaurants and shops that make up daily life. A destination within a five-minute walk earns full marks, while the algorithm also weighs population density, block length and intersection density to capture how pleasant a walk actually feels rather than just how far it is. Among the 130 U.S. cities with populations over 200,000, the average score sits at just 48, which is what makes anything above 70 worth paying attention to. Ten American cities cleared that bar for 2026, and the list traces a rough map of where car-free American life is actually possible. San Francisco, California Natalie Chaney / Unsplash San Francisco's Walk Score of 88.7 is the highest of any major U.S. city, and the ranking holds even with the hills factored in. The city packs an unusual diversity of walkable neighborhoods into a 49-square-mile footprint, from Chinatown's dense grid to the Victorian rowhouses of Hayes Valley. Much of that walkability is now locked in by policy rather than just geography. San Francisco voters made a 1.5-mile stretch of JFK Drive through Golden Gate Park permanently car-free in November 2022, backing the measure by a 63% margin after the road had already spent two pandemic years closed to traffic. The city's Better Streets Plan, along with a wave of pandemic-era parklets that never went away, has kept pushing street space toward pedestrians rather than parking. The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency's pedestrian program continues adding safer crossings, wider sidewalks and red-painted visibility curbs across the city, and both Dolores Park and the Presidio give walkers some of the most scenic car-free ground in the country to cover. Even the hills that define the city's skyline have become part of its pedestrian identity. Historic cable cars exist specifically to carry walkers up the steepest grades rather than around them. Chinatown, the Tenderloin and North Beach anchor the densest, most walkable stretch of the city, while Hayes Valley and Nob Hill offer a quieter version of the same car-optional lifestyle just a short walk away. Polk Gulch and the Mission District round out the list, each dense enough with restaurants, corner stores and transit stops that skipping a car becomes a realistic choice rather than a hardship. Part of what makes all of this work is simple geography. San Francisco covers only about seven miles by seven miles, meaning even a cross-town trip rarely demands more than a bus transfer or two. The Presidio, a former Army post turned national park at the city's northern tip, adds hundreds of acres of forested, mostly car-free trails to that same compact footprint, connecting directly to the Golden Gate Bridge for walkers willing to cover a bit more ground. New York City, New York Luca Bravo / Unsplash New York City's Walk Score sits just behind San Francisco's at 88.0. On one measure the city stands alone, with 55% of households getting by without a car, the highest rate in the nation. The borough's grid system makes navigation almost foolproof, and a scattering of Manhattan neighborhoods, Union Square $SQ, Chinatown, NoHo, Little Italy and NoLita among them, post individual scores between 99 and 100 on the same scale. Round-the-clock subway service across more than 470 stations backs up the walking network for longer trips or bad weather, while continued expansion of the Open Streets program and pedestrian plazas across the five boroughs keeps adding car-free space year over year. New York's biggest recent shift arrived from an unexpected direction, tolls. Congestion pricing launched on January 5, 2025, charging most vehicles to enter Manhattan below 60th Street, and one year in, the program had kept 27 million vehicles out of that zone, an 11% drop in traffic. Cornell researchers later found particulate pollution inside the tolled zone had fallen 22% over the program's first six months, with cleaner air showing up across the wider region as well. The toll revenue, more than $550 million in year one, is now funding transit upgrades including new subway signals and accessibility improvements at stations that previously had none. Beyond Manhattan, Brooklyn's Park Slope and Queens' Astoria extend the same walkable density into the outer boroughs, giving residents there a genuine alternative to driving into the city rather than out of it. Brooklyn Heights' quiet, leafy blocks and the gallery-lined stretches of Chelsea round out a city where almost nothing worth reaching sits more than a few blocks from the nearest door. Chelsea's High Line, a defunct elevated freight rail line converted into a 1.45-mile park that opened in stages starting in 2009, remains one of the clearest examples anywhere of turning abandoned infrastructure into car-free public space, drawing millions of walkers a year along a route that once carried nothing but freight trains above the meatpacking district. Boston, Massachusetts Sean Sweeney / Unsplash Boston's compact core predates the automobile entirely, and that accident of timing is most of the reason the city still ranks near the top of America's walkability list today, with a Walk Score of 82.8. Narrow, winding streets laid out centuries before cars existed naturally favor pedestrians over vehicles, and the entire downtown can be crossed on foot in under an hour. The nation's oldest subway line, known locally as the T, backs up that street design, while Beacon Hill and the Chinatown-Leather District both carry near-perfect scores of 99 on the same scale. History is also the city's biggest tourist draw on foot. The 2.5-mile Freedom Trail links 16 historic sites from the Boston Common to Bunker Hill, tracing the city's Revolutionary War history in a single continuous walk. Much of that walk now passes above what used to be an elevated highway. The Big Dig, completed in 2007, buried Boston's Central Artery underground and replaced it at street level with the Rose Kennedy Greenway, a chain of parks that reconnected downtown neighborhoods that had been cut off from each other by traffic for decades. Beacon Hill's gas-lit streets and the North End's Italian bakeries sit within walking distance of the Greenway on one side, while Back Bay's brownstone-lined blocks and the South End's Victorian rowhouses extend the same walkable pattern further west. Fenway-Kenmore adds a college-town energy to the mix on game days, when thousands of fans walk to Fenway Park rather than searching for parking near one of the oldest ballparks in the country. Boston's subway, opened in 1897, still runs through some of its original tunnels beneath the Common, making it the oldest underground rapid transit system in North America and a foundational reason the city never had to build its downtown around cars in the first place. The Emerald Necklace, a chain of parks designed by Frederick Law Olmsted in the late 19th century, threads through several of these same neighborhoods, giving walkers a green, mostly car-free route between downtown and the surrounding residential districts. Chicago, Illinois Christopher Alvarenga / Unsplash Grid streets, an elevated train and a nearly 20-mile lakefront trail add up to a Walk Score of 77.2 for Chicago, good for fourth place nationally. The city's predictable street layout puts commercial corridors within walking distance of most residents, and its 500-plus parks and world-class museums cluster densely enough in the most walkable districts that an entire day can pass without a car ever entering the picture. The Lakefront Trail itself stretches roughly 18.5 miles along the Lake Michigan shoreline, connecting pedestrian bridges, beaches and skyline views into one long, mostly car-free spine through the city. Away from the lake, Chicago has spent the past decade turning old infrastructure into new walking space. The 606, a 2.7-mile elevated park and trail built on a former freight rail viaduct, opened in 2015 and now links the Bucktown, Wicker Park and Humboldt Park neighborhoods on a car-free path suspended above street level. The elevated L train ties these pedestrian-friendly pockets together across the wider city, and neighborhoods like the West Loop and East Ukrainian Village have kept adding density and foot traffic without losing the walkable scale that defines them. Downtown, the Loop and Near North Side pack museums, theaters and lakefront access into a grid tight enough that entire workdays pass without anyone needing a car, while Lincoln Park and Lakeview extend that same density north along the water into some of the city's most sought-after residential blocks. Millennium Park, home to the reflective Cloud Gate sculpture locals call the Bean, sits directly on the Lakefront Trail and functions as a free, car-free gathering space linking the Loop's office towers to the lake itself. The city's Divvy bike-share network fills in the gaps between L stops for trips just a bit too long to comfortably walk. Chicago's grid itself dates back to the city's post-fire rebuilding in the 1870s, when planners laid out wide, numbered streets running in a strict north-south and east-west pattern that still makes wayfinding almost effortless a century and a half later, even for a first-time visitor without a map. Washington, D.C. Andy He / Unsplash Pierre L'Enfant never designed Washington with a Walk Score in mind, but his diagonal avenues and small park-lined intersections gave the capital a head start most American cities never had, and the district posts a score of 76.7 today. Height restrictions on buildings, in place since the early 20th century, keep the skyline low and human-scaled in a way that's rare among major U.S. cities, and that low profile means street-level storefronts and windows stay in constant view rather than disappearing beneath towers. The Metro system supports genuinely car-free living for a large share of residents, and the Capital Bikeshare program fills in the gaps between subway stops. The National Mall itself functions as miles of pedestrian-priority space linking the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial, and every spring the Tidal Basin at its edge draws crowds on foot for the National Cherry Blossom Festival, held in celebration of the roughly 3,000 trees Japan gifted the city in 1912. Away from the monuments, neighborhoods like Dupont Circle and the U Street Corridor carry their own dense, walkable commercial life, while Navy Yard and the Capitol Riverfront have emerged as newer pedestrian districts built almost entirely from scratch over the past two decades. Georgetown's cobblestone streets and waterfront path draw a different, more historic version of the same walkable pattern, while Adams Morgan and Mount Vernon Square $SQ round out a capital where a walk from a rowhouse to a restaurant rarely takes more than ten minutes. Capitol Hill, home to some of the district's oldest residential blocks, still functions as a genuinely walkable neighborhood in its own right rather than just a backdrop for the buildings that share its name. The Smithsonian museums lining the Mall charge no admission at all, which turns an ordinary afternoon walk into a free tour through some of the country's best collections of art, history and science without ever requiring a car to reach a single one of them. Miami, Florida aurora.kreativ / Unsplash Only a tenth of a point separates Miami from Washington on this ranking, and the city has closed that gap by transforming itself from a car-centric metro into one with genuinely walkable districts within the past five years, arriving at a Walk Score of 76.6. Downtown, Wynwood-Edgewater and Little Havana now anchor the city's strongest pedestrian neighborhoods, while Miami Beach carries the walkability torch for the region on the strength of its Art Deco Historic District, one of the largest concentrated collections of Art Deco architecture anywhere in the world, and its long beachfront promenade. Brickell and Wynwood, both once car-dependent commercial strips on the mainland, have shifted into dense, mixed-use districts where walking has become the default rather than the exception, and the free Metromover circulator ties downtown's walkable core together for anyone who needs to cover more ground than their feet alone allow. Miami's tropical climate cuts both ways for pedestrians. Mild winters make the city one of the country's best warm-weather walking destinations, even as rising sea levels and increasingly frequent street flooding push city planners toward raised roadways and new stormwater pumps to keep those same sidewalks usable. Coconut Grove gives walkers a leafier, lower-density version of the same formula, with tree-canopied streets built around a village-like commercial strip rather than a high-rise skyline. South Beach still draws the largest crowds on foot, where the pastel Art Deco hotels lining Ocean Drive turn a simple beachfront stroll into one of the most photographed walks in the country. Hundreds of those buildings, most dating to the 1920s and 1930s, remain protected within the historic district today, giving South Beach a visual consistency that few other American beach towns can match. Little Havana's Calle Ocho carries a different kind of pedestrian energy entirely, its sidewalks lined with domino parlors, cafecito windows and murals that make an unhurried walk down a single street feel like a genuine cultural destination rather than just a route between two points. Oakland, California Cedric Letsch / Unsplash Oakland spent years living in San Francisco's shadow across the bay, and its arrival in the top 10 for 2026, with a Walk Score of 75.3, is one of this year's more notable shifts. The city's compact downtown, along with the Koreatown-Northgate, Fruitvale Station and Laney College areas, all score well for pedestrian accessibility, and colorful street murals throughout Oakland's walkable districts give those same streets a distinct visual identity beyond the everyday mix of shops and cafes. Much of Oakland's walkability traces back to transit-oriented development around its BART stations, which have anchored the East Bay's rail network since the system opened in 1972. Fruitvale Village, built around the Fruitvale BART stop, became a nationally cited model for pairing a transit station with dense housing, a health clinic and neighborhood retail all within walking distance of the platform. Along the waterfront, Jack London Square $SQ lets visitors move from restaurant to shop to bar without ever leaving the water's edge, and BART itself provides the connective tissue linking Oakland's walkable pockets to the rest of the Bay Area. Temescal has emerged as a genuine dining destination in its own right, its short commercial strip packed tightly enough with restaurants and bars that a single walkable block can anchor an entire evening out. The Koreatown-Northgate district, still widely known by its KONO acronym, has followed a similar path from underused commercial corridor to one of the city's more walkable arts and dining pockets. Lake Merritt, a tidal lagoon ringed by a 3.4-mile paved path in the heart of downtown, gives Oakland something few American cities have this close to their center. It's a genuine loop walk with water on one side and the skyline on the other, connecting several of the city's most walkable neighborhoods without a single car ever needing to be involved. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Prasad Panchakshari / Unsplash America turns 250 this year, and few cities have as much riding on that anniversary as Philadelphia, which ranks eighth nationally with a Walk Score of 74.8. William Penn laid out Philadelphia's street grid in the 17th century, making it one of the earliest planned cities anywhere in the country, and that same grid still delivers dividends for pedestrians in Center City today. Rittenhouse Square $SQ, Center City West and Washington Square West form the city's most walkable core, packing an unusually dense concentration of historic sites, restaurants and cultural institutions into an area most visitors can cross without needing transit at all. Philadelphia became the first American city named a UNESCO World Heritage City back in 2015. The distinction is tied to Independence Hall and the historic district surrounding it, and the city is leaning hard into that history throughout 2026's Semiquincentennial celebrations marking 250 years since the Declaration of Independence was signed there. Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell sit close enough together that the walk between them takes barely two minutes, and this year that short stroll sits at the center of citywide programming that includes the Wawa Welcome America festival, a World Cup match and a full slate of exhibitions tracing the Declaration's global influence. More than 10,000 acres of public parkland and the growing Circuit Trails network round out the walking options beyond the historic core. Old City carries much of that same historic weight within an easily walkable radius, while Fishtown has become the city's newer draw, its converted rowhouses and warehouse blocks now packed with restaurants and bars that draw crowds on foot well into the evening. Avenue of the Arts South rounds out the core with a concentration of theaters and concert halls within easy reach of Center City's hotels. Reading Terminal Market, tucked inside a converted 19th-century train shed a few blocks from Rittenhouse Square, remains one of the city's most walkable food destinations in its own right, packing dozens of vendors under one roof within a few minutes' walk of nearly every hotel in Center City. Seattle, Washington Bruce W / Unsplash Seattle spent 15 years and roughly $800 million tearing down a highway to get here, and the payoff, a new waterfront park connecting downtown to Puget Sound, only fully opened in September 2025. Before that, an elevated freeway called the Alaskan Way Viaduct cut the city off from its own shoreline for decades. Its removal, paired with a new tunnel routing that traffic underground, freed up 20 acres for what's now Waterfront Park, a garden-lined promenade, bike path and habitat beach stretching across 26 blocks from Pioneer Square $SQ to Belltown. A pedestrian bridge called the Overlook Walk now links Pike Place Market directly down to the water and the Seattle Aquarium. That single project helped push Seattle's Walk Score to 74.4 for 2026, and the city's older walkable neighborhoods, the International District, Belltown and First Hill among them, continue to rank highest within Seattle's own boundaries. Further out, the growing Link light rail network keeps adding walkable transit nodes to the city, while neighborhood centers like Capitol Hill, Fremont and the University District each function as largely self-contained pedestrian environments with their own restaurants, shops and services. Columbia City, a few stops south on the light rail line, has quietly become one of the city's more walkable pockets in its own right, its historic main street lined with restaurants representing the neighborhood's long history as one of Seattle's most diverse communities. Pike Place Market, founded in 1907 and among the oldest continuously operating public markets in the country, sits directly above the new waterfront park and remains the anchor that ties the whole redeveloped shoreline together for anyone arriving on foot from downtown. Before the viaduct came down, the market's famous vendors sold fish and produce within earshot of a freeway carrying roughly 100,000 cars a day just below street level. Now that same walk continues uninterrupted down to the water, past the Seattle Aquarium and out onto the piers, in what city planners have called the most significant change to Seattle's downtown geography in a century. Long Beach, California Sandro Giacon / Unsplash Long Beach closes out the top 10 with a Walk Score of 73.3, the only entry on this list built as much around a beach as a downtown grid. Belmont Shore, Central Long Beach and Belmont Heights lead the city's walkable neighborhoods, and downtown's wide sidewalks and dedicated pedestrian zones support a genuine mixed-use core rather than a purely tourist-facing waterfront. A local bike share program and a recent round of completed urban trails have added to the city's pedestrian infrastructure without displacing its beach-town character. The city's signature landmark has had its own long road back to full public access. The retired ocean liner Queen Mary, permanently docked in Long Beach since 1967, spent years closed to visitors during the pandemic while the city carried out extensive structural repairs, and by early 2026 the ship had reopened fully as an operational hotel again after that lengthy hiatus. Nearby, the marine exhibits at the Aquarium of the Pacific and the bars lining Pine Avenue round out a downtown core built almost entirely for walking rather than driving. East Village Arts District has grown into the neighborhood's creative anchor, its converted warehouses now home to galleries and studios within a few blocks of downtown's restaurants. Alamitos Beach connects that core directly to the sand, giving residents a walkable stretch that runs from bars and coffee shops straight onto the boardwalk without a single stretch of parking lot in between. Belmont Shore's Second Street carries much of that same beach-town walkability a few miles down the coast, its boutiques and restaurants packed tightly enough along a single strip that visitors rarely need to move their car all afternoon. A citywide bike-share network fills in the remaining gaps between these walkable pockets, letting residents cover the longer stretches between Belmont Shore and downtown without ever needing to drive.

item.title: OpenAI signed a deal for computing power from Nvidia-backed Firmus's new Malaysia data centers
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.38
OpenAI and Firmus announced a multi-year partnership on Tuesday under which OpenAI will receive dedicated AI computing capacity from two Firmus data center sites in Malaysia, the Australian infrastructure company said. The agreement makes OpenAI an anchor customer of Firmus and brings total contracted capacity across the Australian firm to more than 900 MW The deal makes OpenAI an anchor customer of Firmus and brings the company's total contracted capacity across all customers to more than 900 megawatts, the company said. The partnership also marks Firmus' expansion into Malaysia, extending its Asia-Pacific footprint beyond Australia, Singapore, and Indonesia. Firmus will deploy Nvidia $NVDA's Vera Rubin processors at the Malaysian sites, using Nvidia's DSX AI Factory Platform integrated with Firmus' own HyperCube infrastructure system. The HyperCube combines liquid cooling, mechanical systems, and electrification into a prefabricated unit manufactured in regional New South Wales, the company said. "We're excited to work with Firmus as we expand our global compute capacity. These new data centers in Malaysia will help us serve growing demand for OpenAI's products across the region and around the world," said Sachin Katti, VP of Compute Strategy at OpenAI, in a statement. Firmus currently has two AI data centers in operation — located in Australia and Singapore — and is actively developing five more across the Asia-Pacific region, the company said. The firm said its full portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries and that the five sites under development are targeted to be ready for service within the next 24 months. Nvidia is among Firmus' financial backers, with Jane Street, Blackstone funds, and Coatue Management also holding stakes in the company, according to Reuters. The firm's most recent fundraising round put its valuation at more than $10.5 billion, Reuters reported. The deal is part of a broader push by AI companies to lock in computing infrastructure. OpenAI's agreement with Firmus follows a pattern of large AI labs securing dedicated capacity from Nvidia-backed infrastructure providers. Anthropic, for instance, has signed agreements with Nvidia-backed infrastructure startups including Volta Infra Holdings, and has pursued a series of large computing arrangements as demand for its products has grown. Alongside its OpenAI partnership, Firmus said it intends to establish an Australian AI Access Program to provide computing access to researchers and organizations working on applications in science, education, agriculture, energy efficiency, and climate resilience. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: OpenAI's chief scientist warned AI labs aren't ready to keep scaling safely
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.03
OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that no AI lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a degree that justifies continuing to scale at maximum speed, and said he expects voluntary slowdowns to become common across the industry until shared safety standards are established.

item.title: Jensen Huang declared "AGI has arrived" after OpenAI launched its new model
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.49
Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang declared that artificial general intelligence has arrived following OpenAI's release of its latest AI model, Astra, drawing pushback from researchers who said the claim lacked evidence and a clear definition. "From ChatGPT to o1 to Astra in 4 years," Huang posted on X $TWTR on Sunday. "AGI has arrived. Congratulations @OpenAI team." He also noted that Astra was trained on Nvidia's chips and said "400K GPUs coming online next." OpenAI unveiled Astra last week, billing it as the world's "most intelligent and aligned model" and positioning it as a tool for complex, high-stakes professional tasks. The company said it is rolling out to customers this week. During a call with reporters following the launch, OpenAI president Greg Brockman told journalists: "Welcome to the AGI era." Brockman added that he believes future observers will look back and identify AGI as having been created "about this time, and I think it might be about this model," according to Business Insider. AGI — artificial general intelligence — has no single agreed-upon definition. OpenAI characterizes it as "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work," while Google $GOOGL's definition centers on a machine's capacity to understand or learn any intellectual task a human being can perform, according to Pymnts. Not everyone welcomed Huang's declaration. AI researcher Gary Marcus, writing on his Substack, said Huang had offered neither evidence nor definitions, describing the declaration as "an effort at a takeover of a scientific question by corporate fiat." Marcus applied his own ten-point definition of AGI and concluded that Astra meets only one or two of those benchmarks. "By conventional definitions, Astra still falls short," he wrote, according to Business Insider. The team behind the ARC Prize benchmark, which OpenAI pointed to in its Astra announcement, similarly declined to label the model AGI. While acknowledging Astra's results as a meaningful leap forward, they cautioned that clearing the benchmark's bar was not sufficient evidence of AGI, given that its evaluations unfold in constrained settings far narrower than the open-ended messiness of the real world. It is not the first time Huang has made such a claim. Back in March, Huang told Lex Fridman's podcast that "I think we've achieved AGI," only to soften that position before the conversation ended, according to Pymnts. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has described AGI as "a very poorly defined term." The Astra launch comes as Nvidia's business has expanded alongside surging demand for AI chips. Nvidia's most recent quarterly earnings, reported in August, came in at $96.2 billion — more than double its haul from the same period a year prior — with the data center division, home to its AI chips, accounting for $89 billion of that figure. OpenAI called Nvidia "the foundation of our infrastructure" in a funding announcement earlier this year. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: The best places in the world to plan a trip entirely around coffee
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.47
The best places in the world to plan a trip entirely around coffee Colombia's UNESCO-listed Coffee Triangle, Ethiopia's birthplace-of-coffee farm treks, Panama's rare Geisha beans — the destinations where coffee isn't a stop on the itinerary, it's the whole reason for the trip A quarter of young travelers now consider a destination's coffee scene a major factor in whether they visit at all, according to GetYourGuide's Hidden Trends List, part of a broader shift in which travelers increasingly want to explore the origins and traditions behind a cup rather than simply drinking one somewhere new. This list splits between two distinct versions of coffee travel, origin countries where the bean is actually grown and harvested, and coffee culture cities built around café life and roasting rather than cultivation, since the two experiences offer genuinely different reasons to plan a trip around coffee specifically. Colombia's Coffee Triangle Qingqing Cai / Unsplash Colombia's Eje Cafetero, known internationally as the Coffee Triangle, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site anchored by the towns of Manizales, Armenia, and Pereira, giving visitors direct access to working arabica farms alongside a broader coffee-growing landscape significant enough to have earned this specific international cultural recognition. Farm stays throughout the region allow visitors to actually pick coffee cherries, observe the full processing sequence, and end with tastings of some of the world's most recognized coffee, and a specific "be a farmer for a day" tour from Bogotá gives visitors a hands-on, immersive version of the harvest and processing work rather than a passive walkthrough. Colombia's specific advantage within origin-country coffee tourism is this combination of UNESCO-level cultural significance with genuinely accessible, well-developed tourism infrastructure built specifically around coffee, making it one of the most complete single destinations for travelers wanting the full farm-to-cup experience in one region. Ethiopia's coffee birthplace Zeynep S. / Unsplash Ethiopia holds a specific distinction no other destination on this list can claim: it's widely recognized as the birthplace of coffee itself, giving a visit here a genuine origin-story significance beyond simply touring another coffee-growing region among many. Multi-day treks through Ethiopia's historical coffee routes allow visitors to trace this origin directly, visiting traditional farms and learning the plant's cultivation history in a setting current coffee tourism guides specifically distinguish from the more streamlined, tourist-ready farm tours available in Latin America. Ethiopia's coffee tourism industry remains considerably less developed than Colombia's or Costa Rica's, a specific tradeoff that gives visitors a more raw, unpolished experience of coffee's actual origins at the cost of the more comfortable, established infrastructure that more heavily visited coffee destinations elsewhere on this list provide. Costa Rica's sustainable coffee highlands Vlad D / Unsplash Costa Rica has built its coffee tourism identity specifically around sustainable farming practices, with the coffee-growing highlands of Monteverde, Tarrazú, and the Central Valley offering eco-friendly plantation tours that walk visitors through shade-grown cultivation methods rather than the more intensive, sun-grown methods common elsewhere. Tours here consistently end with tastings overlooking the region's dramatic mountain and forest scenery, giving Costa Rica a specific reputation current coffee tourism guides describe as the perfect balance of environmental stewardship and coffee excellence, distinguishing the destination through its sustainability credentials as much as the coffee itself. Costa Rica's specific appeal for environmentally conscious travelers gives it a distinct identity within origin-country coffee tourism, positioning sustainable and shade-grown practices as the destination's core draw rather than simply an incidental detail of how the coffee happens to be produced there. Panama's Geisha coffee highlands jaime fuentes / Unsplash Panama's Boquete and Volcán regions produce some of the most sought-after and expensive coffee in the world, with farms including Ninety Plus, Altieri, and the Lamastus Family Estates specifically known for cultivating Geisha, a coffee variety that commands prices considerably above standard arabica varieties in specialty coffee markets globally. Visitors can travel easily between farms by rental car, and small, hands-on tours in Boquete specifically give coffee enthusiasts direct access to this premium variety at its source, a level of proximity to genuinely rare, high-value coffee that few other destinations on this list can offer in the same concentrated area. Panama's specific value within coffee tourism is this access to Geisha coffee specifically, making it the clear destination of choice for serious specialty coffee enthusiasts who want direct exposure to one of the most prestigious and expensive coffee varieties in the world rather than a general introduction to coffee cultivation. Kona, Hawaii Nico Smit / Unsplash Kona, on Hawaii's Big Island, offers American travelers a domestic coffee tourism option built around the region's specific volcanic soil and climate conditions, factors current guides credit directly with producing Kona coffee's distinctive character and international reputation. The region concentrates a dozen or more farm tours around Holualoa near Kailua-Kona and around Captain Cook, ranging from free, no-reservation walks at farms like Greenwell to more involved paid tastings, giving visitors genuine flexibility to fit two or three different farm experiences into a single day given how closely the farms sit together. Kona's specific advantage for American travelers is eliminating the international travel that every other origin-country destination on this list requires, pairing genuine coffee farm tourism with Hawaii's broader appeal and infrastructure, a domestic option current guides specifically recommend starting early in the day given how reliably afternoon clouds and rain build up on the volcanic slopes. Melbourne's café culture Jordan Ryskamp / Unsplash Melbourne represents the coffee culture city side of this list directly, internationally recognized for its specialty coffee and distinctive café culture built around independent roasters and baristas rather than coffee cultivation, since Australia grows essentially none of the coffee its café scene has become famous for. Walking tours through Melbourne's laneways give visitors access to the city's most iconic roasters and cafés, and current coffee tourism guides specifically highlight the city's flat whites as a benchmark experience, reflecting Melbourne's specific role in shaping and popularizing this particular espresso-based drink internationally. Melbourne's specific appeal within this broader list is representing an entirely different model of coffee travel, urban café culture and craft rather than farm-to-cup origin tourism, giving travelers without the time or interest in visiting an actual growing region a genuine, deeply developed coffee experience within a single, walkable city. Guatemala's underrated coffee circuit Manuel González Asturias, SJ / Unsplash Guatemala remains what current coffee tourism guides specifically call criminally underrated relative to its actual coffee quality, with the country's volcanic soil producing beans carrying a distinctive chocolate and spice flavor profile that has begun earning the country genuine recognition as a top coffee destination within Central America. The lakeside communities surrounding Lake Atitlán offer coffee tours paired with dramatic volcano and lake views, with lodging options including Hotel Toliman and Porta Hotel Del Lago giving visitors comfortable, well-located bases for exploring the surrounding coffee-growing communities without requiring the more extensive infrastructure Colombia or Costa Rica has already built. Guatemala's specific appeal is this combination of genuinely distinctive coffee flavor and comparatively lower visitor volume than the more established destinations elsewhere on this list, giving travelers specifically seeking an origin-country coffee experience without the crowds that Colombia's UNESCO recognition or Costa Rica's sustainability reputation increasingly attract.

item.title: Perry Mason's creator was a Baja nut
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.35
Perry Mason's creator was a Baja nut His Mexican pilot tells the back stories
Gardner and Muñoz. The two men decided to fly along the coast, about 180 miles south of Ensenada, to see if the rugged beaches could yield access to custom-designed trailers and dune bikes.
In early 1960, the man who created Perry Mason was introduced to an Imperial Beach resident named Francisco Muñoz. Erle Stanley Gardner had many friends, and he particularly liked Mexicans, but the friendship that developed between him and Muñoz appears to have ranked among the most cherished of both men. By 1962 Muñoz had become a main character in Gardner’s travel books and his abettor in adventures like this one, recounted by Gardner in The Hidden Heart of Baja. Erle Stanely Gardner on a Baja trip in the 1960s. “It was great fun flying at a height of 10 or 15 feet over the sand." Gardner had hired Muñoz, introduced to the book’s readers as a “quick-thinking, quick-talking aviator, who has been flying long enough to have developed an uncanny skill as well as an encyclopedic knowledge of the country over which he is flying.” The two men had decided to fly along the Pacific Coast, about 180 miles south of Ensenada, to see if the rugged beaches could yield access to custom-designed trailers and dune bikes in which the septuagenarian Gardner hankered to go exploring. “It was great fun flying at a height of 10 or 15 feet over the sand, with the plane throttled down so that we had just sufficient air speed to give the pilot good control,” Gardner recorded. Muñoz chats with passengers at Bahía de los Angeles. Muñoz moved his family to Imperial Beach in 1955 and began flying over Baja. For “mile after mile,” they traveled in this intimate proximity to the beach, with Muñoz touching down whenever it struck his and the writer’s fancy. They studied coyotes, including one “just preparing to feast on a dead baby whale which had been cast up.” They stopped at fishing camps to gossip with the Mexicans gathering lobster and catching totoaba. Later, realizing they were hungry, and seeing a clam camp, Muñoz “made a quick circle into the wind, came down on the sandy beach, landed, and taxied up to the place where the clam diggers were bringing in the huge clams.” ^^^^^^^^^^^ The Reader has started this series of its best stories from the past 52 years — 2600 cover stories and some remarkable interior features — to help make up for the loss of its physical edition, which was once large enough to hold whole oceans of print. These stories will feature all the original illustrations and photos (plus easy-to-read typography). ^^^^^^^^^^^ Receiving abrazos, Muñoz made his and Gardner’s hunger known, and “in no time at all a young lad was forthcoming with lemons and a large soup plate,” Gardner wrote. “One of the clam diggers, at a signal, brought up a sackful...and Muñoz and I stood by while the clam digger cut open the shells with swift skill and stripped out the meat....” The two men gorged themselves, then realized that the afternoon was waning. “It would be touch-and-go to reach Tijuana before dark.” Although Muñoz was unfazed, Gardner felt worried by the deepening gloom, and his alarm increased when it became obvious that the two were flying into a storm. Muñoz today lives part-time at Crest, east of El Cajon, where a second home overlooks rocky vistas. “[W]e were being borne along by a tail wind which increased until it was blowing at 75 miles an hour,” Gardner later wrote. “Below us the ocean was a churned mass of angry waters, and above us the clouds kept pressing down until we were forced to fly just over the tops of the waves.” Squinting through the torrential rains, Gardner shouted that Muñoz should land in Ensenada, but the storm swept them past the town. La Paz airport, 1950s. In 1964 Gardner had been invited to view some new cave paintings and fish-fossil beds near Santiago, so Muñoz flew him to La Paz. At times “gusts of wind would catch the plane and seem to lift the tail so that it took skillful handling to keep us from being blown over end to end.... We were now flying two or three hundred yards offshore, so low that headlights from the automobiles coming along the highway between Tijuana and Ensenada would dazzle me — darkness above and below, but over on the right there was a faint murky line of surf; a surf which was hitting the shore with terrific fury and sending great clouds of spray high into the air.” Finally Muñoz wrestled the plane down to a landing strip in Rosarito Beach, and the two men made their way, dripping, to the Rosarito Beach Hotel. Muñoz and Gardner stopped at fishing camps to gossip with the Mexicans gathering lobster and catching totoaba. Still the adventure hadn’t quite ended. As Muñoz called for a car to drive up from Tijuana, Gardner insisted on ordering stiff drinks and taking a room in which the two could await the ride north in comfort. “Muñoz insisted that as a customer I was entitled to the first shower, and after wasting some time in argument I stepped out of my wet clothes, leaving them in a soggy mess on the floor....” The mystery writer then entered the shower and turned on the wrong faucet, producing an icy blast. Twisting the alternate faucet, however, caused flakes of rust to jam the shower head; after a moment, only a few drops of warm water trickled out. Muñoz heard Gardner’s curses and came forward to help — not realizing that Gardner had already opened the faucet. “Suddenly he had the shower head off, and water...steaming hot, struck me full in the chest. I ducked, Muñoz jumped. We collided with each other and then the stream of water was pouring over both of us!” Francisco Muñoz and his Baja Airlines planes, c. 1950s. By 1962 Muñoz had become a main character in Gardner’s travel books. Today Francisco Muñoz roars with laughter at the memory. “He was in the nude, and I was dressed. And we both tried to get out at the same time!” Gardner died about 8 years after this incident, in 1970. But Muñoz, now 76, is still an active man with detailed memories of his life. He and his wife, Leysl, spend part of their time at a beach-front mobile home in the community of Bahía de los Angeles, about 100 miles south of San Felipe on the Sea of Cortéz. But every month or two, they drive to Crest, east of El Cajon, where a second home overlooks rocky vistas. “See this?” says Muñoz. He is standing in a jumbled storage area next to his Crest home, hefting a chalky white chunk of material. It’s part of a whale skull, including the ear bone, scavenged from Malarrimo Beach, near Guerrero Negro, on Baja’s Pacific Coast. Close at hand, other cardboard boxes, all labeled, are packed with more whale ear bones. Some of the pieces of Muñoz’s flotsam collection are unique. He shows off a wooden tool that looks like an archaeological artifact. Once, some shrimper used it to scrape his catch from the floor of his boat into an icebox. Along one side of his house, Muñoz has built shelves to hold his hundreds of bottles, once-hard-edged and glittering glass made subtle and milky by the work of seawater and sand and sun. Inside the house, the ceiling has been hung with huge glass balls that held up far-flung Pacific fishing nets and, over time, washed up on the shores of Baja, sea green, and turquoise, pale rose. Muñoz has a buoyancy that surges up through his stories, as when he recalls his first sight of an airplane. “My father subscribed to a magazine in Mexico City called Jueves de Excelsior. And they showed pictures of the Mexican air force. ‘Oh, God!’ ” he gasps, summoning a boy’s voice filled with longing. “ ‘I want to be a flyer!’ ” He was around eight years old. Raised on his grandparents’ ranch in Coahuila, Muñoz remembers going into the pecan orchard. “You had to climb the tree with a pole and you hit the branches, and then somebody picked up the nuts from beneath the tree.” Swinging on the branches, watching the flight of the birds, he says, enhanced his yearning to take to the air. But his parents were appalled by his ambitions. “First they send me to the seminary,” recounts Muñoz, whose still-accented English reflects a casual attitude toward grammatical tense. “They want me to be a priest. But the bishop kicked me out because I was asking too many questions. He told me that I came to the seminary to learn, not to ask questions.” The thought of this still provokes a chuckle. “I only stayed a semester, and then I went to high school in Monterrey, Mexico.” When he finished high school, Muñoz began a course of studies intended to transform him into a doctor. But he learned that flying lessons were available at the Monterrey airport. “I wrote my grandparents for permission to learn to fly and to support me financially,” Muñoz says. “The answer was no. ‘Your mother doesn’t want you to be a pilot. It’s very dangerous.’ ” So he resolved to earn the money. Muñoz dropped out of school and went to work as a butcher, a skill he’d acquired on the ranch. Flight instruction cost 20 pesos an hour. “That was a lot of money,” he says. But after a year he had saved 320 pesos. By then the training plane in Monterrey had crashed, but Muñoz found another small flight school in the city of Chihuahua. “It took me something like eight hours [of instruction] to fly solo,” he says today. “A very short time.” The date of that first time in the air, alone in the cockpit of an antiquated Curtiss Junior pusher was February 7,1937. He was two months short of his 18th birthday. Because he was well educated, he was asked to conduct the aviation ground school in exchange for more time in the air. He also made money by giving plane rides to townspeople willing to pay five pesos for the thrill. Within two years, Muñoz had acquired more than 200 hours, enough to apply for a commercial pilot’s license. He was granted number 237 — the 237th commercial pilot to be licensed in Mexico.
